docs.title: Preface
docs.text:
This is Volume 22 of the series Bhāratīya Jñāna Paramparā: Manas and Śikṣā: Psychology and Education. It brings together two subjects that the Indian sources often treat together: the analysis of the mind — consciousness, perception, memory, emotion, attention, dreams and sleep — in the Upaniṣads, Sāṃkhya and Yoga, Nyāya, the Jain and Buddhist traditions, Vedānta, the medical texts, the theory of rasa, the Sufi masters and the Sikh Gurus; and the history of teaching and learning in India, from the Vedic teacher’s household and the oral transmission of the Veda to the Buddhist monasteries, the Brahmanical and Jain colleges and libraries, the madrasas, the village schools, the first schools for girls and the colonial and modern periods.

Dates are given as the range accepted in current scholarship, with traditional dates labelled as such. The Indian accounts of the mind are presented in their own terms, not as “anticipations” or “proofs” of modern neuroscience and psychology; where modern research on practices such as meditation and yoga is discussed, its results are reported with their limitations and with attention to possible harms. Popular myths about Indian education — Takṣaśilā as “the world’s first university”, the “nine million manuscripts” of Nālandā — are corrected. The volume also tries to give an honest account of who was excluded from learning, and of the women, Buddhist, Jain, Islamic and anti-caste traditions that are often left out of celebratory histories.

The book has no formal parts. Chapters 2 to 8 treat the mind, including a section on the Tamil accounts of inner life and one on what the classical theories said about women’s minds; Chapters 9 to 12 follow the history of learning from the Vedic teacher’s household and the oral tradition to the monasteries, colleges, madrasas and village schools and the manuscript tradition; and Chapter 13 carries the story through the colonial period to modern psychology and education.

References to standard editions, translations and studies are given in the text and collected in the select bibliography; a glossary, a chronology, a list of the editions of the principal texts and an index of quoted passages are provided at the end. No survey of this size can be exhaustive, and this one is weighted towards the classical Sanskrit and Pali sources. Readers should treat it as an introduction, turn to the works cited for the texts themselves, and check every quotation against a critical edition before scholarly use.

Nikhil Kumar Rajput Ramanujan College, University of Delhi Guru Pūrṇimā, 2026

docs.title: Chapter 1: Introduction: Mind and Learning in the Indian Traditions
docs.text: tat karma yan na bandhāya sā vidyā yā vimuktaye | āyāsāyāparaṃ karma vidyānyā śilpanaipuṇam || That is action which does not bind; that is knowledge which leads to liberation. Other action is mere toil; other knowledge is mere skill in a craft. — Viṣṇu Purāṇa 1.19.41

docs.title: 1.1 Two Subjects, One Inquiry
docs.text:
This volume brings together two subjects that modern universities usually keep in separate faculties: the study of the mind and the history of education. In the Sanskrit, Pali and Prakrit sources, and in the institutions that transmitted them, the two were closely linked. The texts that analyse the mind — the Upaniṣads, the Sāṃkhyakārikā, the Yogasūtra, the Buddhist Abhidharma, the medical saṃhitās — were themselves objects of a demanding training, memorised, recited, debated and commented upon. And the purpose of much of that training was understood in psychological terms: to steady attention, to correct mistaken cognition, to weaken habitual craving and aversion, and, in the soteriological traditions, to bring about liberation (mokṣa, nirvāṇa, kaivalya).

The epigraph above, from the Viṣṇu Purāṇa, states the ideal in its strongest form: real knowledge (vidyā) is that which frees; every other kind of learning is merely a skill. The line is often quoted as a motto of Indian education, and it does express an important strand of the tradition. It should not, however, be taken as a description of what most Indian education actually was. Most learning in pre-modern India was practical and hereditary — the training of scribes, accountants, physicians, artisans, musicians, merchants and farmers — and most of it was not written down. The learned traditions that survive in texts were cultivated by small groups, and access to the most prestigious of them was restricted by birth and gender. A history of Indian education must hold both facts in view: the remarkable intellectual achievement of the textual traditions, and the social exclusions that surrounded them.

The book has no formal part divisions, but its chapters fall into two groups and a coda. Chapters 2–8 examine Indian accounts of the mind. Chapters 9–12 follow the history of teaching and learning from the Vedic teacher’s household to the eve of colonial rule. Chapter 13 carries that history through the colonial period to the present, and considers how the traditions of mind have been taken up in modern psychology, medicine and education, and with what evidence (Section 1.8).

docs.title: 1.2 What Counts as “Indian Psychology”?
docs.text:
The phrase “Indian psychology” has been used in two different ways. In one usage, associated with the Handbook of Indian Psychology edited by Rao et al. (2008), it names a contemporary project: the attempt to build a psychology, for use today, out of concepts drawn from Yoga, Vedānta, Buddhism and other Indian traditions. In another usage, which this volume follows, it names a historical subject: what the Indian texts themselves say about perception, memory, emotion, attention, sleep, dreams, the self and the training of the mind. That is the sense of the older surveys, C. A. F. Rhys Davids’s Buddhist Psychology (Rhys Davids 1914) and Jadunath Sinha’s multi-volume Indian Psychology, whose first volume appeared in 1934 (Sinha 1934).

The distinction matters. The texts did not set out to do psychology in the modern sense. The Sāṃkhya analysis of the mind serves an argument about the difference between consciousness and matter; the Abhidharma lists of mental factors serve a path of meditation and a doctrine of no-self; the Nāṭyaśāstra’s analysis of emotion serves the theatre; the medical texts’ account of the mind serves diagnosis and treatment. Their categories are embedded in metaphysical and religious commitments that a modern reader may not share. To call the Buddhist ālayavijñāna “the unconscious” or Patañjali’s citta “the brain” is to translate, and every translation loses something. Throughout this volume the Indian accounts are presented as what the texts say, in their own terms, and comparisons with modern psychology are offered only as comparisons — never as claims that an ancient author “anticipated” or “proved” a modern finding. Where modern research has examined a practice derived from these traditions, such as meditation or yoga, the evidence is reported with its limits.

docs.title: 1.3 Recurring Themes in Indian Accounts of the Mind
docs.text: Despite their differences, the Indian schools share a number of assumptions and problems that recur in the chapters that follow.

docs.title: 1.3.1 The Mind Is Not the Self (for Most Schools)
docs.text: Most Brahmanical schools distinguish between consciousness or the self (ātman, puruṣa) and the mind (manas, citta, antaḥkaraṇa), which they treat as an instrument — subtle, but in Sāṃkhya and Yoga made of the same material nature (prakṛti) as the body. The self illuminates or witnesses mental events but is not itself one of them. Buddhist thinkers reject the permanent self altogether and analyse the person into a stream of momentary physical and mental events; the Jains hold that the soul (jīva) is conscious by nature and that its knowledge is obscured by karmic matter. The disagreement about the self is the main fault-line running through Indian philosophy of mind, and it shapes every account of perception, memory and liberation.

docs.title: 1.3.2 States of Consciousness
docs.text: The Upaniṣads analyse experience into states — waking, dream and dreamless sleep — and the Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad adds a “fourth” (turīya) that underlies the three. Dream and sleep were therefore treated not as marginal phenomena but as evidence about the nature of the self. Chapter 2 and Chapter 7 discuss these analyses.

docs.title: 1.3.3 Latent Impressions
docs.text: Almost all schools hold that experiences leave traces — saṃskāra, vāsanā, bīja, anuśaya — which persist below awareness and condition later perception, memory and action. In the Yoga and Buddhist traditions this theory explains habit, memory and karma; it is also the basis of their methods of mental training, which aim to weaken some impressions and cultivate others (Yogasūtra 2.33: vitarkabādhane pratipakṣabhāvanam, “when troubled by unwholesome thoughts, cultivate the opposite”).

docs.title: 1.3.4 Error and Its Correction
docs.text: Indian epistemology devoted great effort to explaining perceptual error: the rope mistaken for a snake, the shell for silver. The competing theories of error (khyātivāda) discussed in Chapter 3 are at the same time theories of how the mind constructs what it perceives. For several schools the fundamental human predicament is itself a kind of error — avidyā, “ignorance”, the misidentification of self and non-self — and liberation is its correction.

docs.title: 1.3.5 Mind, Body and Conduct
docs.text: Most Indian accounts treat the mind as closely bound up with the body and with conduct. The Sāṃkhya and Yoga schools count the mind among the products of matter; the medical texts hold that bodily humours disturb the mind and that mental states disturb the humours; the Yoga and Buddhist paths begin with ethical restraint, on the view that a mind agitated by harmful action cannot become still. The modern separation of “psychology”, “medicine” and “ethics” into distinct disciplines has no exact counterpart in the classical sources. This integration is often praised as “holistic”. It is worth remembering that it also meant that judgements about mental health were bound up with judgements about moral and ritual purity, and with the social hierarchy that those judgements supported.

docs.title: 1.3.6 Training as Well as Theory
docs.text: Indian accounts of the mind are almost always attached to practices: meditation, breath control, recitation, devotional discipline, ethical restraint. The texts claim that these practices transform the practitioner. Those claims are part of the historical record and are reported as such; whether and how such practices affect health or well-being is a separate, empirical question, taken up in Chapter 13.

docs.title: 1.4.1 Teacher and Student
docs.text: The relationship between teacher (ācārya, guru, upādhyāya) and student (śiṣya, brahmacārin, antevāsin) is the organising unit of Brahmanical, Buddhist and Jain education alike. The Taittirīya Upaniṣad’s instruction to the departing student — mātṛdevo bhava, pitṛdevo bhava, ācāryadevo bhava, atithidevo bhava, “treat your mother, father, teacher and guest as gods” (TU 1.11.2) — expresses the reverence expected; the Dharmasūtras regulate the student’s conduct in detail. Chapter 9 describes this model and its limits.

docs.title: 1.4.2 Orality and Memory
docs.text: The Vedic corpus was transmitted orally for many centuries before it was written down, and the techniques developed for this purpose — the word-by-word padapāṭha and the permuted recitations such as jaṭā and ghana — are among the most remarkable achievements of Indian learning (Chapter 10). Oral transmission remained central even after writing became common, and the manuscript culture that developed alongside it is the subject of Chapter 12.

docs.title: 1.4.3 Institutions
docs.text: Alongside the household of the teacher, India developed larger institutions: Buddhist monasteries that became great centres of learning, such as Nālandā and Vikramaśilā; Brahmanical colleges attached to temples and land grants (ghaṭikā, agrahāra, maṭha); Jain teaching lineages and libraries; and Islamic maktabs and madrasas, which spread with the Delhi Sultanate from the thirteenth century (Section 1.5). Much of the popular literature on these institutions is mythical — Takṣaśilā presented as “the world’s first university”, Nālandā’s library said to have held “nine million manuscripts”. Chapter 11 separates what the sources say from what has been added.

docs.title: 1.4.4 Exclusion
docs.text: Brahmanical normative texts restricted Vedic learning to boys of the three upper varṇas who had undergone initiation (upanayana). Śūdras were excluded, sometimes under threat of savage punishment, and from about the beginning of the common era women were steadily excluded from Vedic study. These rules were never the whole story — Buddhist and Jain communities admitted members of all castes and both sexes to monastic life, women scholars and poets are attested in many periods, and vernacular schools taught reading and arithmetic to a broader population — but they cannot be passed over. They are discussed in Section 9.12.

docs.title: 1.5 A Brief History of Indian Thought about the Mind
1.5.1 The Vedic Hymns
docs.text:
The word manas, “mind”, is already common in the Ṛgveda, where it denotes the inner organ of thought, intention and feeling, and is closely associated with other words for mental activity: dhī, “visionary thought” or “insight”, especially the poet’s inspired insight that becomes a hymn; kratu, “resolve” or “purposive power”; and citta, “thought”. The poets speak of fashioning their hymns “with the mind” and of the gods as knowing the thoughts of men. One hymn (Ṛgveda 10.58) is a charm to call back the mind of a person that has “gone far away” — to the realm of Yama, to the sky, to the waters — so that he may live; the mind is here imagined as something that can wander from the body. A famous later Yajurvedic litany, the Śivasaṅkalpa verses (Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā 34.1–6), describes the mind as the swift “light of lights” that goes far while one is awake and returns while one sleeps, and ends each verse with the prayer tan me manaḥ śivasaṅkalpam astu, “may that mind of mine be of auspicious intent”.

For the student of psychology, the most interesting line of the cosmogonic hymn RV 10.129 (discussed as cosmology in Volume 1, Veda Prakāśa) is its fourth verse, which makes a mental event the first stirring of creation:

Ṛgveda 10.129.4

kāmas tad agre sam avartatādhi manaso retaḥ prathamaṃ yad āsīt | Desire came upon that One in the beginning, which was the first seed of mind.

The genitive manasaḥ can be read in two ways. Desire may be the first seed of mind, so that desire comes before thought and gives rise to it; or it may be the first seed emitted by thought, as in the translation of Jamison and Brereton (2014), so that thought is already present and desire is its first product. The verse does not settle the question, and nothing should be built on either reading alone. What both readings share is the hymn’s choice of a mental event — desire joined to thought — as the first stirring of creation. These passages are not a psychology, but they show that reflection on the mind and its powers is as old as the Indian textual tradition itself.

docs.title: 1.5.2 The Upaniṣads and the Renouncer Movements
docs.text: The oldest Upaniṣads (mid-first millennium BCE) turned from ritual to the self (Chapter 2). In the same period a number of renouncer (śramaṇa) movements — among them the Buddhists, the Jains and the Ājīvikas — rejected the authority of the Veda and taught paths of discipline and insight aimed at liberation from rebirth. The Buddhist analysis of the person into five aggregates, the Jain theory of karmic matter, and the Upaniṣadic search for the self all belong to this creative period, and all three are concerned with the mind as the place where bondage and liberation are decided.

docs.title: 1.5.3 The Classical Systems
docs.text: In the first half of the first millennium CE the philosophical schools produced their root texts: the Nyāyasūtra, the Vaiśeṣikasūtra, the Sāṃkhyakārikā, the Pātañjalayogaśāstra, the Brahmasūtra, the Tattvārthasūtra, Nāgārjuna’s Mūlamadhyamakakārikā, the Abhidharma compendia and the works of Asaṅga and Vasubandhu. The medical compendia of Caraka and Suśruta and the Nāṭyaśāstra took shape between the last centuries BCE and the middle of the first millennium CE. Each of these works contains, among other things, a theory of the mind.

docs.title: 1.5.4 Commentators and Debaters
docs.text: The following thousand years were the age of commentary and debate. The Buddhist epistemologists Dignāga (5th–6th century) and Dharmakīrti (7th century) reshaped Indian theories of perception and inference; their Nyāya and Mīmāṃsā opponents replied; Śaṅkara (c. 700–750) and his successors developed Advaita Vedānta; the Kashmir Śaivas, above all Abhinavagupta (c. 950–1016), developed a philosophy of consciousness and an aesthetics; Rāmānuja and Madhva founded rival schools of Vedānta; and the “new logic” (Navya-Nyāya) of Gaṅgeśa (14th century) and his successors created a technical language of great precision. Devotional (bhakti) movements, flourishing in the regional languages from the Tamil Āḻvārs and Nāyaṉmārs onwards, produced their own rich psychology of love and longing.

docs.title: 1.5.5 The Indo-Islamic Period
docs.text: Arabic learning reached Sindh with Arab rule in the eighth century; Persian Sufi learning was established at Ghaznavid Lahore in the eleventh, where al-Hujwīrī wrote the first Sufi treatise composed in India; and from the thirteenth century the Delhi Sultanate, and later the Mughals, made Arabic and Persian learning a permanent part of Indian intellectual life. Islamic philosophy and medicine (Yūnānī, “Greek”) brought the Greek and Arabic tradition of faculty psychology, and Sufi writers brought a vocabulary of the self — the lower self (nafs), the heart (qalb), the spirit (rūḥ) — and of stages of the spiritual path that interacted with Indian ideas in many ways (Section 8.4.7). In the Panjab, the Sikh Gurus, from Guru Nānak (1469–1539) onwards, composed a scripture with its own analysis of the mind and of self-centredness (haumai). Chapter 8 describes the Islamic, Sufi and Sikh psychologies of the self, and Chapter 11 the maktab, the madrasa and Sikh learning. The Tamil country, meanwhile, had developed its own vocabulary of inner and outer life, its own ethics of the mind in the Tirukkuṟaḷ, and, in Śaiva Siddhānta, a systematic analysis of the bound soul (Section 3.11).

docs.title: 1.5.6 The Modern Period
docs.text:
In the nineteenth and twentieth centuries Indian thinkers — among them Swami Vivekananda, Sri Aurobindo, Rabindranath Tagore, Mohandas Gandhi and B. R. Ambedkar — reinterpreted the traditions in response to colonial rule, Western science and social reform. Academic psychology was introduced in Indian universities from 1915, and meditation and yoga were carried abroad and transformed. Chapter 13 follows these developments. Figure 1.1 sets the two histories, of thought about the mind and of educational institutions, side by side.

Figure 1.1. A simplified timeline of Indian thought about the mind (upper row) and of educational institutions (lower row). All dates are approximate, and the periods are not drawn to scale.

docs.title: 1.6 Who Were the Learned?
docs.text:
The texts discussed in this volume were produced and transmitted by particular groups, and it is worth asking who they were. Vedic and śāstric learning was cultivated above all by Brahmin families, many of which specialised in a particular Veda, ritual tradition or discipline over generations. Buddhist and Jain monks and nuns formed a second learned class, recruited from all castes, whose monasteries became centres of scholarship and whose lay supporters — merchants, artisans and kings — financed them. Physicians formed hereditary lineages of their own; astronomers and astrologers, scribes and accountants (such as the Kāyasthas of north India), musicians and dancers, architects and sculptors each transmitted specialised knowledge within families or guilds. From the eleventh century, and on a large scale from the thirteenth, the Muslim learned class (ʿulamāʾ), Sufi masters and Persian-educated secretaries added further communities of learning.

Literacy itself was unevenly spread. Aśoka addressed his edicts to the general public in the third century BCE, which suggests that a public existed for whom inscriptions could be read aloud; merchants needed writing and accounts; and by the early modern period village schools taught reading and arithmetic to a minority of boys of many castes. But until the twentieth century most Indians — and the overwhelming majority of women — could not read. A history of Indian learning is necessarily a history of minorities, and part of the task of this volume is to keep that fact in view.

docs.title: 1.7 Sources and Methods
docs.text:
The sources for this volume are of several kinds, and each has its own problems.

  1. Philosophical and religious texts in Sanskrit, Pali and Prakrit: the Upaniṣads, the Sāṃkhyakārikā, the Yogasūtra and its commentaries, the Abhidharma literature, the works of Śaṅkara and later Vedāntins, the Nyāya and Buddhist epistemologists, and the Kashmir Śaiva philosophers. Their dates are often uncertain, and many survive in late manuscripts.

  2. Normative texts such as the Dharmasūtras and the Manusmṛti (c. 2nd century CE; (Olivelle 2005)). These prescribe how things should be done; they are not reliable descriptions of practice.

  3. Technical literature: the medical saṃhitās of Caraka and Suśruta, the Nāṭyaśāstra, the phonetic and grammatical treatises (śikṣā, prātiśākhya, vyākaraṇa).

  4. Narrative literature: the epics, the Purāṇas, the Buddhist Jātakas. These preserve valuable incidental information about teachers and students but are not histories.

  5. Travellers’ accounts, above all those of the Chinese pilgrims Xuanzang (travelled 629–645) and Yijing (in India 673–685), and later Tibetan accounts such as the biography of Dharmasvāmin.

  6. Inscriptions and archaeology, which provide the firmest dates for institutions such as Nālandā, the ghaṭikā of Kāñcī and the colleges of the Cōḻa period.

  7. Colonial surveys of indigenous education from the 1820s and 1830s, which provide the first quantitative evidence, with all the biases of their compilers.

Dates in this volume follow current scholarship, with traditional dates labelled as traditional. Thus the Ṛgveda is dated c. 1500–1200 BCE in its core, the later Vedic texts c. 1200–500 BCE, the oldest Upaniṣads (Bṛhadāraṇyaka and Chāndogya) to the middle of the first millennium BCE, the Buddha c. 480–400 BCE (the “short chronology”; the older dates 563–483 or the Theravāda 624–544 BCE are traditional), the Yogasūtra c. 325–425 CE (Maas 2013), and Śaṅkara c. 700–750 CE (the conventional dates 788–820 are traditional).

docs.title: 1.8 The Structure of This Volume
docs.text:
The volume is not divided into formal parts. Its first group of chapters concerns the mind. Chapter 2 examines the Upaniṣadic analysis of consciousness — the states of waking, dream, deep sleep and turīya, the five “selves” of the Taittirīya Upaniṣad — and its later development by Gauḍapāda, the Kashmir Śaivas, the grammarian Bhartṛhari and the Jains. Chapter 3 sets out the models of the mind of Sāṃkhya, Yoga, Nyāya–Vaiśeṣika, Mīmāṃsā, the materialists, the Jains, the Mahābhārata and Āyurveda, together with the Tamil accounts of inner life and the Śaiva Siddhānta analysis of the soul, and asks what the classical theories said about women’s minds. Chapter 4 treats Advaita Vedānta, its Vedāntic rivals and the psychology of devotion. Chapter 5 treats the Buddhist analysis of mind in the Abhidharma, Yogācāra and Madhyamaka and in the meditation manuals. Chapter 6 examines the theory of emotion developed in the Nāṭyaśāstra and by Abhinavagupta. Chapter 7 examines dreams and sleep. Chapter 8 turns to the accounts of the self written in Arabic, Persian and Panjabi: the faculty psychology and ethics of the Muslim philosophers, the Sufi psychology of the lower self, the heart and the subtle centres, and the Sikh teaching on the mind and on haumai.

The second group follows the history of learning in roughly chronological order. Chapter 9 describes the Brahmanical model of the student living with his teacher and the rules that governed it, including its exclusions. Chapter 10 describes the oral transmission of the Veda on which that model rested, and the other oral traditions of India. Chapter 11 examines the larger institutions, from the teachers of Takṣaśilā and the Buddhist monasteries to the temple colleges, the Jain libraries, the madrasas, Sikh learning and the village schools of the eighteenth century. Chapter 12 describes the manuscript tradition and its passage into print. Chapter 13 begins with the colonial surveys, the first modern colleges and the schooling of girls between 1820 and 1930, and then considers the modern afterlife of the traditions: in Indian educational thought and policy, including the National Education Policy of 2020; in academic psychology and psychiatry; and in meditation and yoga research.

docs.title: 1.9 Orientation: Mind, Learning and Their Vocabulary
docs.text:
Sanskrit has many words that are translated “mind”, and they are not interchangeable. A reader of the following chapters will meet them constantly.

  • manas: the most general word; in the systems, a specific inner organ that coordinates the senses and deliberates.

  • citta: “thought”, and in Yoga the whole mental field; in Buddhist Abhidharma, a single moment of consciousness.

  • buddhi: intellect or understanding; in Sāṃkhya, the faculty of ascertainment; in Nyāya, simply “cognition”.

  • antaḥkaraṇa: the “inner instrument”, threefold in Sāṃkhya (intellect, I-maker and mind; Section 3.2) and fourfold in later Vedānta, which adds citta as memory (Section 4.5.1).

  • cetas, cetanā: mind, awareness; in Buddhism cetanā is “volition”, the mental factor that constitutes karma.

  • vijñāna (Pali viññāṇa): consciousness or discernment; in the Upaniṣads also “understanding”.

  • jñāna: knowledge or cognition, in the sense both of an act and of its content.

  • cit, caitanya, saṃvit: consciousness as such, especially in Vedānta and Kashmir Śaivism.

  • hṛdaya: “heart”, often the seat of the self and of feeling.

Where is the mind located? The Upaniṣads repeatedly place the self “in the cavity of the heart”, and the Carakasaṃhitā makes the heart the seat of consciousness and of the vital essence (ojas). Other medical writers, and the later yogic literature with its centres along the spine culminating at the crown of the head, located mental functions in the head. Neither view was based on experiment in the modern sense, and the texts often combine them. The Indian analyses of the mind were functional and introspective, not anatomical.

Three ideas link the two halves of the volume. The first is memory (smṛti). Patañjali defines it as “the not-losing of an object that has been experienced” (YS 1.11), and most epistemologists, Nyāya and Mīmāṃsā among them, refused it the status of a means of valid knowledge, because it only reproduces a previous cognition. Yet the same culture invested extraordinary effort in the training of verbal memory (Chapter 10). The second is the idea that understanding grows in stages, from hearing a teaching through reflection to contemplation: the Upaniṣadic triad of śravaṇa, manana and nididhyāsana, which has a close Buddhist counterpart (Section 4.8). The third is eligibility (adhikāra): the principle that a teaching suits only a student who is ready for it, which was also, in the Mīmāṃsā and Dharmaśāstra traditions, a right to study defined by caste and gender (Sections 4.8 and 9.12). Many schools, finally, frame their analysis of the mind as a diagnosis of suffering and a prescription for its cure; Table 8.3 sets five of these diagnoses side by side.

docs.title: 1.10 Indian and Modern Psychology: A Note on Comparison
docs.text:
Comparison between Indian and modern psychology is unavoidable and can be illuminating, provided that it is done carefully. Parallels of the kind met in this volume — the inner instrument and executive control, the Yoga cultivation of opposite thoughts and cognitive restructuring, the Buddhist life-continuum and the brain’s “default mode”, the storehouse consciousness and the unconscious, the redundancy of Vedic recitation and error-detecting codes — are common in the literature that presents “Indian psychology” as a contemporary project (Section 1.2) and in popular writing. Four cautions guide this volume. They apply to every comparison mentioned in the later chapters, which is why those chapters note such comparisons only briefly.

First, “Indian” and “Western” are not unified positions. The Indian schools are divided on the most basic questions — whether there is a self, whether consciousness is intrinsically active or passive, whether the world is real — and so are modern psychologists. Generalisations such as “Indian psychology treats consciousness as primary” are true of Advaita Vedānta and Kashmir Śaivism, false of Buddhism and Nyāya.

Secondly, similarity of structure is not identity of content. The Abhidharma list of mental factors and a modern taxonomy of cognitive functions may both distinguish attention from feeling, but they do so for different purposes and on different evidence. The Indian categories were arrived at by philosophical analysis and trained introspection within metaphysical and soteriological frameworks; they do not map onto brain regions or clinical diagnoses.

Thirdly, the antiquity of an idea does not establish its truth, and a modern finding does not “confirm” an ancient text. Where a practice derived from the traditions has been tested, the test concerns the modern practice, not the doctrine from which it came. No parallel noted in passing in this volume should be read as a claim that a text “anticipated” a modern discovery.

Fourthly, the most productive dialogues treat the traditions as sources of careful first-person description and of hypotheses to be tested, not as authorities whose conclusions are already known to be right. That is the approach of Francisco Varela, Evan Thompson and the contributors to recent collaborative work between philosophers of mind and Indologists (Thompson 2015; Siderits et al. 2011; Ganeri 2012).

docs.title: 1.11 The Living Traditions
docs.text:
Many practices discussed in this volume continue today: Vedic recitation in traditional schools (pāṭhaśālās), the study of Sanskrit śāstra with traditional teachers, monastic education in Buddhist and Jain communities, meditation and yoga in forms both traditional and modern. Some have been adapted far from their origins — the mindfulness programmes used in clinics are a well-known case. Chapter 13 discusses these developments, distinguishing what research supports from what is claimed for them. It also places the revival of interest in “Indian Knowledge Systems” in its historical context: the colonial reorganisation of education, the nationalist responses to it, and the policies of independent India.

Īśā Upaniṣad 5

tad ejati tan naijati tad dūre tad v antike | tad antar asya sarvasya tad u sarvasyāsya bāhyataḥ || It moves, it does not move; it is far, and it is near. It is within all this, and it is outside all this.

docs.title: 1.12 What This Volume Does Not Cover
docs.text: Some limits of the volume should be stated plainly. It concentrates on the classical Sanskrit and Pali sources and on the history of institutions of learning; it treats the Tamil and other regional-language traditions in a single section on the mind (Section 3.11) and in passing elsewhere, though they contain their own reflections on the mind and their own histories of teaching, and its account of the Persian, Arabic and Panjabi sources (Chapter 8) is a survey of a large literature. It gives only brief sketches of the history of Indian psychiatry and of modern Indian schooling (Chapter 13), both of which are large subjects in their own right, and it touches only in passing on the knowledge of tribal and nomadic communities, and on the craft and agricultural knowledge transmitted outside schools. These subjects are treated, where possible, in other volumes of the series. Readers should therefore take the picture presented here as one part of a larger and more varied whole.

docs.title: 1.13 A Note on Terms and Transliteration
docs.text: Sanskrit, Pali and Prakrit words are given in the International Alphabet of Sanskrit Transliteration (IAST). Pali forms are used for Theravāda material (sati, citta, cetasika), Sanskrit forms for the northern Buddhist traditions (smṛti, caitta). Arabic and Persian words in Chapters 8 and 11 are given in a simplified scholarly transliteration, and Panjabi terms of the Sikh scripture in the form usual in Sikh studies. Key terms are explained at their first occurrence and collected in the Glossary. Translations of verses are made for this volume unless otherwise stated; they aim at accuracy rather than elegance, and readers should consult the editions and translations listed at the end of the volume (Editions and Translations of the Principal Texts) for the full texts. Tamil words are transliterated in the system of the Tamil Lexicon (ḻ, ṟ, ṉ), and couplets of the Tirukkuṟaḷ are cited by their traditional numbers.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text:
• Rao et al. (2008): a large collection of essays presenting “Indian psychology” as a contemporary project; useful but often advocacy rather than history.

  • Paranjpe (1998): a careful comparison of Indian and Western theories of the self.

  • Dasgupta (1922): still the most detailed history of the philosophical schools.

  • Scharfe (2002): the standard scholarly account of education in ancient India; supersedes Altekar (1965) and Mookerji (1947) on many points.

  • Thompson (2015): a philosopher’s dialogue between Indian contemplative traditions and cognitive science, written with attention to the differences.

docs.title: Chapter 2: The Dimensions of Consciousness
docs.text: prajñānaṃ brahma Brahman is consciousness. — Aitareya Upaniṣad 3.3

docs.title: 2.1 The Upaniṣadic Turn Inward
docs.text:
The oldest Upaniṣads, composed in the middle centuries of the first millennium BCE, shift the focus of Vedic speculation from the ritual and the cosmos to the person who performs the ritual and knows the cosmos. Their central question is “what is the self (ātman)?”, and their central claim, stated in many forms, is that the self in its true nature is identical with Brahman, the ground of all that exists. In pursuing this question the Upaniṣadic teachers produced the earliest sustained analyses of consciousness in Indian literature: of the difference between the knower and the known, of the states of waking, dream and sleep, and of the layers that make up a person.

These texts are not treatises. They are collections of dialogues, teachings and ritual speculations, composed and transmitted by different Vedic schools over several centuries, and they do not present a single system (Olivelle 1998). Later commentators — above all Śaṅkara and the Vedāntins who followed him — read them as a unified doctrine, and much of the modern literature reads them through Advaita eyes. This chapter tries to present first what the texts say, and then how later schools developed them.

docs.title: 2.2 Four “Great Sayings”
docs.text:
Later Vedānta singled out four sentences, one from an Upaniṣad of each Veda, as “great sayings” (mahāvākya) that express the identity of self and Brahman (Table 2.1).

Table 2.1. The four mahāvākyas of later Vedānta. Saying Meaning Source prajñānaṃ brahma Brahman is consciousness Aitareya Up. 3.3 (Ṛgveda) ahaṃ brahmāsmi I am Brahman Bṛhadāraṇyaka Up. 1.4.10 (Yajurveda) tat tvam asi You are that Chāndogya Up. 6.8.7 (Sāmaveda) ayam ātmā brahma This self is Brahman Māṇḍūkya Up. 2 (Atharvaveda)

The grouping is late — it is not found in the Upaniṣads themselves — and in their original contexts the sentences do different work. “You are that” is the refrain of Uddālaka Āruṇi’s instruction to his son Śvetaketu in Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6, where “that” refers to the subtle essence (aṇiman) underlying all things:

Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.7

sa ya eṣo ’ṇimaitadātmyam idaṃ sarvaṃ tat satyaṃ sa ātmā tat tvam asi śvetaketo That which is this finest essence — the whole world has it as its self. That is the truth; that is the self. You are that, Śvetaketu.

How can a sentence identify the limited individual (“you”) with the unlimited ground of the world (“that”)? Later Advaitins answered with a theory of interpretation. In an ordinary sentence such as “this is that Devadatta”, said of a man seen now and once before in another place, we set aside the incompatible features of the two occasions (here and there, now and then) and retain the person who is common to both. In the same way, they argued, tat tvam asi sets aside the limiting features of the individual (finitude, embodiment) and of the cosmic lord (omniscience, rulership over the world) and points to the pure consciousness common to both. This “partial” secondary meaning (jahadajahallakṣaṇā) became a standard part of Advaita exegesis and shows how closely the doctrine of consciousness was tied to a theory of language.

Uddālaka’s method is pedagogically striking: he teaches through demonstrations — salt dissolved in water that can be tasted but not seen, the seed of a banyan split open to reveal nothing visible, a blindfolded man finding his way home — each followed by the same refrain. The teaching proceeds by repeated concrete examples rather than by definition, a method to which Chapter 9 returns.

docs.title: 2.3 Light, the Seer and the Seen
docs.text:
In the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad (4.3), King Janaka asks Yājñavalkya what light a person has. The sun, Yājñavalkya answers; when the sun has set, the moon; then fire; then speech; and when all these have ceased, “the self is his light” (ātmaivāsya jyotir bhavati). The self is the light by which everything else is seen and which is not itself an object of seeing. In another passage Yājñavalkya argues that “you cannot see the seer of seeing, you cannot hear the hearer of hearing” (BU 3.4.2): the subject of experience cannot become its own object.

These arguments became the foundation of the Vedāntic doctrine of the self as the witness (sākṣin) and as self-luminous (svaprakāśa), discussed in Chapter 4. They also set a problem that occupied Indian philosophers for two thousand years: if the self is never an object, how is it known at all? The Buddhists answered that there is no such self to know; the Nyāya philosophers that the self is known by inference and by inner perception of its qualities; the Advaitins that it is known not as an object but as the very fact of awareness.

docs.title: 2.4 The Chariot of the Self: The Kaṭha Upaniṣad
docs.text:
The Kaṭha Upaniṣad, one of the most widely read of the verse Upaniṣads, frames its teaching as a dialogue between the boy Naciketas and Yama, the lord of death. In its third section it offers the most influential image of the person in Indian literature:

Kaṭha Upaniṣad 1.3.3–4

ātmānaṃ rathinaṃ viddhi śarīraṃ ratham eva tu | buddhiṃ tu sārathiṃ viddhi manaḥ pragraham eva ca || indriyāṇi hayān āhur viṣayāṃs teṣu gocarān | ātmendriyamanoyuktaṃ bhoktety āhur manīṣiṇaḥ || Know the self as the rider in the chariot, and the body as the chariot. Know the intellect as the charioteer and the mind as the reins. The senses, they say, are the horses, and the objects of sense the paths they range over. The self joined with body, senses and mind the wise call “the enjoyer”.

The verses that follow draw out the image: one who lacks understanding and whose mind is never controlled has senses like the vicious horses of a bad charioteer; one who has understanding and a controlled mind has senses like the good horses of a skilled driver, and reaches the end of the road, “the highest step of Viṣṇu”. The Upaniṣad then sets out a hierarchy:

Kaṭha Upaniṣad 1.3.10–11

indriyebhyaḥ parā hy arthā arthebhyaś ca paraṃ manaḥ | manasas tu parā buddhir buddher ātmā mahān paraḥ || mahataḥ param avyaktam avyaktāt puruṣaḥ paraḥ | puruṣān na paraṃ kiṃcit sā kāṣṭhā sā parā gatiḥ || Higher than the senses are their objects; higher than the objects is the mind; higher than the mind is the intellect; higher than the intellect is the great self. Higher than the great is the unmanifest; higher than the unmanifest is the person. There is nothing higher than the person: that is the goal, that the highest way.

This sequence — senses, mind, intellect, the “great” (mahat), the unmanifest (avyakta), the person (puruṣa) — shares its vocabulary with the later system of Sāṃkhya (Chapter 3), and scholars have long seen in it an early stage of that system’s development. The chariot image, with its picture of the intellect controlling the mind as a driver controls horses through the reins, became a commonplace of later Indian ethics and psychology. It has a striking parallel in Plato’s Phaedrus, where the soul is likened to a charioteer driving two horses. No contact between the two texts is documented, and the resemblance is best treated as a parallel, not as evidence of borrowing in either direction.

docs.title: 2.5 The Four States: The Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad
docs.text:
The Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad, a text of only twelve short prose sections, analyses the syllable oṃ and the states of the self in parallel. Its date is uncertain but it is later than the oldest Upaniṣads.

Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad 1

om ity etad akṣaram idaṃ sarvaṃ tasyopavyākhyānaṃ bhūtaṃ bhavad bhaviṣyad iti sarvam oṃkāra eva | yac cānyat trikālātītaṃ tad apy oṃkāra eva || Oṃ — this syllable is all this. Its explanation: the past, the present and the future — all this is oṃ. And whatever else lies beyond the three times, that too is oṃ.

The text then distinguishes four “quarters” (pāda) of the self.

  1. Waking (jāgarita). The self as Vaiśvānara, “common to all men”, whose cognition is turned outward (bahiṣprajña) and who enjoys gross objects.

  2. Dream (svapna). The self as Taijasa, “the luminous”, whose cognition is turned inward (antaḥprajña) and who enjoys subtle objects.

  3. Deep sleep (suṣupta). The self as Prājña, “the knowing”, in whom cognition has become a single mass (prajñānaghana), “made of bliss and enjoying bliss”.

  4. The fourth (caturtha, later turīya). Not a further state alongside the others but the self as such.

The description of deep sleep is precise:

Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad 5

yatra supto na kañcana kāmaṃ kāmayate na kañcana svapnaṃ paśyati tat suṣuptam When one asleep desires no desire and sees no dream, that is deep sleep.

The fourth is described almost entirely by negation:

Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad 7

nāntaḥprajñaṃ na bahiṣprajñaṃ nobhayataḥprajñaṃ na prajñānaghanaṃ na prajñaṃ nāprajñam | adṛṣṭam avyavahāryam agrāhyam alakṣaṇam acintyam avyapadeśyam ekātmapratyayasāraṃ prapañcopaśamaṃ śāntaṃ śivam advaitaṃ caturthaṃ manyante sa ātmā sa vijñeyaḥ || Not inwardly cognitive, not outwardly cognitive, not cognitive both ways, not a mass of cognition, neither cognitive nor non-cognitive; unseen, beyond transaction, ungraspable, without marks, unthinkable, indescribable, whose essence is the cognition of the one self, the cessation of the world, peaceful, auspicious, non-dual — this they consider the fourth. That is the self; that is what is to be known.

The final sections map the three states onto the three sounds of oṃ (a, u, m) and the fourth onto the soundless syllable as a whole:

Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad 12

amātraś caturtho ’vyavahāryaḥ prapañcopaśamaḥ śivo ’dvaita evam oṃkāra ātmaiva saṃviśaty ātmanātmānaṃ ya evaṃ veda || The fourth is without measure, beyond transaction, the cessation of the world, auspicious, non-dual. Thus oṃ is the self. One who knows this enters the self by the self.

Figure 2.1. The four “quarters” of the self in the Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad.

docs.title: 2.5.1 The Philosophical Point
docs.text:
The argument implicit in the Māṇḍūkya (Figure 2.1) — and made explicit by its commentators — is that the contents of experience change completely from waking to dream to dreamless sleep, while something remains constant: the one to whom these states belong. Since the self persists through all three, it cannot be identified with any of them. Deep sleep is particularly important: on waking we say “I slept happily, I knew nothing”, and the Vedāntins took this as evidence that awareness, and a kind of bliss, were present even in the absence of any object.

Other Upaniṣads describe sleep in physiological-sounding terms. The Praśna Upaniṣad (4.2–3) compares the senses in sleep to the rays of the setting sun, which gather into the sun’s disc: in sleep the senses become one in the mind, “the highest god”, so that a person “does not hear, does not see, does not smell”, while the vital breaths remain awake like fires keeping watch in a sleeping house. The Bṛhadāraṇyaka (2.1.19) and Chāndogya (8.6) Upaniṣads speak of the self in deep sleep as resting in the channels (nāḍī) of the heart. These images belong to a family of ideas about breath and the body that later developed into the medical and yogic theories of the channels.

Other schools rejected the Vedāntic reading of deep sleep. The Nyāya philosophers held that in dreamless sleep there is no cognition at all, since cognition arises only when the mind is in contact with the self and a sense organ; the memory of having “slept well” is an inference from the refreshed state of the body. The Buddhists explained deep sleep in terms of a subtle continuing stream of consciousness (Pali bhavaṅga) without positing a self. The question is still debated by philosophers working on sleep and consciousness (Thompson 2015).

docs.title: 2.5.2 The Three States and Sleep Science
docs.text: Modern sleep research distinguishes waking, rapid-eye-movement (REM) sleep, in which vivid dreaming is most common, and non-REM sleep, whose deepest stage is associated with little reportable mental content. The correspondence with the Upaniṣadic triad is loose: dreaming also occurs in non-REM sleep, the modern stages are defined by physiological measurement rather than by the content of experience, and turīya has no counterpart in sleep science. The Upaniṣadic scheme is a phenomenological and metaphysical analysis, not an early version of polysomnography.

docs.title: 2.6 Gauḍapāda’s Kārikā
docs.text:
The Māṇḍūkyakārikā (also called Āgamaśāstra), attributed to Gauḍapāda, whom tradition makes the teacher of Śaṅkara’s teacher, is a verse treatise in four chapters of 29, 38, 48 and 100 verses. It is usually dated to the sixth century CE. Only the first chapter comments on the Māṇḍūkya; the others develop an independent argument, with clear debts to Buddhist Madhyamaka and Yogācāra thought (Potter 1981). Table 2.2 summarises the four chapters.

Table 2.2. The four chapters (prakaraṇa) of Gauḍapāda’s Māṇḍūkyakārikā. Name Verses Theme I Āgama 29 Exposition of the Māṇḍūkya; oṃ and the four states II Vaitathya 38 “Unreality”: waking objects are as unreal as dream objects III Advaita 48 Non-duality; critique of theories of causation IV Alātaśānti 100 “Quenching of the firebrand”; non-origination (ajātivāda)

Gauḍapāda’s central doctrine is ajātivāda, “non-origination”: nothing real ever comes into being. His argument in the second chapter starts from dreams: the marks by which we judge waking objects real are present in dreams too, and so cannot prove the reality of the waking world (the argument is set out in Chapter 7). The conclusion is stated with deliberate starkness:

Māṇḍūkyakārikā 2.32

na nirodho na cotpattir na baddho na ca sādhakaḥ | na mumukṣur na vai mukta ity eṣā paramārthatā || There is no dissolution, no origination; no one bound and no one striving; no seeker of liberation and no one liberated. This is the highest truth.

Gauḍapāda also recommends a contemplative practice he calls “touchless yoga” (asparśayoga, GK 3.39), which he admits is “difficult to see” and of which yogins are afraid, “seeing fear where there is no fear”. The term, and much of the vocabulary of the fourth chapter, closely resembles that of Mahāyāna Buddhism, and scholars have long debated how far Gauḍapāda borrowed from Buddhist sources. Later Advaitins were sensitive to the charge that their doctrine was “Buddhism in disguise”, a charge pressed by their Vedāntic opponents.

The image of the fourth chapter’s title is that of a burning torch whirled in the air: the circles and lines we see are produced by the movement of a single point of fire, and when the movement stops they vanish. So, Gauḍapāda argues, the world of multiplicity is a “vibration” (spandita) of consciousness.

docs.title: 2.7 The Five Sheaths: The Taittirīya Upaniṣad
docs.text:
The second chapter of the Taittirīya Upaniṣad (the Brahmānandavallī) describes the person as a series of selves, each “made of” (-maya) a different substance and each contained within the previous one: the self made of food (annamaya), of breath (prāṇamaya), of mind (manomaya), of understanding (vijñānamaya) and of bliss (ānandamaya). The Upaniṣad does not use the word “sheath” (kośa); that term comes from later Vedānta, which treated the five as coverings to be distinguished from the true self (Table 2.3 and Figure 2.2).

Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1

brahmavid āpnoti param | tad eṣābhyuktā | satyaṃ jñānam anantaṃ brahma One who knows Brahman attains the highest. On this there is the verse: “Brahman is truth, knowledge, infinite.”

Table 2.3. The five selves of the Taittirīya Upaniṣad and their later interpretation. Self (kośa) Made of Later Vedāntic interpretation annamaya Food The physical body (gross body) prāṇamaya Breath, the five vital winds Vital functions (part of the subtle body) manomaya Mind Manas with the organs of perception vijñānamaya Understanding Buddhi, the sense of agency ānandamaya Bliss The causal body, experienced in deep sleep Figure 2.2. The five “selves” of the Taittirīya Upaniṣad (2.1–5), each said to be contained within the preceding one; later Vedānta calls them “sheaths” (kośa) covering the true self.

The third chapter of the same Upaniṣad (the Bhṛguvallī) presents the teaching as a process of discovery. Bhṛgu asks his father Varuṇa to teach him Brahman. Varuṇa gives him only a definition — “that from which these beings are born, by which, once born, they live, and into which they pass on dying: seek to know that; that is Brahman” (TU 3.1) — and sends him to practise austerity (tapas). Bhṛgu returns five times, having concluded successively that Brahman is food, breath, mind, understanding and finally bliss. The episode is often cited as an example of teaching by guided inquiry rather than by instruction.

The five sheaths are widely used today as a framework for “holistic” health or education, mapped onto physical, emotional, intellectual and spiritual development. That is a modern adaptation: the Upaniṣad’s purpose is to lead the student to Brahman, not to provide a model of human development.

docs.title: 2.8 The Three Bodies
docs.text: Later Vedānta combined the five sheaths and the three states into the doctrine of three bodies (śarīratraya): the gross body (sthūla), corresponding to the food-sheath and the waking state; the subtle body (sūkṣma or liṅga), comprising the vital, mental and intellectual sheaths and associated with dreaming; and the causal body (kāraṇa), identified with the bliss-sheath and with deep sleep. The self, the witness of all three, is identified with turīya. The scheme is a scholastic systematisation of the Upaniṣadic material, found in manuals such as Sadānanda’s Vedāntasāra; it is not present as such in the Upaniṣads.

docs.title: 2.9 Consciousness and the Body in Āyurveda
docs.text:
The physicians had to explain consciousness in a way that fitted the living body they treated. The Carakasaṃhitā (Śārīrasthāna 1) describes the person (puruṣa) as a combination of the self, the mind and the elements, and argues that knowledge arises only when the self, the mind, a sense organ and its object are brought together; when the mind is not joined to a sense, no knowledge arises even if the object is present. The self is said to be the cause of consciousness, but it is conscious only when joined with the mind and the body; in itself it is without awareness. The analysis is close to that of the Nyāya–Vaiśeṣika school (Chapter 3). Caraka also discusses why the self, though in principle all-pervading, experiences pleasure and pain only in one body, and how the mind’s contact with impurities produces suffering.

This medical account is important because it shows the Upaniṣadic and philosophical vocabulary of self and mind put to practical use. For the physician, consciousness was not an abstract absolute but something whose presence, absence and disturbance in a particular patient had to be assessed — in fainting, in delirium, in insanity, in the approach of death.

docs.title: 2.10 The Five Vital Breaths
docs.text: From the Upaniṣads onwards Indian texts distinguish five “breaths” or vital winds (prāṇa) with different functions in the body. Their names are stable, though their functions are described somewhat differently in different texts: prāṇa, the breath of the chest and head, associated with inhalation; apāna, the downward breath, associated with excretion and reproduction; vyāna, the diffused breath that pervades the body; udāna, the upward breath, associated with speech and, in some Upaniṣads, with the departure of the self at death; and samāna, the “equalising” breath in the middle of the body, associated with digestion. The medical texts and the yogic literature developed this scheme further. It is a physiological theory of its time; the psychological meanings assigned to each breath in some modern yoga manuals go beyond the sources.

docs.title: 2.11 Breath and Mind
docs.text:
From the Upaniṣads onwards, Indian texts link the mind (manas) closely with the breath (prāṇa). Several Upaniṣadic passages describe a contest among the bodily powers — speech, sight, hearing, mind and breath — in which breath proves indispensable (e.g. BU 6.1, ChU 5.1). The later Haṭha Yoga texts make the connection the basis of their practice:

Haṭhayogapradīpikā 2.2

cale vāte calaṃ cittaṃ niścale niścalaṃ bhavet | yogī sthāṇutvam āpnoti tato vāyuṃ nirodhayet || When the breath moves, the mind moves; when the breath is still, the mind becomes still. The yogin attains steadiness; therefore he should restrain the breath.

The Haṭhayogapradīpikā is a fifteenth-century text, and its claims concern the yogin’s progress towards absorption. Modern physiology has found that breathing does interact with brain activity — for example, nasal breathing has been reported to modulate oscillations in limbic brain regions and to affect performance on memory tasks (Zelano et al. 2016) — and slow breathing is studied for its effects on the autonomic nervous system. Such findings make the traditional association of breath and mind intelligible without validating the specific claims of Haṭha Yoga (Section 1.10).

docs.title: 2.12 Consciousness in Kashmir Śaivism
docs.text: The non-dual Śaiva philosophers of Kashmir — Somānanda (early 10th century), his pupil Utpaladeva (c. 925–975), Abhinavagupta (c. 950–1016) and Abhinavagupta’s pupil Kṣemarāja — developed a theory of consciousness that is consciously opposed to the Vedāntic picture of a passive witness. Consciousness (cit, saṃvit), for them, is not only luminous (prakāśa) but also reflexively aware of itself (vimarśa); it is intrinsically active, free and creative. The world is its self-manifestation, not an illusion superimposed on it.

docs.title: 2.12.1 The Thirty-Six Principles
docs.text: The Śaiva systems extend the twenty-five principles (tattva) of Sāṃkhya (Chapter 3) to thirty-six by adding eleven above them: five “pure” principles — Śiva, Śakti, Sadāśiva, Īśvara and Śuddhavidyā — in which consciousness experiences itself as “I” with progressively more articulated awareness of “this”; then Māyā, the power of limitation; and five “sheaths” (kañcuka) through which Māyā restricts the universal consciousness to a finite subject: limitation of agency (kalā), of knowledge (vidyā), of satisfaction (rāga), of time (kāla), and restriction by causal order and place (niyati). The five kañcukas are, in effect, an analysis of what it is to be a finite knower and agent.

docs.title: 2.12.2 Vibration
docs.text: A related strand of Kashmir Śaivism, the doctrine of “vibration” (spanda), goes back to the Spandakārikā, a short verse text attributed to Vasugupta or his pupil Bhaṭṭa Kallaṭa (9th century). It describes consciousness as a subtle, pulsating movement that is the source of all activity, perception and emotion. The practitioner is taught to notice the moments in which this vibration becomes palpable — at the start of an intense emotion such as anger or joy, at the moment of a sudden surprise, at the junction between waking and sleep — and to recognise in them the activity of universal consciousness. The doctrine is thus also a contemplative technique for working with emotion: strong feelings are not suppressed but used as gateways (Dyczkowski 1987).

docs.title: 2.12.3 Recognition
docs.text:
The school takes its name from Utpaladeva’s Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā, “Verses on the Recognition of the Lord”. Liberation is not the acquisition of anything new but the recognition (pratyabhijñā) that one’s own consciousness is already the universal consciousness. Kṣemarāja’s short manual, the Pratyabhijñāhṛdaya, opens with a sūtra that summarises the doctrine:

Kṣemarāja, Pratyabhijñāhṛdaya, sūtra 1

citiḥ svatantrā viśvasiddhihetuḥ Consciousness, free, is the cause of the accomplishment of the universe.

The Śaiva texts also describe consciousness as performing five acts (pañcakṛtya): emission, maintenance and withdrawal of the world, concealment of its own nature, and grace (self-revelation). And some Śaiva and Śākta authors speak of a state “beyond the fourth” (turyātīta), in which the awareness glimpsed in turīya pervades all three ordinary states. Abhinavagupta’s aesthetics, discussed in Chapter 6, is built on this philosophy of consciousness (Dyczkowski 1987). His vast Tantrāloka (“Light on the Tantras”) sets out the whole Śaiva system of ritual and contemplative practice, arranged according to the means (upāya) suited to students of different capacities — from the “non-means” of sudden recognition for the most gifted, through means centred on will and on knowledge, to ritual and bodily means for those who need them. The graded scheme is another example of the Indian principle that teaching must be matched to the student.

docs.title: 2.13 Consciousness and Language: Bhartṛhari
docs.text:
The grammarian-philosopher Bhartṛhari (c. 5th century CE), in his Vākyapadīya, argued that all cognition is interpenetrated by language: “there is no cognition in the world that does not follow language” (Vākyapadīya 1.131 in Rau’s edition, 1.123 in Iyer’s: na so ’sti pratyayo loke yaḥ śabdānugamād ṛte). Meaning, on his account, is grasped as a whole — the sphoṭa, the unitary linguistic entity manifested by the sequence of sounds — rather than being assembled piece by piece from sounds or words (Iyer 1969).

Bhartṛhari distinguished three levels of speech: articulated speech (vaikharī), the intermediate level of speech in the mind (madhyamā), and the “seeing” level (paśyantī) at which meaning exists as an undivided whole. The Kashmir Śaivas later added a fourth and highest level, “supreme speech” (parā vāk), identified with consciousness itself; this fourth level is not found in Bhartṛhari. The theory’s holism about meaning has interested modern philosophers of language; it is a philosophical theory about language and cognition, not an account of language processing.

docs.title: 2.14 Consciousness in Jain Thought
docs.text:
For the Jains, consciousness is the defining mark of the soul (jīva), and every soul is in its pure state omniscient. Jain philosophers distinguish two aspects of conscious activity (upayoga): “seeing” (darśana), an undifferentiated, general awareness of an object, and “knowing” (jñāna), a differentiated cognition of its particular features. In ordinary beings “seeing” precedes “knowing”; in the omniscient they occur together, or — the point was debated between the Śvetāmbara and Digambara traditions — in alternate moments. The distinction resembles the Nyāya and Buddhist distinction between indeterminate and determinate perception (Chapter 3), but is framed in terms of the soul’s own activity rather than of the relation between the senses and their objects.

Jain thinkers also graded living beings by the number of their senses, from one-sensed beings such as plants and earth-bodies, which have only touch, to five-sensed beings, some of which possess a mind (saṃjñin) capable of reflection. Consciousness, on this view, is present in all living beings, but in very different degrees of development — a hierarchy that underlay the Jain ethic of non-violence towards all life (Jaini 1979).

docs.title: 2.15 Is Consciousness Self-Revealing?
docs.text:
A question debated across all the schools was whether a cognition makes itself known, or whether it needs to be known by something else. When I see a pot, do I also, in the same act, know that I am seeing it? The answers divided the schools along lines that cut across the division between “orthodox” and “heterodox” (Matilal 1986).

  • Nyāya held that a cognition is not self-aware. The first cognition (“this is a pot”) is known, if at all, by a second, introspective cognition (anuvyavasāya: “I am aware of the pot”), produced through the mind as an inner sense. Cognitions can therefore occur without being known.

  • The Buddhist epistemologists Dignāga and Dharmakīrti held that every cognition is aware of itself (svasaṃvedana): it has an aspect that presents the object and an aspect that presents the cognition. One of their arguments is from memory: we can later remember not only the object but our having seen it, which would be impossible if the experience had not been registered at the time.

  • Mīmāṃsā was divided. Kumārila held that a cognition is not perceived but inferred from the “cognisedness” (jñātatā) it produces in its object; Prabhākara held that every cognition reveals at once the knower, the known and the knowing (the “triple perception”, tripuṭī).

  • Advaita Vedānta held that consciousness itself is self-luminous (svaprakāśa) and never an object, while particular mental states are revealed by it (Chapter 4).

The debate is one of the most sophisticated in Indian philosophy, and it bears on issues still discussed in philosophy of mind: whether consciousness essentially involves self-awareness, whether there can be unconscious mental states, and how introspection works. Philosophers working on “pre-reflective self-awareness” have engaged with the Indian arguments as live philosophical positions, notably in the collaborative volume edited by Mark Siderits, Evan Thompson and Dan Zahavi (Siderits et al. 2011) and in Jonardon Ganeri’s study of the self (Ganeri 2012).

docs.title: 2.16 Knowing Other Minds
docs.text: How do we know that others are conscious? The Nyāya philosophers answered that we infer other minds from the purposive behaviour of other bodies, by analogy with our own case. The Buddhist logician Dharmakīrti (7th century) devoted a short treatise, the Santānāntarasiddhi (“Proof of Other Streams”), to the question, arguing that even an idealist must accept other mental streams on the basis of inference from their effects. Advaita Vedānta, for which there is ultimately only one consciousness, treats the plurality of minds as a feature of the empirical level of reality. The Jains, for whom each soul is a distinct centre of consciousness, list direct knowledge of others’ thoughts (manaḥparyāya jñāna) among the supernormal forms of knowledge available to advanced ascetics. The range of positions shows that Indian philosophers recognised the problem and treated it with the same seriousness as other questions of epistemology.

docs.title: 2.17 Assessment
docs.text:
The Upaniṣads and their successors offer a sustained reflection on consciousness that is unusual among ancient literatures for its attention to dream and dreamless sleep, for its arguments about the subject that cannot be made an object, and for its development into rival philosophical systems. Its claims are metaphysical claims, argued by their authors on the basis of scripture, reasoning and contemplative experience. Modern consciousness studies can engage with them as philosophical positions — the idea that consciousness is fundamental, for example, has modern defenders as well as critics — but no neuroscientific finding has shown them to be true or false, and presenting them as anticipations of modern science misrepresents both.

What the Indian traditions can offer contemporary discussion is something different: a long record of careful description of states of consciousness by people who trained their attention intensively, a range of rival theories argued with great sophistication, and a set of questions — about the self that persists through sleep, about whether awareness is reflexive, about the relation between consciousness and its objects — that remain open. Read in that way, the material in this chapter belongs not to the prehistory of neuroscience but to the history of philosophy, where it stands comparison with any tradition.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text:
• Olivelle (1998): text and translation of the early Upaniṣads, with a valuable introduction; Radhakrishnan (1953) for a wider selection with an Advaita-leaning commentary.

  • Potter (1981): summaries of Gauḍapāda’s and Śaṅkara’s works, with a historical introduction.

  • Dyczkowski (1987): the Kashmir Śaiva doctrine of vibration and its theory of consciousness; Singh (1963) for a translation of the Pratyabhijñāhṛdaya.

  • Iyer (1969): Bhartṛhari’s philosophy of language.

  • Thompson (2015): a dialogue between Indian theories of waking, dreaming and sleep and contemporary cognitive science.

docs.title: Chapter 3: Models of the Mind
docs.text: yogaś cittavṛttinirodhaḥ Yoga is the stilling of the fluctuations of the mind. — Yogasūtra 1.2

docs.title: 3.1 Introduction
docs.text: The Upaniṣads ask what the self is; the philosophical schools (darśana) that took shape in the following centuries ask, in addition, how the mind works. Each school developed a model of the mind — its components, its relation to the self and the body, the process by which it knows — that fitted its wider metaphysics. This chapter presents five such models: the Sāṃkhya account of the evolutes of matter, the Yoga account of the mind and its fluctuations, the Nyāya–Vaiśeṣika account of the mind as an atomic inner sense, the Jain account of the soul and its karmic coverings, and the Āyurvedic account of the mind as an object of medical care. It also considers the materialist dissent, the theories of error, the pre-systematic psychology of the Mahābhārata and the subtle body of Tantra, and two subjects that the Sanskrit schools leave out: the Tamil accounts of inner life (Section 3.11) and what the classical theories said about women’s minds (Section 3.12). The Buddhist models are treated separately in Chapter 5, and Vedānta in Chapter 4.

docs.title: 3.2 Sāṃkhya: Consciousness and the Evolutes of Matter
3.2.1 The Framework
docs.text:
Sāṃkhya is one of the oldest systematic schools of Indian thought. Its ideas appear in the Upaniṣads and the Mahābhārata, and it was given classical form in Īśvarakṛṣṇa’s Sāṃkhyakārikā, a work of seventy-two verses usually dated to the fourth or fifth century CE (Larson 1979; Larson and Bhattacharya 1987). The tradition names the sage Kapila as its founder.

Sāṃkhya is a dualism. There are two kinds of reality: consciousness (puruṣa), of which there are many, each pure, inactive and merely witnessing; and primal matter (prakṛti), one, unconscious and constantly changing. Everything other than consciousness — including the intellect, the ego and the mind — is a product of matter. The distinctive and, to modern readers, surprising feature of Sāṃkhya is thus that it counts the mind on the material side of its dualism. What makes mental events conscious is not the mind itself but the proximity of the puruṣa, whose light, as it were, is reflected in the intellect.

docs.title: 3.2.2 The Three Strands
docs.text:
Matter consists of three strands or qualities (guṇa): sattva (lightness, illumination, pleasure), rajas (activity, stimulation, pain) and tamas (heaviness, obstruction, dullness). Every thing and every mental state is a particular balance of the three.

Sāṃkhyakārikā 13

sattvaṃ laghu prakāśakam iṣṭam upaṣṭambhakaṃ calaṃ ca rajaḥ | guru varaṇakam eva tamaḥ pradīpavac cārthato vṛttiḥ || Sattva is held to be light and illuminating, rajas stimulating and moving, tamas heavy and enveloping. Their functioning serves a single purpose, like a lamp.

The final simile — a lamp, in which oil, wick and flame, though different, cooperate to give light — explains how three opposed qualities can work together. The theory of the guṇas became common property of Indian thought; the Bhagavad Gītā (chapters 14, 17 and 18) uses it to classify food, faith, knowledge, action and temperament, and Āyurveda uses it to classify minds.

docs.title: 3.2.3 The Twenty-Five Principles
docs.text:
From unmanifest matter evolve twenty-three manifest principles. Together with matter itself and consciousness, they make the twenty-five principles (tattva) of the system (Table 3.1); Figure 3.1 shows the order in which they evolve.

Table 3.1. The twenty-five principles (tattva) of classical Sāṃkhya. Principle Number Notes puruṣa (consciousness) 1 Neither produced nor productive; many prakṛti (primal matter) 1 Productive but not produced buddhi or mahat (intellect) 1 First evolute; ascertainment ahaṃkāra (I-maker) 1 Self-appropriation manas (mind) 1 Inner sense; deliberation organs of perception 5 Hearing, touch, sight, taste, smell organs of action 5 Speech, hands, feet, excretion, generation subtle elements (tanmātra) 5 Sound, touch, form, taste, smell gross elements (mahābhūta) 5 Space, air, fire, water, earth Total 25 puruṣa + prakṛti + 23 evolutes Figure 3.1. The evolution of the principles (tattva) in classical Sāṃkhya, after Sāṃkhyakārikā 22–25.

docs.title: 3.2.4 Arguments for Consciousness and Matter
docs.text: Sāṃkhya did not simply assert its dualism; it argued for it. Against those who held that effects are new creations, it defended the doctrine that the effect pre-exists in its material cause (satkāryavāda): what is non-existent cannot be brought into being (SK 9), just as, the commentators add, oil can be pressed from sesame but not from sand. Hence the world of experience must pre-exist in an unmanifest cause, primal matter. For the existence of consciousness distinct from matter, the Kārikā gives five reasons (SK 17): composite things exist for the sake of something else, as a bed exists for a sleeper; there must be something that is the opposite of the three guṇas; there must be a controller; there must be an experiencer; and there is activity directed towards isolation, which implies someone to be isolated. The first argument — that the complex apparatus of body and mind is “for another” and must therefore serve a being that is not itself complex — became a standard argument for the self in Indian philosophy.

docs.title: 3.2.5 The Inner Organ
docs.text:
The intellect, the I-maker and the mind together form the “inner organ” (antaḥkaraṇa). The Sāṃkhyakārikā defines each by its function:

  • The intellect is ascertainment (adhyavasāyo buddhiḥ, SK 23). In its sāttvika form it has four dispositions — virtue, knowledge, dispassion and mastery — and in its tāmasa form their opposites; these eight dispositions (bhāva) determine the course of a person’s life.

  • The I-maker is self-appropriation (abhimāno ’haṃkāraḥ, SK 24). It produces two series of evolutes: from its sāttvika aspect the mind and the ten organs, from its tāmasa aspect the five subtle elements, with its rājasa aspect energising both (SK 25).

  • The mind is “of the nature of both” (organ of perception and of action) and is characterised by deliberation (saṅkalpaka, SK 27).

The process of cognition runs in a fixed order (SK 30–36): the external organs grasp their objects; the mind deliberates on what they present; the I-maker appropriates it; and the intellect ascertains it, presenting the whole to the puruṣa. The organs, the Kārikā says, are like lamps that illuminate the object and hand it on to the intellect for the sake of the puruṣa.

Because the puruṣa is the opposite of the three guṇas, the Kārikā (SK 19) ascribes to it the character of a witness (sākṣitva), isolation, neutrality, the nature of a seer and non-agency. Yet in ordinary experience the qualities of the two are confused: the unconscious intellect appears conscious, and the inactive puruṣa appears to act, “as it were” (SK 20). This mutual misattribution is the Sāṃkhya counterpart of the Advaita doctrine of superimposition (Chapter 4).

The goal of the system is discriminative knowledge: the realisation that the puruṣa is not the intellect or any other product of matter. When that knowledge arises, matter, “like a dancer who has shown herself to the audience” (SK 59), ceases to perform for that puruṣa, which abides in isolation (kaivalya).

docs.title: 3.3 Yoga: The Mind and Its Fluctuations
3.3.1 Text and Date
docs.text: The Pātañjalayogaśāstra — the 195 sūtras attributed to Patañjali together with the commentary (bhāṣya) traditionally ascribed to Vyāsa — is now generally regarded by scholars as a single work, composed c. 325–425 CE (Maas 2013). It adopts much of the Sāṃkhya metaphysics but adds a personal Lord (īśvara) and, above all, a detailed analysis of meditation. Its psychology is centred on citta, “mind”, a term that covers the whole inner organ.

docs.title: 3.3.2 The Five Fluctuations
docs.text:
The mind is constantly modified by “fluctuations” or “turnings” (vṛtti), of which there are five kinds (YS 1.5–11), each of which may be afflicted (kliṣṭa) or unafflicted (akliṣṭa) (Table 3.2).

Table 3.2. The five fluctuations (vṛtti) of the mind in the Yogasūtra. Vṛtti Translation Definition (paraphrased) YS pramāṇa Valid cognition Perception, inference and testimony 1.7 viparyaya Error False knowledge not based on the real form of the object 1.8 vikalpa Conceptual construction Cognition following words, without a corresponding object 1.9 nidrā Sleep The fluctuation whose support is the cognition of absence 1.10 smṛti Memory The not-losing of an experienced object 1.11

The inclusion of sleep among the fluctuations is notable. Patañjali holds that dreamless sleep is itself a modification of the mind, a cognition whose support is absence, since on waking one remembers having slept. The Advaitins of the Vivaraṇa school also treat deep sleep as an experience that is later remembered — an experience of bliss and of ignorance (Section 4.4) — but they assign it to the witness-consciousness and to a mode of ignorance, not to the mind, which they hold to be withdrawn into its cause in sleep. The Naiyāyikas, by contrast, deny that there is any cognition in dreamless sleep at all (Section 2.5).

docs.title: 3.3.3 Practice and Dispassion
docs.text: The fluctuations are stilled “by practice and dispassion” (abhyāsavairāgyābhyāṃ tannirodhaḥ, YS 1.12). Practice is the effort to remain in stillness, made firm by long, uninterrupted and respectful cultivation (YS 1.14); dispassion is the mastery of one who no longer thirsts for seen or heard-of objects (YS 1.15). The pairing of a positive discipline with a withdrawal of craving recurs throughout Indian contemplative literature.

docs.title: 3.3.4 The Afflictions
docs.text:
The second chapter of the Yogasūtra analyses the roots of suffering as five afflictions (kleśa).

Yogasūtra 2.3

avidyāsmitārāgadveṣābhiniveśāḥ kleśāḥ The afflictions are ignorance, I-am-ness, attachment, aversion and clinging to life.

Ignorance is the field of the others, and is defined as taking the impermanent, impure, painful and not-self to be permanent, pure, pleasant and self (YS 2.5). I-am-ness (asmitā) is the identification of the power of seeing with the instrument of seeing (YS 2.6); attachment and aversion follow on pleasure and pain (YS 2.7–8); and clinging to life (abhiniveśa) is present “even in the wise” (YS 2.9). The afflictions may be dormant, attenuated, interrupted or active (YS 2.4), and the purpose of the practices of the second chapter — austerity, self-study and devotion to the Lord (kriyāyoga, YS 2.1), and the eight limbs (YS 2.29) — is to attenuate them.

docs.title: 3.3.5 Obstacles and Remedies
docs.text:
Patañjali lists nine obstacles (antarāya) that distract the mind (YS 1.30): sickness, mental inertia, doubt, carelessness, sloth, lack of detachment, false perception, failure to attain a stage of practice, and instability in a stage once attained. They are accompanied, he says, by pain, dejection, trembling of the body and irregular breathing (YS 1.31). Among the remedies he recommends is the cultivation of four attitudes towards others:

Yogasūtra 1.33

maitrīkaruṇāmuditopekṣāṇāṃ sukhaduḥkhapuṇyāpuṇyaviṣayāṇāṃ bhāvanātaś cittaprasādanam The mind becomes clear through cultivating friendliness towards the happy, compassion towards the suffering, gladness towards the virtuous and equanimity towards the wicked.

The four attitudes are the same as the Buddhist “divine abidings” (Chapter 5), one of many points at which Yoga and Buddhism share a vocabulary of practice. The passage is notable for its recognition that the clarity of the mind depends on one’s emotional relations with others, not only on solitary concentration.

docs.title: 3.3.6 The Eight Limbs
docs.text:
The best-known part of the Yogasūtra is its scheme of eight limbs (aṣṭāṅga, YS 2.29), which became the standard outline of yogic practice (Table 3.3 and Figure 3.2).

Table 3.3. The eight limbs of yoga (Yogasūtra 2.29–3.3). Limb Content 1 yama (restraints) Non-violence, truthfulness, not stealing, sexual restraint, non-possessiveness (YS 2.30) 2 niyama (observances) Purity, contentment, austerity, self-study, devotion to the Lord (YS 2.32) 3 āsana (posture) A posture that is steady and comfortable (YS 2.46) 4 prāṇāyāma Regulation of inhalation and exhalation (YS 2.49) 5 pratyāhāra Withdrawal of the senses from their objects (YS 2.54) 6 dhāraṇā Fixing the mind on one place (YS 3.1) 7 dhyāna Continuous flow of cognition on that object (YS 3.2) 8 samādhi The object alone shining forth, as if empty of its own form (YS 3.3)

Two points deserve emphasis. First, the scheme begins with ethics: the restraints and observances are prerequisites for the meditative limbs, and the restraints are described as a “great vow” valid for all times and places (YS 2.31).
