docs.title: Chapter 4: Vedāntic Psychology
docs.text: brahma satyaṃ jagan mithyā jīvo brahmaiva nāparaḥ Brahman is real, the world is false; the individual self is Brahman alone, not other. — A half-verse traditionally attributed to Śaṅkara (from the Brahmajñānāvalīmālā, whose authorship is doubtful)

docs.title: 4.1 Introduction
docs.text:
Vedānta, “the end of the Veda”, is the name of the exegetical tradition that interprets the Upaniṣads, the Brahmasūtra and the Bhagavad Gītā (the “triple foundation”, prasthānatraya). Its most influential branch, Advaita (“non-dual”) Vedānta, received its classical formulation from Śaṅkara, whom most scholars now date to c. 700–750 CE; the conventional dates 788–820 derive from later hagiography and are best treated as traditional. Śaṅkara’s central thesis is that the self (ātman) is identical with Brahman, pure consciousness, and that the experience of being a limited, embodied individual results from ignorance (avidyā). This chapter describes the account of the mind that follows from that thesis, and then the rival Vedāntic schools that rejected it.

Advaita is a theology and a metaphysics, not a psychology in the modern sense. But because it locates the human predicament in a cognitive error, and because it prescribes a discipline of study and contemplation to correct it, it contains a detailed theory of perception, error, the self and the mind.

docs.title: 4.2 Superimposition
docs.text:
Śaṅkara opens his commentary on the Brahmasūtra with a preamble on superimposition (adhyāsa). Self and not-self, he says, are as opposed as light and darkness; yet in everyday life we constantly confuse them, saying “I am fat”, “I am blind”, “I am happy”, attributing the properties of body, senses and mind to the self, and the consciousness of the self to body, senses and mind. He defines superimposition as follows:

Śaṅkara, Brahmasūtrabhāṣya, preamble

smṛtirūpaḥ paratra pūrvadṛṣṭāvabhāsaḥ The appearance, in the form of memory, of something previously seen in something else.

The model case is perceptual error: a rope seen in dim light as a snake, mother-of-pearl as silver. Something previously experienced (snake, silver) is projected onto what is present. Śaṅkara argues that the mutual superimposition of self and not-self is of the same kind, but beginningless, and that all ordinary knowledge and action — including the use of scripture and ritual — presupposes it. Liberation is the removal of this superimposition by knowledge.

docs.title: 4.2.1 Error and the Indeterminable
docs.text: What is the status of the snake seen in the rope? It is not real, since it is contradicted when the light improves; but it is not simply unreal like a “hare’s horn”, since it was actually experienced and caused fear. Later Advaitins called it “indeterminable” (anirvacanīya) — neither real nor unreal — and extended the description to the world as a whole. This theory of error (anirvacanīyakhyāti) set Advaita against the realist theories of Nyāya and Mīmāṃsā described in Chapter 3.

docs.title: 4.2.2 Levels of Reality
docs.text: Post-Śaṅkara Advaita systematised these ideas into three levels of reality: the ultimate (pāramārthika), which is Brahman alone; the empirical or transactional (vyāvahārika), the world of ordinary experience, valid for all practical purposes but sublated by knowledge of Brahman; and the apparent (prātibhāsika), the world of dreams and illusions, sublated even within ordinary experience. The scheme allowed Advaitins to affirm the practical validity of ordinary knowledge while denying its ultimate truth.

docs.title: 4.2.3 Veiling and Projection
docs.text: Later manuals such as Sadānanda’s Vedāntasāra attribute two powers to ignorance: veiling (āvaraṇa), which conceals the real nature of the self, and projection (vikṣepa), which creates the appearance of something else in its place — as darkness conceals the rope and the mind projects a snake. Whatever its resemblance to accounts of self-deception, the “ignorance” in question is for Advaita a cosmic, beginningless principle, not a defence mechanism of an individual mind.

docs.title: 4.3 The Witness
docs.text:
If every experience is an appearance to consciousness, consciousness itself cannot be one of the appearances. Advaita therefore distinguishes the mind and its modifications, which change constantly, from the witness (sākṣin), the consciousness that is aware of them. The witness is described as:

  • self-luminous (svaprakāśa): it does not need another awareness to be known;

  • unchanging (kūṭastha): it is present unaltered in waking, dream and deep sleep;

  • unattached (asaṅga): it is not affected by the pleasures and pains it witnesses;

  • never an object: it is the knower, never the known.

The doctrine draws on the Upaniṣadic arguments discussed in Chapter 2 and on verses of the Bhagavad Gītā that describe the self as unborn and indestructible:

Bhagavad Gītā 2.20

na jāyate mriyate vā kadācin nāyaṃ bhūtvā bhavitā vā na bhūyaḥ | ajo nityaḥ śāśvato ’yaṃ purāṇo na hanyate hanyamāne śarīre || It is never born and never dies; it did not come into being and will not cease to be. Unborn, eternal, everlasting and primeval, it is not killed when the body is killed.

A careful philosophical study of the witness doctrine is Gupta (1998). The “observing self” of some modern therapies has a different history, drawn partly from Buddhist rather than Vedāntic sources (Section 13.14), and the Advaita doctrine has not been clinically tested.

docs.title: 4.4 The Analysis of the Three States
docs.text:
Advaitins developed the Upaniṣadic analysis of waking, dream and deep sleep (Chapter 2) into a standard method of argument, the “examination of the three states” (avasthātrayaparīkṣā). The method uses the whole of a person’s experience, not only waking life, as evidence about the self. Three steps are typical.

  1. The objects of waking experience are absent in dream, and the objects of dream are absent in waking; each state “sublates” the other. What varies from state to state cannot be the self.

  2. In deep sleep there are no objects at all, yet on waking one says, “I slept happily; I knew nothing.” The Advaitins (especially the Vivaraṇa school) took this remembrance as evidence that in deep sleep there was an experience — of bliss and of ignorance — and therefore an experiencer, since only what has been experienced can be remembered.

  3. The witness that is present in all three states, and that is aware of their coming and going, is the self.

The argument depends on contested premises — above all the claim that the waking report is a memory rather than an inference — and the Naiyāyikas and Buddhists rejected it (Chapter 2). But it is a serious attempt to take the whole range of human experience into account in thinking about the self, and it remains a central teaching method in Advaita.

docs.title: 4.5 The Individual Self
docs.text:
How is the one consciousness related to the many individual selves (jīva)? Advaitins answered with analogies, and the choice of analogy divided the later schools (Table 4.1).

Table 4.1. Analogies for the relation of Brahman and the individual self. Analogy Image Point Rope and snake A rope seen as a snake The individual self is an error superimposed on Brahman Space in a pot (avaccheda) Space enclosed by a pot is not different from space The individual is consciousness “limited” by the mind; developed by Vācaspati Miśra’s Bhāmatī school Reflection (pratibimba) The one sun reflected in many pools The individual is consciousness reflected in the mind; developed by the Vivaraṇa school Dream The dreamer appears as many characters Plurality is an appearance within one consciousness

On either the “limitation” or the “reflection” theory, the mind (antaḥkaraṇa) is what individuates: it is the adjunct (upādhi) through which the one consciousness appears as many. The mind is thus indispensable to the Advaita account of personhood, even though it is, ultimately, not the self.

docs.title: 4.5.1 The Fourfold Inner Instrument
docs.text:
Sāṃkhya names three inner faculties — intellect (buddhi), the I-maker (ahaṃkāra) and the mind (manas) (Section 3.2). The later Vedānta manuals add a fourth, citta, the faculty of memory, to form the fourfold model that is now the best-known Indian description of the mind’s functions.

The fourfold inner instrument (antaḥkaraṇa catuṣṭaya)

manas The mind in the narrow sense: it attends to the reports of the senses and entertains alternatives (saṅkalpa–vikalpa), “is it this or that?”. buddhi The intellect: it ascertains and decides (niścaya, adhyavasāya). ahaṃkāra The “I-maker”: it appropriates experience as “mine” (abhimāna). citta The faculty of memory and stored impressions (smaraṇa).

Sadānanda’s Vedāntasāra (15th century) defines manas and buddhi as two modes (vṛtti) of a single inner organ — the one characterised by doubt, the other by certainty — and assigns citta and ahaṃkāra to them. The point of the scheme is not to locate separate organs but to distinguish functions of one instrument, which in Advaita remains, however subtle, an object of the witness and not the witness itself.

docs.title: 4.6 The Advaita Theory of Perception
docs.text: The most developed Advaita theory of perception is found in Dharmarāja Adhvarin’s Vedāntaparibhāṣā (17th century). In perception, the mind goes out through a sense organ to the object and takes on its form; this “mode” of the mind (vṛtti) removes the ignorance that conceals the object. Consciousness is then present in three forms — as delimited by the object, by the mental mode and by the mind — and when these coincide in one place, the object is directly perceived. The theory is designed to explain how a single, all-pervading consciousness can nonetheless know particular objects at particular times. It shares with the Sāṃkhya and Yoga accounts the idea that the mind “takes the form” of what it knows.

docs.title: 4.7 Means of Knowledge
docs.text: Advaita adopted, with modifications, the epistemology of the Bhāṭṭa school of Mīmāṃsā, which recognised six means of valid knowledge (pramāṇa): perception, inference, comparison (upamāna), verbal testimony (śabda), postulation (arthāpatti) — as when one concludes that a man who is fat but does not eat by day must eat at night — and non-apprehension (anupalabdhi), by which one knows the absence of something. The Vedāntaparibhāṣā discusses each in turn. For Advaita, all of them are valid at the level of everyday experience; but knowledge of Brahman comes only from testimony, the sentences of the Upaniṣads, since Brahman is not an object of perception or inference. The theory gives Advaita a carefully argued place for ordinary knowledge within a philosophy that ultimately denies the reality of plurality.

docs.title: 4.8 The Path of Knowledge
docs.text:
For Advaita, liberation comes through knowledge (jñāna), and knowledge of Brahman comes through the Upaniṣads, studied with a teacher. The student must first be qualified by the fourfold preparation (sādhanacatuṣṭaya):

  1. discrimination between the eternal and the non-eternal (nityānityavastuviveka);

  2. dispassion towards the enjoyment of rewards here and hereafter (ihāmutrārtha­bhoga­virāga);

  3. the six virtues (śamādiṣaṭkasampatti): calm, self-control, withdrawal, forbearance, faith and concentration;

  4. the desire for liberation (mumukṣutva).

The list is an application of the principle of eligibility (adhikāra): a teaching is given only to a student who is ready for it. The Bhagavad Gītā states the qualities of such a student:

Bhagavad Gītā 4.39

śraddhāvāṃl labhate jñānaṃ tatparaḥ saṃyatendriyaḥ | jñānaṃ labdhvā parāṃ śāntim acireṇādhigacchati || The one who has faith, who is intent on it and has mastered the senses, gains knowledge; having gained knowledge, he soon attains the highest peace.

The student then undertakes hearing (śravaṇa), reflection (manana) and contemplation (nididhyāsana). The three verbs come from Yājñavalkya’s words to his wife Maitreyī:

Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.5

ātmā vā are draṣṭavyaḥ śrotavyo mantavyo nididhyāsitavyo maitreyi It is the self, Maitreyī, that should be seen, heard, reflected upon and meditated upon.

Advaita turned them into a discipline: śravaṇa, hearing the teaching from a competent teacher and determining the meaning of the texts; manana, removing doubts by reasoning; and nididhyāsana, sustained contemplation until the understanding becomes stable. A closely similar scheme appears in Buddhist thought, which distinguishes wisdom arising from hearing (śrutamayī), from reflection (cintāmayī) and from meditative cultivation (bhāvanāmayī prajñā); Vasubandhu’s Abhidharmakośa (chapter 6) makes them successive stages of the path. The convergence suggests a widely shared Indian view of how understanding deepens — from received teaching, through critical reflection, to transformed experience — although the Advaita sequence is not a general theory of learning but a prescription for the study of the Upaniṣads by a qualified student. In Śaṅkara’s own view these are not stages of a meditative technique leading to a new experience: knowledge of Brahman arises directly from understanding the Upaniṣadic sentences, and reflection and contemplation serve to remove the doubts and contrary habits that obstruct it. Later Advaitins disagreed about how far contemplation is itself a cause of liberation.

docs.title: 4.8.1 Śaṅkara as Teacher
docs.text: Śaṅkara’s independent work, the Upadeśasāhasrī (“A Thousand Teachings”), whose authenticity is generally accepted, opens its prose part with a chapter on “the method of enlightening the student”. The teacher, Śaṅkara says, should teach this knowledge to a student who has become dispassionate, is calm and self-controlled, has approached him in the prescribed way and has been examined as to his caste, conduct and qualities; he should teach repeatedly, until the student grasps it firmly. The teacher himself should be able to grasp arguments for and against, to retain what he has learned and to explain it, and should be calm, self-controlled, compassionate, free from pride, deceit and envy, and devoted to helping others. The following chapters are dialogues in which a student raises questions about the self, bondage and liberation, and the teacher answers by drawing out the implications of the student’s own experience — the method of reasoned instruction from the student’s standpoint that later Advaita teachers continued.

docs.title: 4.8.2 Knowledge and Meditation
docs.text:
Śaṅkara’s contemporaries and successors argued about the role of meditation in this process. Maṇḍana Miśra, in his Brahmasiddhi, held that the knowledge produced by the Upaniṣadic sentences is at first indirect and verbal, and must be made direct by repeated meditative contemplation (prasaṅkhyāna); Śaṅkara’s pupil Sureśvara rejected this, insisting that the sentences themselves produce direct knowledge in a qualified hearer. The debate concerns a question with obvious psychological interest: whether understanding a truth intellectually is enough to transform a person, or whether a further discipline is needed to make it effective. Later Advaita, as in Vidyāraṇya’s work discussed below, tended in practice to combine study with sustained meditative practice.

Advaitins also distinguished liberation in life (jīvanmukti), in which knowledge has removed ignorance while the body continues to live out the karma that produced it, “like a potter’s wheel that keeps turning after the potter has stopped”, from the final liberation that follows death (videhamukti).

The social limits of this path should be noted. Śaṅkara restricts the study of the Upaniṣads to men of the three upper classes who have undergone initiation; in his commentary on Brahmasūtra 1.3.34–38 he denies that Śūdras are eligible, citing the Dharmasūtra penalties for a Śūdra who hears the Veda (Section 9.12), while allowing that Śūdras may attain knowledge through the epics and Purāṇas. Here the pedagogical sense of adhikāra merges with its social sense, the right to study defined by caste and gender, and presentations that offer adhikāra only as an early version of “readiness for learning” leave out half of its history. Later Advaita teachers and modern exponents such as Vivekananda rejected or reinterpreted these restrictions.

docs.title: 4.9 Desire, Anger and the Collapse of Judgement
docs.text:
The Bhagavad Gītā, which all schools of Vedānta treat as authoritative, contains the best-known Indian analysis of how attachment leads to the loss of judgement:

Bhagavad Gītā 2.62–63

dhyāyato viṣayān puṃsaḥ saṅgas teṣūpajāyate | saṅgāt saṃjāyate kāmaḥ kāmāt krodho ’bhijāyate || krodhād bhavati saṃmohaḥ saṃmohāt smṛtivibhramaḥ | smṛtibhraṃśād buddhināśo buddhināśāt praṇaśyati || When a man dwells on the objects of sense, attachment to them arises; from attachment comes desire, and from desire anger. From anger comes delusion, from delusion the confusion of memory; from the loss of memory the ruin of the intellect, and with the ruin of the intellect he perishes.

The Gītā’s answer to the problem of desire is not the abandonment of action but a change in the motive of action. Kṛṣṇa tells Arjuna:

Bhagavad Gītā 2.47

karmaṇy evādhikāras te mā phaleṣu kadācana | mā karmaphalahetur bhūr mā te saṅgo ’stv akarmaṇi || Your concern is with the action alone, never with its fruits. Do not let the fruit of action be your motive, and do not be attached to inaction.

This is the core of the “discipline of action” (karmayoga): one should do one’s duty with a mind that is even in success and failure (samatva, BG 2.48), offering the action to God and renouncing attachment to its results. Psychologically, the teaching locates freedom not in the absence of activity but in the absence of craving for outcomes; it also, in its original context, urges a warrior to fight and affirms the duties of one’s own social station (svadharma), a point that modern readers — including Gandhi and Ambedkar, who read the Gītā very differently — have debated intensely.

The same chapter describes the opposite condition, the person “of steady wisdom” (sthitaprajña, BG 2.54–72), who has withdrawn the senses from their objects:

Bhagavad Gītā 2.58

yadā saṃharate cāyaṃ kūrmo ’ṅgānīva sarvaśaḥ | indriyāṇīndriyārthebhyas tasya prajñā pratiṣṭhitā || When he withdraws his senses from their objects entirely, as a tortoise draws in its limbs, his wisdom stands firm.

The Gītā also classifies temperaments, foods, kinds of knowledge, action and happiness according to the three guṇas (chapters 14, 17 and 18): sattva is associated with clarity, knowledge and contentment, rajas with desire, activity and restlessness, tamas with confusion, sloth and negligence. The ideal is not the predominance of sattva as such but freedom from all three (nistraiguṇya, BG 2.45). Later Vedāntic and Āyurvedic writers built on this classification, and it remains influential in modern Indian discussions of personality and well-being.

An Upaniṣadic verse, much quoted in Vedāntic literature, sums up the view that bondage and freedom are matters of the mind:

Brahmabindu (Amṛtabindu) Upaniṣad 2

mana eva manuṣyāṇāṃ kāraṇaṃ bandhamokṣayoḥ | bandhāya viṣayāsaktaṃ muktyai nirviṣayaṃ smṛtam || For human beings the mind alone is the cause of bondage and liberation: attached to objects it is held to lead to bondage; free of objects, to liberation.

docs.title: 4.10.1 The Pañcadaśī
docs.text: The Pañcadaśī (“Fifteen Chapters”), attributed to Vidyāraṇya (14th century, associated with the Śṛṅgeri monastery and the early Vijayanagara court), is a widely studied verse manual of Advaita. Its chapters fall into three groups of five: on discrimination (viveka), on illumination (dīpa) and on bliss (ānanda). The last group discusses the bliss of Brahman under the headings of the bliss of yoga, of the self, of non-duality, of knowledge and of objects. It distinguishes the bliss of Brahman experienced in deep sleep, the residual “bliss of impressions” (vāsanānanda) that lingers on waking, and the bliss of objects (viṣayānanda), which it explains as a momentary glimpse of the self’s own bliss when desire is temporarily stilled. The analysis is a philosophical theory of happiness: pleasure from objects is real but derivative, a reflection of the bliss that is the self’s nature.

docs.title: 4.10.2 Liberation in Life: The Jīvanmuktiviveka
docs.text: Vidyāraṇya also wrote the Jīvanmuktiviveka (“Discrimination of Liberation in Life”), a treatise on the condition of one who is liberated while still embodied and on the discipline that leads to it. It argues that knowledge of the truth (tattvajñāna) must be accompanied by two further practices: the “destruction of the mind” (manonāśa), meaning not its annihilation but the cessation of its restless fluctuation, and the “elimination of latent tendencies” (vāsanākṣaya). The three are said to support one another and to be practised together. Vidyāraṇya draws freely on the Yogasūtra and the Yogavāsiṣṭha, and his treatise shows how later Advaita integrated yogic methods of mental discipline into a path that, in principle, depends on knowledge alone. For the history of psychology it is notable as a sustained discussion of how insight, once gained, can be stabilised against the persistence of old habits — a problem that Śaṅkara himself had acknowledged.

docs.title: 4.10.3 The Yogavāsiṣṭha
docs.text: The Yogavāsiṣṭha is a very long dialogue (traditionally of 32,000 verses) between the sage Vasiṣṭha and the young prince Rāma, full of stories in which worlds are revealed within worlds and dreams within dreams. Research by Walter Slaje has shown that it is a Vedāntic reworking (Slaje 1994) of an earlier Kashmiri work, the Mokṣopāya, composed around the tenth century. Its central teaching is that the world is a creation of the mind and that liberation comes through understanding (vicāra) rather than ritual or austerity. Its famous story of Queen Līlā, who travels in consciousness through the worlds contained in her dead husband’s memories, is discussed in Chapter 7. The work also describes seven stages of knowledge (jñānabhūmikā), from right desire (śubhecchā) and inquiry (vicāraṇā) to the “fourth” (turyagā) (Venkatesananda 1984).

docs.title: 4.10.4 The Vivekacūḍāmaṇi
docs.text: The Vivekacūḍāmaṇi (“Crest-jewel of Discrimination”) is a popular verse manual cast as a dialogue between a teacher and a disciple who seeks release from the suffering of transmigration. It is traditionally attributed to Śaṅkara, but most modern scholars regard the attribution as doubtful, partly because its doctrine and vocabulary are closer to later Advaita. It is valued in the tradition for its systematic exposition of the five sheaths, the three bodies and the method of discriminating the self from what it is not (“not this, not this”, neti neti, a phrase from BU 2.3.6). It is sometimes called a “therapeutic” text today; it is better described as a manual of Advaita instruction whose structure — diagnosis of the student’s condition, instruction, practice, realisation — follows the logic of the soteriological path.

docs.title: 4.11 Other Vedāntas
docs.text: Advaita was strongly contested within Vedānta itself, and the rival schools developed psychologies in which individual persons and their emotions are real.

docs.title: 4.11.1 Viśiṣṭādvaita: Rāmānuja
docs.text:
Rāmānuja (traditional dates 1017–1137, which most reference works retain; a later dating to c. 1077–1157 has been proposed but is a minority view) taught a “non-dualism of the qualified”: Brahman, identified with the personal God Viṣṇu–Nārāyaṇa, is one, but includes within himself the real individual selves and the real world as his body. In his Śrībhāṣya Rāmānuja attacked Advaita’s doctrine of ignorance with a series of objections (the “seven untenabilities”), arguing, among other things, that ignorance cannot reside either in Brahman, which is pure knowledge, or in the individual self, which is itself supposed to be a product of ignorance. His theory of error is that all cognition is of the real (satkhyāti). For Rāmānuja the individual self is a real knower whose knowledge expands and contracts, and liberation is a state of loving service to God; devotion (bhakti), understood as a continuous remembrance, is the means.

Rāmānuja’s account of knowledge differs from Advaita’s in a way that matters for psychology. For him consciousness is not the self’s essence alone but also its attribute: the self is a knower, and its knowledge is an “attributive consciousness” (dharmabhūtajñāna) that flows out towards objects and can expand or contract. In bondage this attributive knowledge is contracted by karma; in liberation it expands to embrace everything. Knowledge is thus always someone’s knowledge of something, and there is no pure, objectless consciousness of the Advaita kind. Rāmānuja also rejected the Advaita ideal of liberation in this life (jīvanmukti): as long as the body continues, he held, karma continues, and full liberation comes only after death.

docs.title: 4.11.2 Dvaita: Madhva
docs.text:
Madhva (c. 1238–1317, the dates argued by B. N. K. Sharma on epigraphic and literary evidence and given in most reference works (Sharma 2000); the Mādhva tradition’s own reckoning gives 1199–1278) taught an uncompromising dualism. There are five real and eternal differences (pañcabheda): between God and souls, God and matter, soul and soul, soul and matter, and matter and matter. Souls are eternally distinct and eternally dependent on God; Madhva even held that souls differ in their intrinsic natures, some being destined for liberation and others not — a doctrine unusual in Indian thought.

Madhva too spoke of a “witness” (sākṣin), but in a sense quite different from that of Advaita: for him the witness is the soul’s own faculty of intuitive awareness, by which it directly and infallibly knows itself, its own states and certain basic truths, such as the reality of time and space. Where the senses and the mind may err, the witness cannot. The same word thus names, in the two schools, the impersonal consciousness of Advaita and an individual soul’s intrinsic faculty of certainty.

Madhva’s theology also had a distinctive account of human difference. Because souls differ in their intrinsic natures, some are fit for liberation, some for continued transmigration and some for eternal darkness, and their dispositions show themselves in their attitudes to God and to truth. The doctrine has been much discussed by modern scholars as an Indian form of predestination; within the tradition it served to explain the observed variety of human character and devotion.

docs.title: 4.11.3 The Devotional Vedāntas
docs.text: The Vedāntas of Nimbārka, Vallabha (1479–1531) and the school of Caitanya (1486–1534) developed theologies of devotion in which emotion is not something to be transcended but the very medium of relation to God. The Caitanya school’s “inconceivable difference-in-identity” (acintyabhedābheda) and Rūpa Gosvāmin’s theory of devotional rasa (Chapter 6) produced an elaborate analysis of the varieties of love. In these traditions the psychology of the devotee — longing, humility, the moods of servant, friend, parent and lover — becomes a central theological subject.

docs.title: 4.12 The Psychology of Devotion
docs.text:
Devotion (bhakti) is the most widespread form of Indian religious life, and its literature contains a rich psychology of emotion. Its roots lie in the Bhagavad Gītā, which offers devotion as a path open to all, “even women, Vaiśyas and Śūdras” (BG 9.32) — a sentence that at once widens access and reflects the hierarchy of its time. From the sixth century onwards the Tamil poet-saints, the Vaiṣṇava Āḻvārs and the Śaiva Nāyaṉmārs, composed hymns in which the devotee’s longing for God is expressed in the language of human love, especially the love of a woman separated from her beloved (viraha). The Bhāgavata Purāṇa (perhaps 9th–10th century) made the love of the cowherd women (gopī) for Kṛṣṇa the model of devotion and listed nine forms of devotional practice:

Bhāgavata Purāṇa 7.5.23

śravaṇaṃ kīrtanaṃ viṣṇoḥ smaraṇaṃ pādasevanam | arcanaṃ vandanaṃ dāsyaṃ sakhyam ātmanivedanam || Hearing about Viṣṇu, singing his praise, remembering him, serving his feet, worshipping him, saluting him, being his servant, being his friend, and offering oneself to him.

The Nāradabhaktisūtra, a later aphoristic text, defines devotion as “supreme love” (paramapremarūpā, sūtra 2) for God and describes its signs: the devotee is absorbed in God, finds all else tasteless, and is “like one intoxicated”. The theologians of the Caitanya school gave the most elaborate analysis, applying the categories of rasa theory to the devotee’s emotions (Chapter 6).

The devotional movements in the regional languages — from the Vārkarī poets of Maharashtra to the sants of north India and the Vīraśaivas of Karnataka — also had a social dimension. Many of their poets came from artisan, peasant or “untouchable” communities, composed in the vernacular rather than Sanskrit, and questioned the value of ritual and caste in the face of devotion. At the same time devotion often coexisted with caste hierarchy in practice, within the devotional communities as well as outside them. The psychology of bhakti — its emphasis on emotion, surrender, longing and the equality of devotees before God — is thus also a social history.

The meeting of Vedānta and devotion with the Sufi psychology of the heart, in Dārā Shukōh’s comparisons and in the poetry of the regional languages, is described in Section 8.4.7.

docs.title: 4.13 Vedānta in Modern Thought
docs.text:
Vedānta, especially Advaita, became in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries the most widely known form of Indian philosophy, largely through the work of Swami Vivekananda (1863–1902), who presented it as a universal religion compatible with science, and through modern teachers such as Ramana Maharshi (1879–1950), whose method of self-inquiry (“Who am I?”) is a simplified form of Advaitic discrimination. Sri Aurobindo (1872–1950) developed an “integral” philosophy in which consciousness evolves through matter, life and mind towards a “supramental” level; his followers have written extensively on its implications for psychology and education (Dalal 2001).

Vedāntic ideas have also influenced Western humanistic and transpersonal psychology. Two cautions apply. First, the Vedānta that reached the West was largely the modern, universalised Vedānta of Vivekananda and his successors, which differs in important respects from that of Śaṅkara. Secondly, the claim that Vedānta “solves” the hard problem of consciousness, or that its account of the witness has been confirmed by therapy research, goes beyond the evidence. Vedānta offers a serious philosophical position — that consciousness is fundamental and cannot be reduced to its objects — which deserves discussion on its merits.

The variety of the Vedāntic schools is itself instructive. Advaita, Viśiṣṭādvaita, Dvaita and the devotional Vedāntas all claimed to interpret the same Upaniṣads, the same Brahmasūtra and the same Gītā, and they reached opposite conclusions about the reality of the individual self, the value of emotion and the nature of liberation. Any presentation of “the Vedāntic view of the mind” should therefore specify which Vedānta is meant.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text:
• Deutsch (1969): a concise philosophical reconstruction of Advaita.

  • Potter (1981): summaries of the works of Śaṅkara and his early followers, with a long introduction.

  • Gupta (1998): the Advaita doctrine of the witness.

  • Dasgupta (1922): still useful for the later Vedāntic schools (volumes 3 and 4 of the full work).

  • Venkatesananda (1984): an abridged translation of the Yogavāsiṣṭha.

docs.title: Chapter 5: Buddhist Psychology
docs.text: manopubbaṅgamā dhammā manoseṭṭhā manomayā | manasā ce paduṭṭhena bhāsati vā karoti vā | tato naṃ dukkham anveti cakkaṃ va vahato padaṃ || Mind goes before all states; mind is their chief; of mind they are made. Speak or act with a mind gone bad, and pain trails after you like the cart-wheel behind the draught-ox’s hoof. — Dhammapada 1

docs.title: 5.1 Introduction
docs.text:
The Buddha, Siddhattha Gotama, lived in the Ganges plain in the fifth century BCE; on the “short chronology” now favoured by most historians he died c. 400 BCE (the older dates 563–483 BCE and the Theravāda dates 624–544 BCE are traditional). His teaching is concerned above all with suffering (dukkha) and its ending, and it locates the origin of suffering in the mind. Over the following fifteen centuries Buddhist scholars developed the most detailed analyses of mental events produced in pre-modern India: the Abhidharma (Pali Abhidhamma) catalogues of mental factors and moments of consciousness, the Yogācāra theory of a “storehouse” consciousness, the Madhyamaka critique of fixed essences, and a vast literature on meditation (Gethin 1998).

The opening verse of the Dhammapada, quoted at the head of this chapter, is often read as a claim that the mind creates the world. The Pali commentary reads it more narrowly: the “states” (dhammā) are the mental factors of feeling, perception and volition that arise together with a moment of consciousness, and “mind” is that consciousness, which leads them as a chief leads followers. Read in this way the verse is a statement about moral psychology: the quality of the mind from which speech and action spring determines what follows from them, a point the Buddha makes elsewhere in the words “it is intention, monks, that I call karma” (cetanāhaṃ bhikkhave kammaṃ vadāmi, Aṅguttara Nikāya 6.63). The verse’s place in Pali literature and its grammar are discussed in Volume 8, Kāvya Kalpalatā, and Volume 10, Śabda Vidyā.

These analyses were produced for a purpose: to support a path of ethical discipline, meditation and insight leading to liberation (nibbāna, Sanskrit nirvāṇa). They rest on doctrines — karma, rebirth, the absence of a permanent self — that are religious commitments as well as philosophical theses. The often-repeated description of the Buddha as “the first psychologist” captures his interest in the mind but obscures this context. This chapter presents the main Buddhist accounts on their own terms; modern research on Buddhist-derived meditation is discussed in Chapter 13. On Buddhist history and institutions more generally see Volume 4 of this series.

docs.title: 5.2 The Four Noble Truths
docs.text:
The Buddha’s first sermon, the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta (Saṃyutta Nikāya 56.11), sets out four “noble truths”: (1) the truth of suffering — birth, ageing, sickness, death, separation from what is dear and, in short, the five aggregates of clinging are suffering; (2) the truth of its origin — craving (taṇhā) for sensual pleasure, for existence and for non-existence; (3) the truth of its cessation — the complete fading away of that craving; and (4) the truth of the path — the Noble Eightfold Path of right view, intention, speech, action, livelihood, effort, mindfulness and concentration.

Buddhist literature itself often compares the Buddha to a physician and his teaching to medicine, and the four truths follow the order of diagnosis, cause, prognosis and treatment. The “disease”, however, is the whole condition of conditioned existence and rebirth, not a particular mental disorder.

docs.title: 5.3 The Five Aggregates and Not-Self
docs.text:
Buddhism analyses the person into five “aggregates” or “heaps” (khandha, Sanskrit skandha; Table 5.1).

Table 5.1. The five aggregates (khandha). Pali Translation Scope rūpa Form, matter The body and the material world vedanā Feeling The pleasant, unpleasant or neutral tone of experience saññā Perception, recognition Identifying and labelling (“blue”, “a friend”) saṅkhāra Volitional formations Intentions and other active mental factors viññāṇa Consciousness Awareness through the six senses

In the Anattalakkhaṇa Sutta (Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.59), traditionally the Buddha’s second discourse, each aggregate is examined in turn: if form were the self, it would not lead to affliction and one could say “let my form be thus”; but form is impermanent, what is impermanent is unsatisfactory, and what is impermanent and unsatisfactory is not fit to be regarded as “this is mine, this I am, this is my self”. The same reasoning is applied to feeling, perception, formations and consciousness. The conclusion is not that there is no person in any sense — the Buddha uses personal language freely — but that nothing in experience answers to the idea of a permanent, independent, controlling self.

docs.title: 5.3.1 The “Person” Controversy
docs.text: The doctrine of not-self was not accepted in the same form by all Buddhists. One group of early schools, the Pudgalavādins (“proponents of the person”), of whom the Vātsīputrīyas and Sāṃmitīyas were the best known, held that there is a “person” (pudgala) that is neither identical with the aggregates nor different from them, and that is needed to explain who transmigrates, who remembers and who attains liberation. The other schools regarded this as a return to the self by the back door, and Vasubandhu devoted the ninth chapter of his Abhidharmakośabhāṣya to refuting it. The Pudgalavāda was nonetheless widespread: Xuanzang found the Sāṃmitīya school to be among the most numerous in India in the seventh century. The controversy shows that the problem of personal identity was debated within Buddhism as fiercely as between Buddhists and Brahmins.

docs.title: 5.4 Dependent Origination
docs.text:
The doctrine of dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda, Sanskrit pratītyasamutpāda) explains how suffering arises from conditions. Its standard form has twelve links (Table 5.2).

Table 5.2. The twelve links of dependent origination. Pali Translation Gloss 1 avijjā Ignorance Not knowing the four truths 2 saṅkhārā Formations Volitional activity, karma 3 viññāṇa Consciousness Including the consciousness that links to a new life 4 nāmarūpa Name-and-form The psycho-physical person 5 saḷāyatana Six sense bases Eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, mind 6 phassa Contact Meeting of sense, object and consciousness 7 vedanā Feeling Pleasant, unpleasant, neutral 8 taṇhā Craving For sense pleasures, existence, non-existence 9 upādāna Clinging Grasping at pleasures, views, rules, self 10 bhava Becoming The process leading to rebirth 11 jāti Birth 12 jarāmaraṇa Ageing and death With sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, despair

A well-known discourse, the Sallatha Sutta (“The Arrow”, Saṃyutta Nikāya 36.6), illustrates the point with an image. When an untaught person is touched by a painful bodily feeling, he grieves, laments and becomes distraught; he thus feels two feelings, a bodily one and a mental one, like a man struck by one arrow and then by a second. The well-taught disciple, touched by the same painful feeling, does not grieve or lament: he feels only the bodily feeling, “one arrow”. The discourse adds that the untaught person, struck by pain, seeks relief in sensual pleasure because he knows no other escape, and so strengthens the underlying tendencies to lust and aversion. The distinction between pain and the suffering added to it by reaction has become central to modern mindfulness-based pain programmes, which have drawn on it explicitly.

The commentarial tradition reads the twelve links as spanning three lives, but the sequence also lends itself to a reading in terms of a single moment of experience, and much contemporary meditation teaching emphasises the junction between feeling and craving: a pleasant feeling tends to provoke craving, an unpleasant one aversion, and mindfulness of feeling is said to allow the practitioner to notice the feeling without being carried into the reaction. This “present-moment” reading is a legitimate development of the texts, though it is not the only traditional one.

docs.title: 5.5 The Abhidharma
docs.text: In the centuries after the Buddha, monastic scholars systematised the teachings into the Abhidharma (“higher teaching”), which analyses all experience into its ultimate constituents (dhamma, Sanskrit dharma) and specifies how they combine and condition one another. Two Abhidharma traditions survive in full: the Theravāda, whose canonical Abhidhammapiṭaka in seven books was given a standard summary in Anuruddha’s Abhidhammatthasaṅgaha (probably 11th–12th century) (Bodhi 1993); and the Sarvāstivāda, whose system is best known from Vasubandhu’s Abhidharmakośa and its auto-commentary (4th–5th century) (Vasubandhu 1988–1990).

docs.title: 5.5.1 Consciousness and Its Factors
docs.text:
The Theravāda Abhidhamma distinguishes four kinds of ultimate reality: consciousness (citta), mental factors (cetasika), matter (rūpa, of 28 kinds) and the unconditioned, nibbāna. Consciousness is the bare knowing of an object; it never occurs alone but always with a set of mental factors that give each moment its specific character. Consciousness is classified into 89 types (or 121, when the supramundane types are counted in relation to the meditative absorptions; Table 5.3).

Table 5.3. The 89 types of consciousness (citta) of the Theravāda Abhidhamma. Sphere Number Subdivisions Sense sphere (kāmāvacara) 54 12 unwholesome, 18 rootless, 24 beautiful Fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara) 15 5 wholesome, 5 resultant, 5 functional Immaterial sphere (arūpāvacara) 12 4 wholesome, 4 resultant, 4 functional Supramundane (lokuttara) 8 4 path, 4 fruition (40 in the expanded count) Total 89 (121 in the expanded count)

The 52 mental factors fall into four groups (Table 5.4).

Table 5.4. The 52 mental factors (cetasika) of the Theravāda Abhidhamma. Group No. Members Universals 7 Contact, feeling, perception, volition, one-pointedness, life faculty, attention Occasionals 6 Applied thought (vitakka), sustained thought (vicāra), decision, energy, zest (pīti), desire to act (chanda) Unwholesome 14 Delusion, shamelessness, fearlessness of wrongdoing, restlessness; greed, wrong view, conceit; hatred, envy, avarice, remorse; sloth, torpor; doubt Beautiful 25 19 universal beautiful factors (faith, mindfulness, shame, fear of wrongdoing, non-greed, non-hatred, equanimity, and six pairs of tranquillity, lightness, malleability, wieldiness, proficiency and rectitude of body and mind); 3 abstinences; 2 illimitables (compassion, sympathetic joy); wisdom

The first two groups (thirteen factors) are “ethically variable”: they take on the quality of the consciousness they accompany. Combinatorial rules state which factors can occur together — greed and hatred, for example, never arise in the same moment, while every unwholesome consciousness contains delusion — and the 89 types of consciousness are defined by their factor profiles. The Sarvāstivāda system, as presented in the Abhidharmakośa, counts 46 mental factors in a different arrangement.

The Abhidharma’s list of universal factors amounts to a theory of the minimal structure of any moment of experience: there is always an object contacted, a hedonic tone, a recognition, an intention, a degree of focus, a sustaining vitality and an orientation of attention. The analysis was arrived at through doctrinal reasoning and introspective practice, and it has interested phenomenologists and cognitive scientists (Thompson 2015); it remains a scholastic system with its own aims. Maria Heim has shown how Buddhaghosa’s commentaries use this analysis to develop a sophisticated account of intention and agency (Heim 2014), and C. A. F. Rhys Davids’s Buddhist Psychology remains a pioneering, if dated, survey of the Pali material (Rhys Davids 1914).

docs.title: 5.5.2 The Sarvāstivāda Scheme
docs.text:
The Sarvāstivāda school, dominant in north-west India and Kashmir, classified all phenomena into seventy-five dharmas in five groups, as set out in Vasubandhu’s Abhidharmakośa (Vasubandhu 1988–1990) (Table 5.5).

Table 5.5. The seventy-five dharmas of the Sarvāstivāda (after the Abhidharmakośa). Group No. Contents Matter (rūpa) 11 Five sense organs, five sense objects, and “unmanifest” matter (avijñapti) Mind (citta) 1 Consciousness Mental factors (caitta) 46 Universal, wholesome, defiled, unwholesome, minor defilements and indeterminate factors Factors dissociated from mind (cittaviprayukta) 14 E.g. possession (prāpti), life-force, the marks of arising and ceasing, names and phrases Unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) 3 Space, and two kinds of cessation (including nirvāṇa) Total 75

The school’s name, “those who say everything exists”, refers to its distinctive doctrine that dharmas exist in the past and future as well as the present — a doctrine designed to explain memory and the delayed effects of karma without a self, and vigorously contested by the Sautrāntikas.

docs.title: 5.5.3 The Cognitive Process
docs.text:
The Theravāda commentaries describe perception as a series of mind-moments. In the case of a strong object presented at one of the five sense doors, the process has seventeen moments (Figure 5.1):

Figure 5.1. The seventeen mind-moments of a complete five-door cognitive process in the Theravāda commentaries.

  1. a passing moment of the life-continuum (atīta bhavaṅga);

  2. vibration of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga calana);

  3. arrest of the life-continuum (bhavaṅgupaccheda);

  4. adverting to the five sense doors (pañcadvārāvajjana);

  5. the relevant sense consciousness (e.g. eye-consciousness);

  6. receiving (sampaṭicchana);

  7. investigating (santīraṇa);

  8. determining (voṭṭhapana);

  9. seven moments of “impulsion” (javana), in which the karmically significant response occurs;

  10. two moments of registration (tadārammaṇa),

after which the mind lapses back into the life-continuum. The commentaries say that the whole process takes place in an instant, many such moments arising and passing in the time of a finger-snap. They illustrate it with the simile of a man asleep under a mango tree: a ripe mango falls beside him (the object strikes the sense door); he wakes (adverting), sees it (eye-consciousness), picks it up (receiving), examines it (investigating), decides that it is ripe (determining), eats it (impulsion), swallows the last morsels (registration), and goes back to sleep (life-continuum).

docs.title: 5.5.4 The Life-Continuum
docs.text: The life-continuum (bhavaṅga) is the passive flow of consciousness that continues whenever no active cognitive process is taking place — in dreamless sleep and between perceptions. It is a resultant consciousness, determined by the karma that produced the present life, and it maintains the continuity of the individual stream without requiring a permanent self. It is defined within a theory of karma and rebirth, which limits any comparison with the unconscious or with resting brain activity (Section 1.10).

docs.title: 5.5.5 The Theory of Conditions
docs.text: The last and largest book of the Theravāda Abhidhammapiṭaka, the Paṭṭhāna (“Conditional Relations”), analyses how phenomena condition one another in twenty-four kinds of relation (paccaya). They include the relation of root (hetu) — greed, hatred and delusion and their opposites as the roots of action; of object (ārammaṇa); of predominance (adhipati); of contiguity and immediate succession (anantara, samanantara), by which each moment of consciousness gives rise to the next; of co-arising and mutuality (sahajāta, aññamañña); of support and decisive support (nissaya, upanissaya); of repetition (āsevana), by which a mental state is strengthened by recurring; of karma and its result; of nutriment, faculty, absorption and path; of association and dissociation; and of presence, absence, disappearance and non-disappearance. The scheme is an attempt to state, without reference to a self, all the ways in which mental and physical events can influence one another — including, in the condition of repetition, a principle of habit formation (Bodhi 1993).

docs.title: 5.5.6 Latent Tendencies
docs.text: The Pali texts speak of seven latent tendencies (anusaya): sensual lust, aversion, views, doubt, conceit, lust for existence and ignorance (Aṅguttara Nikāya 7.11–12). They lie dormant and become active when conditions provoke them; the path aims to uproot them, not merely to suppress their outbreaks. The concept occupies in Buddhist thought something like the place that saṃskāra and vāsanā occupy in Yoga.

docs.title: 5.5.7 Momentariness
docs.text: Most Abhidharma schools held that all conditioned things, mental and material, are momentary (khaṇika), arising, enduring for an instant and ceasing; the apparent continuity of a person or a thing is a series of causally connected moments. The Sautrāntikas and later Buddhist logicians argued that a thing perishes in the very moment of its arising. The doctrine of momentariness was attacked at length by Nyāya and Mīmāṃsā philosophers, who argued that memory and recognition (“this is the same pot I saw yesterday”) require an enduring self.

docs.title: 5.6 Yogācāra: The Storehouse Consciousness
docs.text:
The Yogācāra school, associated with the brothers Asaṅga and Vasubandhu (4th–5th century CE), held that what we experience as external objects are representations (vijñapti) in consciousness. To explain how karma, memory and the continuity of the person work without a self and without external objects, it introduced the “storehouse consciousness” (ālayavijñāna) (Waldron 2003; Lusthaus 2002), the eighth of the consciousnesses listed in Table 5.6.

Table 5.6. The eight consciousnesses of Yogācāra. Consciousness Function 1–5 Five sense consciousnesses Seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, touching 6 Mental consciousness (manovijñāna) Thought, judgement, imagination; cognises the objects of the other senses 7 Afflicted mind (kliṣṭamanas) Constantly takes the storehouse consciousness as “I” 8 Storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) Holds the “seeds” (bīja) of all experience; continuous, subliminal, morally neutral

Vasubandhu’s Triṃśikā (“Thirty Verses”) describes the transformation (pariṇāma) of consciousness in three forms: the storehouse consciousness, which ripens as the result of past actions; the afflicted mind, which “thinks” it as a self; and the six active consciousnesses, which present objects. Every experience “perfumes” the storehouse with seeds (bīja) that later ripen into further experience. Liberation is described as a “transformation of the basis” (āśrayaparāvṛtti) in which the storehouse is purified.

Yogācāra also analysed experience in terms of three natures (trisvabhāva): the imagined nature (parikalpita), the world as falsely constructed into subjects and objects; the dependent nature (paratantra), the flow of causally conditioned mental events; and the perfected nature (pariniṣpanna), the dependent nature empty of the imagined.

The ālayavijñāna is often likened to the Freudian or Jungian unconscious, but Waldron (2003) has shown that it is better understood within its own context: it was introduced to solve specific problems in Abhidharma theory — the continuity of the mind in deep meditative states and between lives, the persistence of latent tendencies — and its “contents” are karmic seeds rather than repressed wishes or archetypes.

docs.title: 5.7 The Epistemologists: Perception and Concept
docs.text:
From the sixth century, the Buddhist epistemologists Dignāga and Dharmakīrti developed a theory of knowledge that profoundly influenced all Indian philosophy (Matilal 1986). They recognised only two means of valid knowledge: perception (pratyakṣa) and inference (anumāna). Perception, Dignāga held, is “free from conceptual construction” (kalpanāpoḍha): it grasps the unique, momentary particular (svalakṣaṇa). Everything that involves concepts and words — recognising the thing as a pot, as blue, as the same pot as yesterday — is a construction of the mind that grasps only universals, which are themselves mental constructs defined by exclusion (apoha). The theory sharply distinguishes the given from the constructed in experience, and its implications for the psychology of perception were debated for centuries.

The epistemologists also held, as described in Chapter 2, that every cognition is aware of itself (svasaṃvedana), and some of them argued for a form of idealism. Their works became the core of the curriculum in logic at Nālandā and in the Tibetan monastic colleges that inherited it (Chapter 11).

docs.title: 5.8 Madhyamaka: Emptiness
docs.text:
Nāgārjuna (c. 2nd century CE), founder of the Madhyamaka (“middle”) school, argued in his Mūlamadhyamakakārikā that nothing, including the Abhidharma’s ultimate constituents, has intrinsic nature (svabhāva). Everything is “empty” (śūnya) because everything arises dependently.

Nāgārjuna, Mūlamadhyamakakārikā 24.18

yaḥ pratītyasamutpādaḥ śūnyatāṃ tāṃ pracakṣmahe | sā prajñaptir upādāya pratipat saiva madhyamā || Dependent origination is what we call emptiness. That is a dependent designation; it is itself the middle way.

Chapter 18 of the same work examines the self: if the self were identical with the aggregates, it would arise and perish like them; if it were different from them, it would be without their characteristics. Later Mādhyamikas such as Candrakīrti (7th century) developed the classic “sevenfold” analysis of the chariot and its parts to show that a person is a conventional designation dependent on the aggregates, real for practical purposes but without an intrinsic essence (Garfield 1995).

A psychological moral is easily drawn: if one’s states and self-image are dependently arisen, they are not fixed. The inference is fair, but the Madhyamaka argument itself is metaphysical and soteriological, aimed at the uprooting of all grasping, including grasping at emptiness.

docs.title: 5.9.1 Sati
docs.text:
The Pali word sati (Sanskrit smṛti) originally means “memory”, and in Buddhist usage it denotes the keeping in mind of the present object and of what is wholesome and unwholesome. The Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta (Majjhima Nikāya 10; also Dīgha Nikāya 22 in an expanded form) sets out four “establishments of mindfulness” (Table 5.7). Its opening sentence, which calls them the ekāyana path to purification and to the ending of sorrow, grief and pain, is discussed with the rest of the discourse in Volume 4, Buddha–Jina Prabhā; the older rendering “the only way” has largely given place to “the direct path” or “the path that goes to one point” (Ñāṇamoli and Bodhi 1995).

What interests the psychologist is the method. The same instruction recurs for each object: the practitioner observes it “internally” and “externally”, watches it arising and passing away, and establishes mindfulness “only to the extent needed for knowledge and recollection”, dwelling “independent, not clinging to anything in the world”. Mindfulness here is not a free-floating awareness but a disciplined observation of particular objects, directed by doctrine (the body as composed of parts and elements, feelings as pleasant or unpleasant, the mind as with or without lust) towards seeing them as impermanent and not-self.

Table 5.7. The four establishments of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna). Domain Pali Contemplations Body kāyānupassanā Breathing, postures, clear comprehension of activities, parts of the body, elements, the stages of a corpse Feelings vedanānupassanā Pleasant, unpleasant and neutral feelings, worldly and unworldly Mind cittānupassanā The state of mind: with or without lust, hatred, delusion; contracted or distracted; concentrated or not Dhammas dhammānupassanā The hindrances, aggregates, sense bases, factors of awakening, four truths

docs.title: 5.9.2 Calm and Insight
docs.text: Buddhist texts distinguish two aspects of meditative development: calm (samatha), which unifies the mind through concentration and leads to the meditative absorptions (jhāna), and insight (vipassanā), which sees phenomena as impermanent, unsatisfactory and not-self. The four jhānas are described by the progressive dropping away of factors: applied and sustained thought, then zest, then happiness, leaving equanimity and one-pointedness. Whether insight requires prior absorption, and how the two relate, has been debated within the tradition and in modern scholarship.

docs.title: 5.9.3 Training Attention: The Nine Stages
docs.text: Mahāyāna manuals of meditation analysed the training of attention in fine detail. A scheme found in Asaṅga’s Śrāvakabhūmi and in the Mahāyānasūtrālaṅkāra describes nine stages in the stabilisation of the mind (cittasthiti), from first placing the mind on its object, through continuous and repeated placement, close placement, taming, pacifying and thorough pacifying, to one-pointedness and finally effortless equipoise. The Madhyāntavibhāga lists five faults that obstruct calm — laziness, forgetting the instructions, sinking and agitation, failure to apply a remedy, and over-application of a remedy — together with eight antidotes, among them faith, aspiration, effort, mindfulness and vigilant awareness. Kamalaśīla’s Bhāvanākrama (8th century), composed for the Tibetan court, sets out the stages of calm and insight on this basis. These texts show a detailed practical knowledge of the vicissitudes of attention — dullness and excitement, the need for both effort and relaxation — developed for the purposes of meditation.

docs.title: 5.9.4 Wholesome Desire and Right Effort
docs.text: Buddhism is often summarised as teaching the elimination of desire, but its psychology is more discriminating. It distinguishes craving (taṇhā), which binds, from the “desire to act” (chanda), one of the ethically variable mental factors, which can be wholesome: the desire to practise, to understand and to attain liberation is necessary for the path. The “four right efforts” (sammappadhāna) describe how that energy should be directed: to prevent unwholesome states that have not yet arisen, to abandon those that have arisen, to develop wholesome states that have not yet arisen, and to maintain and increase those that have. The scheme recognises that mental training involves both restraint and cultivation, and that the will to change is itself a mental state that can be strengthened.

docs.title: 5.9.5 Hindrances and Factors of Awakening
docs.text: The Pali discourses list five “hindrances” (nīvaraṇa) that obstruct concentration: sensual desire, ill will, sloth and torpor, restlessness and remorse, and doubt. The texts compare a mind freed of them to a man released from debt, recovered from illness, freed from prison, freed from slavery and safely across a desert. Opposed to the hindrances are the seven “factors of awakening” (bojjhaṅga): mindfulness, investigation of phenomena, energy, joy, tranquillity, concentration and equanimity. The texts advise that when the mind is sluggish one should cultivate investigation, energy and joy, and when it is agitated, tranquillity, concentration and equanimity — an early example of matching a remedy to a mental state.

docs.title: 5.9.6 Stages of the Path
docs.text: The Buddhist path is described as a sequence of attainments in which “fetters” (saṃyojana) are progressively destroyed. The “stream-enterer” (sotāpanna) has abandoned belief in a permanent self, doubt and attachment to rules and rituals; the “once-returner” has weakened sensual desire and ill will; the “non-returner” has abandoned them; and the arahant has abandoned the subtler fetters of desire for refined existence, conceit, restlessness and ignorance. The scheme amounts to a developmental account of the person in terms of the weakening of particular cognitive and emotional dispositions. In the Mahāyāna traditions it was supplemented or replaced by the path of the bodhisattva, who seeks awakening for the sake of all beings and passes through ten stages (bhūmi).

docs.title: 5.9.7 Matching Practice to Temperament
docs.text:
Buddhaghosa’s Visuddhimagga (5th century; (Buddhaghosa 1956)) classifies practitioners into six temperaments (carita) and recommends meditation subjects for each (Visuddhimagga III; Table 5.8).

Table 5.8. The six temperaments (carita) of the Visuddhimagga and suitable subjects of meditation. Temperament Suitable subjects (selection) Greedy (rāga) The ten kinds of foulness; mindfulness of the body Hating (dosa) The four divine abidings; the four colour kasiṇas Deluded (moha) Mindfulness of breathing Faithful (saddhā) The first six recollections (of the Buddha, Dhamma, Saṅgha, virtue, generosity, deities) Intelligent (buddhi) Recollection of death and of peace; the defining of the four elements; repulsiveness of food Speculative (vitakka) Mindfulness of breathing

The principle that teaching should be matched to the student is a recurrent theme in Indian pedagogy (Section 4.8), and Buddhist tradition describes the Buddha himself as adapting his teaching to his audience (upāya, “skilful means”).

docs.title: 5.9.8 The Divine Abidings
docs.text:
The four “divine abidings” (brahmavihāra) or “immeasurables” are loving-kindness (mettā), compassion (karuṇā), sympathetic joy (muditā) and equanimity (upekkhā). The Visuddhimagga (IX) identifies for each a “far enemy”, its opposite, and a “near enemy”, a state that resembles it and can be mistaken for it (Table 5.9).

Table 5.9. The divine abidings and their “enemies” according to the Visuddhimagga. Abiding Near enemy Far enemy Loving-kindness Greed (attached affection) Ill will Compassion Grief based on worldly life Cruelty Sympathetic joy Worldly joy (exhilaration) Aversion, discontent Equanimity Equanimity of unknowing (indifference) Greed and resentment

The analysis of “near enemies” is a subtle piece of moral psychology: it recognises that a counterfeit of a virtue may be harder to detect than its opposite. Modern research groups have studied compassion and loving-kindness training adapted from these practices; that research and its limits are discussed in Chapter 13.

docs.title: 5.10 Working with Emotion: Śāntideva
docs.text:
The Mahāyāna poet-philosopher Śāntideva (8th century), traditionally associated with Nālandā, wrote in his Bodhicaryāvatāra (“Entering the Path of Awakening”) one of the most influential Buddhist treatments of the emotions. Its sixth chapter, on patience (kṣānti), analyses anger. Anger, Śāntideva argues, destroys the merit of aeons; it arises from frustration; and it rests on a misunderstanding of causation. If I am struck with a stick, I do not blame the stick but the person who wields it; yet that person is himself driven by anger, as the stick is driven by his hand, so I should rather direct my anger at anger itself. An enemy, moreover, is a rare opportunity to practise patience, and so a kind of benefactor. The chapter is a sustained exercise in cognitive reappraisal, aimed not at suppressing anger but at undermining the judgements on which it rests.

The eighth chapter, on meditation, develops the practices of “equalising self and others” and “exchanging self and others” (parātmasamatā, parātmaparivartana): since suffering is bad whoever it belongs to, there is no reason to prefer the removal of my own suffering to that of another’s, and one should train oneself to regard others’ welfare as one’s own. These ideas became the basis of the Tibetan “mind-training” (blo sbyong) literature, which has been a source for modern compassion-training programmes. Śāntideva’s work shows the Buddhist analysis of mind applied to the transformation of emotion through argument and imagination.

docs.title: 5.11 Assessment
docs.text:
Buddhist psychology offers a non-substantial account of the person, a detailed taxonomy of mental states and their ethical qualities, a theory of how experience conditions later experience, and a body of practical methods for training attention and emotion. These contributions are widely recognised. Their transfer into modern clinical contexts — above all through mindfulness-based programmes — has been productive, but it has also involved simplification: the removal of ethical and doctrinal context, the redefinition of sati as non-judgemental awareness, and claims for clinical effectiveness that sometimes outrun the evidence. A historical presentation should keep these two things distinct: what the Buddhist texts teach, and what modern adaptations of them have been shown to do.

It should also remember that Buddhist psychology developed in India over some fifteen centuries, in debate with Brahmanical, Jain and materialist rivals, and that its later history unfolded largely outside India — in Sri Lanka, Southeast Asia, Tibet, China, Korea and Japan. The Abhidharma, the Yogācāra and the meditation manuals discussed in this chapter are part of India’s intellectual heritage even though, after the decline of Buddhism in India, they were preserved and developed mainly by others.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text:
