  • Bodhi (1993): the Abhidhammatthasaṅgaha with explanatory guide and charts; the clearest presentation of the Theravāda Abhidhamma.

  • Buddhaghosa (1956): translation of the Visuddhimagga; Ñāṇamoli and Bodhi (1995) for the Majjhima Nikāya, including the Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta.

  • Vasubandhu (1988–1990): English translation of the Abhidharmakośabhāṣya.

  • Waldron (2003) and Lusthaus (2002): the Yogācāra theory of mind.

  • Garfield (1995): translation and commentary of Nāgārjuna’s Mūla­madhyamaka­kārikā.

  • Warder (2000): a history of Indian Buddhism and its schools.

docs.title: Chapter 6: Rasa: Emotion and Aesthetic Experience
docs.text: na hi rasād ṛte kaścid arthaḥ pravartate For no meaning proceeds without rasa. — Nāṭyaśāstra, chapter 6 (prose following verse 31)

docs.title: 6.1 Introduction
docs.text:
The most detailed analysis of emotion in classical Indian literature is found not in a philosophical or medical text but in a treatise on theatre. The Nāṭyaśāstra, attributed to the sage Bharata, is a compilation whose main body is usually dated between about 200 BCE and 200 CE (Ghosh 1950). Its sixth and seventh chapters set out a theory of how a performance produces in its audience a distinctive aesthetic experience, called rasa — literally “taste”, “flavour” or “essence” — and in doing so they classify the emotions, their causes, their bodily expressions and their accompanying transient states. Over the following millennium the theory was debated and refined by the theorists of poetry, culminating in the work of the Kashmiri philosopher Abhinavagupta (c. 950–1016), who made it the basis of a philosophy of aesthetic consciousness.

This chapter presents rasa theory as a contribution to the understanding of emotion. Its fuller place in the history of literature and theatre is treated in Volumes 8 and 9 of this series.

docs.title: 6.2 The Rasa-Sūtra
docs.text:
The core of the theory is a single sentence in prose:

Nāṭyaśāstra, chapter 6 (prose following v. 31)

vibhāvānubhāvavyabhicārisaṃyogād rasaniṣpattiḥ Rasa arises from the combination of the determinants, the consequents and the transitory states.

  • The determinants (vibhāva) are the causes of an emotion as represented on stage: the characters and situations that occasion it. Later theorists distinguished the “supporting” determinant (ālambana), such as the beloved in love, from the “stimulating” determinant (uddīpana), such as moonlight or a garden.

  • The consequents (anubhāva) are the outward signs by which the emotion is expressed and recognised: glances, gestures, changes of voice.

  • The transitory states (vyabhicāribhāva, also sañcāribhāva) are passing emotional and physical conditions that accompany and colour the dominant emotion.

When these are combined in a performance, the “stable emotion” (sthāyibhāva) latent in the spectator is brought to the condition of rasa (Figure 6.1). Bharata explains the term by an analogy with food: just as a discerning person, eating food prepared with various spices, tastes its flavours and feels pleasure, so cultured spectators “taste” the stable emotions brought out by the various elements of a performance.

Figure 6.1. The rasa-sūtra of the Nāṭyaśāstra as a process: the three elements presented on stage combine to awaken the stable emotion latent in the spectator, which is relished as rasa. The terms vāsanā and sahṛdaya, and the idea of generalisation, come from the later theorists, above all Abhinavagupta (Section 6.8).

docs.title: 6.3 The Stable Emotions and Their Rasas
docs.text:
Bharata lists eight rasas, each grounded in a stable emotion. Each is also assigned a colour and a presiding deity (Nāṭyaśāstra 6.42–45; Table 6.1).

Table 6.1. The rasas, their stable emotions, colours and deities in the Nāṭyaśāstra. Rasa Stable emotion Colour Deity śṛṅgāra (erotic) rati (love) śyāma (dark) Viṣṇu hāsya (comic) hāsa (laughter) sita (white) Pramatha karuṇa (pathetic) śoka (sorrow) kapota (dove-grey) Yama raudra (furious) krodha (anger) rakta (red) Rudra vīra (heroic) utsāha (energy) gaura (pale gold) Mahendra bhayānaka (fearful) bhaya (fear) kṛṣṇa (black) Kāla bībhatsa (odious) jugupsā (disgust) nīla (blue) Mahākāla adbhuta (marvellous) vismaya (astonishment) pīta (yellow) Brahmā śānta (tranquil) śama or nirveda (later additions) (later additions)

docs.title: 6.3.1 The Debate over Śānta
docs.text: Whether there is a ninth, “tranquil” rasa was one of the great debates of Indian aesthetics. The critical edition of the Nāṭyaśāstra lists eight; some manuscripts contain a passage on śānta which is generally regarded as an interpolation. Udbhaṭa (c. 800) is the first known theorist to count nine, and Ānandavardhana argued that the dominant rasa of the Mahābhārata is śānta. Opponents objected that tranquillity, the cessation of all emotion, cannot be represented on stage or relished. Abhinavagupta defended śānta at length, identifying its stable emotion with the knowledge of truth (tattvajñāna) or the self, and arguing that it is in a sense the ground of all the other rasas (Masson and Patwardhan 1969). After him the “nine rasas” (navarasa) became standard.

docs.title: 6.4 The Classification of Emotional States
docs.text:
Besides the eight stable emotions, Bharata lists thirty-three transitory states and eight “involuntary” or “sāttvika” states — forty-nine bhāvas in all. The transitory states are listed in Table 6.2.

Table 6.2. The thirty-three transitory states (vyabhicāribhāva) of the Nāṭyaśāstra. Term Translation Term Translation nirveda despondency garva pride glāni weakness viṣāda despair śaṅkā apprehension autsukya longing, impatience asūyā envy nidrā sleepiness mada intoxication apasmāra epileptic fit śrama weariness supta dreaming ālasya indolence vibodha awakening dainya dejection amarṣa indignation cintā anxiety avahitthā dissimulation moha distraction, bewilderment ugratā ferocity smṛti recollection mati resolve, understanding dhṛti contentment vyādhi sickness vrīḍā shame unmāda madness capalatā inconstancy maraṇa death harṣa joy trāsa fright āvega agitation vitarka deliberation jaḍatā stupor

The eight sāttvika states — freezing, sweating, gooseflesh, a breaking voice, trembling, change of colour, tears and fainting (stambha, sveda, romāñca, svarabheda, vepathu, vaivarṇya, aśru, pralaya) — are psychologically the most interesting of Bharata’s lists (its performance technique is treated in Volume 9, Saṅgīta–Nāṭya). These are the signs that the body gives of strong feeling without the person willing them; a modern psychologist would call them autonomic. Bharata’s name for them reflects his view that they cannot be faked by technique alone: the actor must produce them from an absorbed, concentrated mind (sattva). The theory thus recognises a layer of emotion below voluntary control, and treats access to it as a matter of trained inner attention.

The classification is notable for its range. It includes emotions in the narrow sense (envy, shame, joy, anxiety), cognitive states (recollection, deliberation, resolve), bodily states (weariness, sickness, sleepiness) and extreme conditions (madness, death) — everything, in short, that an actor might have to represent. For each state Bharata gives its determinants and the means of representing it. The Nāṭyaśāstra’s interest is practical: it is a manual for performers, and its analysis of emotion is an analysis of how emotion is caused, expressed and recognised.

docs.title: 6.5 The Actor’s Craft
docs.text:
Because the Nāṭyaśāstra is a manual for performers, its analysis of emotion is tied to a detailed account of how emotion is represented. Representation (abhinaya) is of four kinds: bodily (āṅgika), through movements of the head, eyes, eyebrows, hands, feet and body; verbal (vācika), through speech, song, intonation and metre; “ornamental” (āhārya), through costume, make-up and stage properties; and “involuntary” (sāttvika), through the bodily signs of genuine feeling described above. The text catalogues dozens of glances, each suited to a particular emotion, and many single and combined hand gestures (hasta) that became the basis of the gestural vocabulary of Indian classical dance.

The analysis presupposes a view about emotion and its expression: that emotions have characteristic outward signs, which can be learned, reproduced and recognised by others, and that a skilled performer can evoke in an audience an emotion that he does not himself feel in the ordinary way. Later theorists debated whether the actor himself experiences rasa; Abhinavagupta held that he can, as a spectator of his own performance, but that his task is to present the determinants and consequents, not to suffer the emotion. The question is close to the modern debate about whether actors should “live” or “present” the emotions of their roles.

docs.title: 6.6 Situations of Love: The Heroines
docs.text:
The Nāṭyaśāstra and later works on drama and poetry, such as Dhanañjaya’s Daśarūpaka (10th century), classify heroines (nāyikā) according to their situation in love. The best-known list has eight: the woman whose lover is devoted to her (svādhīnapatikā), the woman dressed and waiting for her lover (vāsakasajjā), the woman longing in separation (virahotkaṇṭhitā), the woman who finds her lover unfaithful (khaṇḍitā), the woman who has quarrelled with him and repents (kalahāntaritā), the woman disappointed when he fails to come (vipralabdhā), the woman whose lover is abroad (proṣitapriyā), and the woman who goes out to meet him (abhisārikā).

The classification is a typology of emotional situations rather than of personalities: each defines a constellation of circumstances, feelings and expressions that poets, painters and dancers could represent. It was immensely productive in later Indian art, from Sanskrit and Hindi poetry to miniature painting and classical dance. It also reflects the perspective of its male authors and audiences, in which women’s emotions are defined largely by their relation to a man — a limitation that modern feminist critics have noted.

docs.title: 6.7 Four Interpretations
docs.text:
The rasa-sūtra is brief, and its interpretation became the central problem of Indian aesthetics. Abhinavagupta’s commentary on the Nāṭyaśāstra, the Abhinavabhāratī, summarises the views of earlier commentators whose own works are lost (Gnoli 1956; Pollock 2016).

  1. Bhaṭṭa Lollaṭa held that rasa is the stable emotion of the original character (Rāma, for example) intensified by the determinants and other factors, and present secondarily in the actor who imitates him.

  2. Śrī Śaṅkuka held that the spectator infers the emotion from the actor’s representation, much as one infers that a painted horse is a horse; rasa is an imitation of emotion, apprehended by a special kind of inference.

  3. Bhaṭṭa Nāyaka (10th century) objected that emotion that belongs to someone else cannot be relished, and argued that poetry and drama have two special powers beyond denotation: a power of “generalisation” (bhāvakatva), by which the determinants and the emotion are made common (sādhāraṇīkṛta) and freed from their connection with particular persons, and a power of “enjoyment” (bhojakatva), by which the spectator relishes the emotion in a state of tranquil self-awareness.

  4. Abhinavagupta accepted Bhaṭṭa Nāyaka’s notion of generalisation but rejected his special powers. For Abhinavagupta rasa is suggested (vyaṅgya) in the sense developed by Ānandavardhana: the spectator’s own latent emotional impressions (vāsanā) are awakened by the generalised situation, and rasa is the relishing of one’s own consciousness as coloured by them.

docs.title: 6.8.1 Generalisation
docs.text: Generalisation (sādhāraṇīkaraṇa) is the key to Abhinavagupta’s account. A spectator watching a scene of grief on stage does not grieve as he would at a personal loss; nor does he merely observe another person’s grief. The emotion is detached from the particular “I” and “he”, from particular times and places, and becomes, as it were, grief as such — available to be savoured rather than suffered. This is why even painful emotions can be the material of aesthetic pleasure: the karuṇa rasa of a tragic play is enjoyed, though the grief it is based on would be painful in life.

docs.title: 6.8.2 Obstacles
docs.text: Abhinavagupta lists seven obstacles (vighna) that prevent the arising of rasa, and explains the conventions of theatre as means of removing them. They include the lack of credibility of what is presented; the spectator’s absorption in the particular circumstances of his own or another person’s situation; his being overwhelmed by his own pleasure or pain; the inadequacy of the means of perception; lack of clarity; the subordination of the main emotion; and doubt about which emotion is intended. The music, costume, stylised gesture and stage conventions of theatre, he argues, serve to detach the spectator from ordinary concerns and to focus his attention.

docs.title: 6.8.3 The Receptive Spectator
docs.text: The ideal audience is the sahṛdaya, “one with heart” — a term taken from Ānandavardhana. Abhinavagupta describes such people as those in whom long familiarity with poetry has made the “mirror of the mind” clear, so that they are able to become absorbed in what is described and respond with their own hearts. Aesthetic capacity, on this view, is cultivated, not innate; it depends on education and practice. The theory thus has an educational dimension that is easily overlooked.

docs.title: 6.8.4 Rasa and the Bliss of Brahman
docs.text: Abhinavagupta describes the relishing of rasa as a state of absorbed, self-aware delight (camatkāra), free of practical concerns, and compares it with the bliss of the self. He does not, however, identify the two: aesthetic experience is temporary, dependent on the performance, and coloured by particular emotions, whereas liberation is none of these. The comparison is older than Abhinavagupta: in his own report of Bhaṭṭa Nāyaka’s view, the relishing of rasa is already likened to the tasting of the supreme Brahman (Pollock 2016). The later theorist Viśvanātha (14th century) in his Sāhityadarpaṇa (3.2) gave the comparison its most famous formulation: rasa is “a twin brother of the tasting of Brahman” (brahmāsvādasahodara). That phrase is often attributed to Abhinavagupta; it is Viśvanātha’s, though the idea goes back through Abhinavagupta to Bhaṭṭa Nāyaka.

docs.title: 6.9 The Education of the Poet
docs.text:
If the spectator’s sensibility had to be cultivated, so did the poet’s. The theorists agreed that poetry requires three things: innate talent (śakti or pratibhā), learning and worldly experience (vyutpatti, nipuṇatā), and practice under the guidance of those who know poetry (abhyāsa). Mammaṭa’s Kāvyaprakāśa (11th century) states the triad at the beginning of his treatise, and most later writers follow him.

The fullest account of a poet’s education is Rājaśekhara’s Kāvyamīmāṃsā (early 10th century). It describes the sciences a poet should study — grammar, lexicons, metrics, poetics, the epics and Purāṇas, the arts — and the daily routine of a poet’s household, from morning study to evening assemblies; it classifies poets by their talents and stages of development, and pupils by their capacities. Rājaśekhara also remarks that women, too, can be poets, since cultivation belongs to the self and not to sex, and mentions princesses, daughters of ministers and courtesans who were accomplished poets. The work shows that in the courtly culture of the late first millennium the making of a poet was understood as a deliberate education of talent, knowledge and sensibility — a counterpart, on the side of the artist, of the cultivated sahṛdaya described above.

docs.title: 6.10 Suggestion: Dhvani
docs.text:
Ānandavardhana (c. 850), in his Dhvanyāloka, argued that the essence of poetry lies in what is suggested rather than stated:

Ānandavardhana, Dhvanyāloka 1.1 (opening)

kāvyasyātmā dhvanir iti budhair yaḥ samāmnātapūrvaḥ The soul of poetry is suggestion — so the wise have declared before.

Ānandavardhana distinguished the literal meaning (vācya), the secondary or figurative meaning (lakṣya) and the suggested meaning (vyaṅgya), and held that rasa can only ever be suggested: a poem that names an emotion (“she was sad”) does not thereby evoke it, whereas one that presents its causes and signs does. Abhinavagupta’s commentary on the Dhvanyāloka, the Locana, united the theory of suggestion with the theory of rasa (Ingalls et al. 1990). As a theory of how emotion is communicated indirectly — through situations, signs and associations rather than labels — it remains of interest to students of literature and of the psychology of art.

docs.title: 6.11 Other Voices: Bhoja and the Tamil Tradition
docs.text:
Not all theorists accepted the plurality of rasas. The eleventh-century king and polymath Bhoja of Dhārā, in his Śṛṅgāraprakāśa, argued that there is in reality only one rasa, which he called śṛṅgāra but understood not as erotic love alone but as a fundamental sense of self, “self-regard” or “pride” (abhimāna, ahaṃkāra), which underlies and colours all the emotions. The various “rasas” of Bharata’s list are, for Bhoja, emotional states (bhāva) through which this single rasa is experienced. His theory, little followed in later Sanskrit poetics, is an interesting attempt to ground the emotions in a single principle of personal investment (Pollock 2016).

The Tamil grammatical tradition developed an independent analysis. The section on “bodily manifestations” (meyppāṭu) in the Tolkāppiyam, the oldest surviving Tamil grammar and poetics (whose date is disputed), lists eight manifest emotional states — laughter, weeping, contempt, wonder, fear, pride, anger and joy — which overlap with Bharata’s list but are not derived from it. The parallel suggests a widely shared interest in classifying emotions and their bodily signs, developed in different literary cultures of the subcontinent. The Tamil poetics of inner and outer life, of which the meyppāṭu form a part, is described in Section 3.11; on Tamil literature more broadly see Volume 8 of this series.

docs.title: 6.12 Devotional Rasa
docs.text: In the sixteenth century the Bengal Vaiṣṇava theologian Rūpa Gosvāmin, a follower of Caitanya, applied rasa theory to religious devotion in his Bhaktirasāmṛtasindhu and Ujjvalanīlamaṇi. Devotion to Kṛṣṇa (bhakti) becomes the master rasa, with five primary forms according to the devotee’s relation to God: peaceful (śānta), servant-like (prīta or dāsya), friendly (preyas or sakhya), parental (vatsala) and amorous (madhura), the last regarded as the highest. The aesthetic theory of the theatre thus became a theology of emotion, in which the feelings of the devotee are not obstacles to be transcended but the substance of religious life.

docs.title: 6.13 Rasa in Music and Dance
docs.text:
Later musical treatises, such as Śārṅgadeva’s Saṅgītaratnākara (13th century), associated melodic types with particular rasas, and the classical dance traditions use the rasa–bhāva framework as the basis of expressive dance (abhinaya). In the later Hindustani tradition, rāgas came to be associated with times of day and seasons, and the rāgamālā paintings of the sixteenth to nineteenth centuries personified rāgas as heroes and heroines in characteristic moods. These associations are part of the history of Indian music and are discussed in Volume 9.

In the twentieth century the rasa–bhāva framework became the theoretical backbone of the revival and reconstruction of the classical dance forms. Teachers such as Rukmini Devi Arundale, who founded the Kalakshetra school in Madras in 1936, reshaped the hereditary dance of the temple and court traditions into the concert form now called Bharatanatyam, drawing on the Nāṭyaśāstra and later treatises for its vocabulary of expression. Training in Kathakali and Kūṭiyāṭṭam includes intensive exercises in the facial expression of the nine rasas. The revival was also a social transformation: it moved dance from the hereditary communities of women performers (devadāsīs), whose practice was stigmatised and legally suppressed, to the urban middle classes — a history whose costs have been the subject of much recent scholarship.

The theory also reached the visual arts. The Citrasūtra section of the Viṣṇudharmottara Purāṇa (perhaps 6th–8th century), the oldest surviving Indian treatise on painting, lists nine rasas that a painting can express and advises which subjects suit which rasa — erotic scenes for the erotic, battle for the heroic, and so on — as well as which subjects should not be painted in a house.

Claims are sometimes made that particular rāgas have specific therapeutic effects (“rāga therapy”). The historical sources do contain such associations, but the modern evidence for specific clinical effects of particular rāgas is limited to small studies, and no such effect should be presented as established. Music in general has well-documented effects on mood and arousal; whether Indian rāgas have distinctive effects beyond these is an open empirical question.

docs.title: 6.14 Emotion in Medicine and Ethics
docs.text:
The theatre was not the only place where Indian authors analysed emotion. The physicians treated strong emotions as causes and symptoms of disease. The Carakasaṃhitā lists grief, fear, anger and similar states among the causes of fevers and other disorders, attributes some forms of insanity to the loss of a loved one or of wealth, and in its account of healthy conduct recommends restraining the “urges” of greed, grief, fear, anger, pride, shamelessness, envy and excessive attachment, as opposed to the bodily urges, which must never be suppressed. The distinction between bodily urges that must be allowed and mental impulses that should be restrained is a characteristic feature of its ethics of health (Wujastyk 2003).

The religious traditions, for their part, classified emotions according to their moral and soteriological value: the Buddhist unwholesome roots of greed, hatred and delusion and their opposites (Chapter 5), the Jain passions (Chapter 3), and the Bhagavad Gītā’s analysis of desire and anger as the “enemy” that covers knowledge (BG 3.37–39). What distinguishes rasa theory from all these is that it values emotion aesthetically: it asks not whether an emotion is healthy or virtuous, but how it can be savoured.

docs.title: 6.15 Rasa Theory and Modern Emotion Research
docs.text:
Rasa theory invites comparison with modern psychology of emotion, and several scholars have made such comparisons, for example in cognitive literary studies (Hogan 2003). Some parallels are clear:

  • The distinction between a small number of stable emotions and many transient states resembles modern distinctions between basic emotions and more complex or blended states, although the lists differ and Bharata’s list is constructed for the stage.

  • The analysis of each emotion into causes (vibhāva), expressions (anubhāva) and accompanying states parallels componential theories of emotion, which distinguish eliciting situations, appraisals, expressions and physiological changes.

  • The sāttvika states recognise the involuntary bodily side of emotion.

  • Generalisation and the enjoyment of painful emotions in art address what modern aesthetics calls the “paradox of tragedy”.

The differences are equally important. Rasa theory is a theory of aesthetic response, not of everyday emotion; it rests on a doctrine of latent impressions and, in Abhinavagupta, on a metaphysics of consciousness; and its categories were derived from the analysis of performance and poetry, not from observation of people in ordinary life. It is best read as a sophisticated theory of the arts that contains insights into emotion, rather than as an early version of affective science.

Modern emotion research is itself divided. One influential tradition holds that a small set of “basic” emotions, with characteristic facial expressions, is universal across cultures; another, constructionist approach argues that emotion categories are built from more general processes and vary considerably between cultures and languages. Bharata’s catalogue, with its culturally specific conventions of gesture and its mixture of emotions, moods and bodily states, can be cited in support of either view. It is perhaps most valuable as evidence of how one sophisticated culture chose to divide and name the emotional life.

docs.title: 6.16 Drama and the Mind
docs.text:
The first chapter of the Nāṭyaśāstra tells how Brahmā created drama as a “fifth Veda” open to all classes, combining instruction and entertainment, and says that it will bring rest to those afflicted by suffering, weariness and grief. Kālidāsa, in his play Mālavikāgnimitra, has a character praise drama as “a single entertainment for people of diverse tastes” (nāṭyaṃ bhinnarucer janasya bahudhāpy ekaṃ samārādhanam, Act 1). Such passages express a view of the arts as morally and emotionally formative, which runs through Indian literary culture.

Modern drama therapy, music therapy and dance-movement therapy have their own histories. Indian practitioners of these therapies have drawn on the rasa–bhāva framework, and the theory’s emphasis on the cultivated, distanced experience of emotion offers a useful vocabulary for reflecting on what the arts can do.

  • Pollock (2016): translations of the principal texts on rasa, from Bharata to Jagannātha, with a substantial introduction.

  • Gnoli (1956): Abhinavagupta’s discussion of the rasa-sūtra, with translation.

  • Ingalls et al. (1990): the Dhvanyāloka with Abhinavagupta’s Locana.

  • Hogan (2003): an attempt to bring rasa theory into dialogue with cognitive science.

docs.title: Chapter 7: Dreams, Sleep and the States Between
docs.text: na tatra rathā na rathayogā na panthāno bhavanti | atha rathān rathayogān pathaḥ sṛjate There are no chariots there, no harnessings, no roads; but he creates chariots, harnessings and roads. — Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.10

docs.title: 7.1 Introduction
docs.text: Few ancient traditions took dreams and sleep as seriously as the Indian. For the Upaniṣadic teachers the dream state showed that the self can create a world from its own resources; for Gauḍapāda and the Buddhist idealists it was the decisive argument about the status of the waking world; for the physicians it was a source of diagnostic and prognostic signs and sleep was one of the three supports of life; for the dream-interpreters it was a field of omens; and for the yogins it was a state to be traversed with awareness. This chapter surveys these approaches and reports the claims of each tradition as claims; modern sleep science, whose methods and questions are different, neither inherits nor confirms them (Section 1.10).

docs.title: 7.2.1 Yājñavalkya on the Dreaming Self
docs.text:
The fullest Upaniṣadic treatment of dreams is Yājñavalkya’s instruction of King Janaka in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad (4.3.9–18). The person has two places, this world and the other world, and a third, the place of dream, which is the “junction” (sandhya) between them. When he dreams, he takes material from this world, “himself breaks it down and himself builds it up”, and dreams by his own light; there the person becomes self-illuminated. The dreamer creates chariots and roads, joys and delights, ponds and rivers — “for he is a creator” (BU 4.3.10, quoted at the head of this chapter).

Yājñavalkya illustrates the movement between states with an image:

Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.18

tad yathā mahāmatsya ubhe kūle anusaṃcarati pūrvaṃ cāparaṃ ca | evam evāyaṃ puruṣa etāv ubhāv antāv anusaṃcarati svapnāntaṃ ca buddhāntaṃ ca || As a great fish moves along both banks of a river, the near and the far, so this person moves along both these realms, the realm of dream and the realm of waking.

Beyond dream lies the state “where, asleep, he desires no desire and sees no dream”, to which the self hastens like a falcon that, tired of flying, folds its wings and settles in its nest (BU 4.3.19); there, embraced by the self of knowledge, it knows nothing within or without (BU 4.3.21).

docs.title: 7.2.2 Indra and Virocana
docs.text: The Chāndogya Upaniṣad (8.7–12) tells how the god Indra and the demon Virocana came to the creator Prajāpati to learn about the self. Prajāpati first identifies the self with the body seen in a reflection; Virocana is satisfied and leaves, but Indra returns, troubled. Prajāpati then identifies the self with the one who moves about happily in dreams; Indra objects that the dream self, though not blinded when the body is blind, still seems to be struck, chased and to weep. The self in dreamless sleep is offered next; Indra objects that in that state one does not know oneself at all and seems to be annihilated. Only then does Prajāpati teach the self beyond all three. The story is an early example of teaching by stages, with the student’s own objections driving the inquiry forward (see Chapter 9).

docs.title: 7.2.3 The Māṇḍūkya
docs.text: As described in Chapter 2, the Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad assigns the dream state to the “luminous” self (taijasa), whose cognition is turned inward and which enjoys subtle objects, and correlates it with the sound u of oṃ.

docs.title: 7.3.1 Gauḍapāda
docs.text:
Gauḍapāda’s Māṇḍūkyakārikā (chapter 2; see Chapter 2) uses dreams to argue that the waking world is unreal. Dream objects are experienced as external and spatially located, yet they are within the body and are contradicted on waking; and the features that seem to make waking objects real — their location, their apparent usefulness — are present in dreams too, judged from within the dream. Waking objects are equally “seen”, and therefore equally unreal.

Māṇḍūkyakārikā 2.31

svapnamāye yathā dṛṣṭaṃ gandharvanagaraṃ yathā | tathā viśvam idaṃ dṛṣṭaṃ vedānteṣu vicakṣaṇaiḥ || As a dream and a magic show are seen, and as a city of the Gandharvas in the clouds, so this whole world is seen by those versed in the Vedānta.

docs.title: 7.3.2 The Buddhist Idealists
docs.text: The Yogācāra philosopher Vasubandhu, in his Viṃśatikā (“Twenty Verses”), used dreams to answer objections to the doctrine that there are no external objects. If there are no external objects, the objector asks, why are experiences restricted to particular places and times, why do many people perceive the same things, and why do objects have real effects? Vasubandhu replies that in dreams, too, things appear in particular places and times, and dream experiences can have physical effects; and that in the hells described by Buddhist cosmology many beings perceive the same infernal guardians without these being external to their minds. Dreams thus show that the marks of reality do not require external objects.

docs.title: 7.3.3 The Realists on Dreams
docs.text: The realist schools explained dreams without making them a problem for the reality of the world. The Vaiśeṣika philosopher Praśastapāda (6th century) defined the dream as a cognition that arises, through the contact of the self with the mind, when the senses have ceased to function. He attributed dreams to three causes: the strength of impressions left by previous experience (as when a person who has been thinking intensely of something dreams of it), disorders of the bodily humours (as when one affected by wind dreams of flying), and unseen merit and demerit, which produce auspicious and inauspicious dreams. Dreams are thus a species of memory-based cognition, erroneous because what is remembered is experienced as present. The Naiyāyikas argued, against the idealists, that dream objects are themselves fragments of things experienced in waking life; dreams therefore presuppose a real external world rather than casting doubt on it.

docs.title: 7.3.4 Śaṅkara’s Reply
docs.text: Śaṅkara, although a non-dualist, rejected the Buddhist argument. Commenting on Brahmasūtra 2.2.29 (“and because of difference in nature, [waking cognition] is not like dream”), he argued that dream cognitions are contradicted on waking whereas waking cognitions are not contradicted in the same way; that dreams are a form of memory, while waking experience is direct perception; and that the Buddhist cannot deny the external world while relying on its regularities. The debate shows how dreams were used on both sides of a central metaphysical controversy, and why Śaṅkara distinguished the “empirical” reality of the waking world from the “apparent” reality of dreams (Chapter 4).

docs.title: 7.3.5 The Yogavāsiṣṭha
docs.text: The Yogavāsiṣṭha turns the philosophical argument into narrative. In the story of Līlā, a queen grieving for her dead husband, King Padma, is granted by the goddess Sarasvatī the power to travel in consciousness. She discovers that his mind contains a whole world in which he has been reborn as another king, with a long history of his own — and that the world in which she herself lives is in turn contained in another’s mind. The work’s stories of nested worlds, in which a moment in one corresponds to years in another, are literary explorations of the claim that the world is a projection of mind, works of imaginative philosophy in their own right (Venkatesananda 1984; O’Flaherty 1984).

docs.title: 7.4 The Physicians on Dreams
docs.text:
The medical saṃhitās treat dreams as signs. The Carakasaṃhitā (Indriyasthāna 5.43) distinguishes seven kinds of dream (Table 7.1): what has been seen (dṛṣṭa), heard (śruta) or experienced (anubhūta) in waking life; what has been wished for (prārthita); what is imagined (kalpita); what is prophetic (bhāvika); and what arises from the disordered doṣas (doṣaja). The first five, Caraka says, are without significance; only the prophetic dream and the dream caused by disease are meaningful. A dream seen in the first part of the night bears little fruit; one after which the dreamer does not fall asleep again bears great fruit at once (5.44–45).

Table 7.1. The seven kinds of dream in the Carakasaṃhitā (Indriyasthāna 5). Kind Meaning Significance according to Caraka dṛṣṭa Of what has been seen Without consequence śruta Of what has been heard Without consequence anubhūta Of what has been experienced Without consequence prārthita Of what has been wished for Without consequence kalpita Of what has been imagined Without consequence bhāvika Prophetic Indicates what is to come doṣaja Arising from the doṣas Indicates disease

Caraka’s recognition that most dreams simply rework waking experience, wishes and imagination is striking; his interest, however, lies in the two kinds he considers meaningful. The prophetic dreams that most concern the physician are omens of death (ariṣṭa), listed at length in the same chapter — travelling south with dogs, camels or donkeys, being carried off by a woman while garlanded and dressed in red, and many others. The Indriyasthāna as a whole is a manual of fatal prognosis, and these dream images belong to a wider culture of omens shared with the dream-interpretation manuals. Later Āyurvedic writers associated dream content with the predominant doṣa: dreams of flying and wandering with vāta, of fire and gold with pitta, of water and lotuses with kapha.

These classifications are historical evidence of how physicians thought; they are not a validated diagnostic method. Modern research has examined whether dream content changes with illness, but the claim that dreams can be used to diagnose disease or predict death has no reliable support.

docs.title: 7.5 Dreams in Buddhist and Jain Literature
docs.text:
• The Milindapañha. In this dialogue between the Greek king Menander (Milinda) and the monk Nāgasena, Nāgasena distinguishes six kinds of dreamer: those affected by wind, by bile or by phlegm; those influenced by a deity; those who dream of what they are used to; and those who receive a prognostic dream. Only the last kind, he says, is true; and the dream occurs neither in deep sleep nor in waking but in the light sleep between them.

  • Queen Māyā’s dream. According to the Buddhist biographical tradition, the Buddha’s mother dreamed at his conception that a white elephant entered her side; Brahmin interpreters at the court explained that she would bear a son who would become either a universal ruler or a Buddha. The scene became one of the most frequently depicted in Buddhist art, from the early stūpa railings onwards.

  • The Buddha’s dreams. The Aṅguttara Nikāya (5.196) records five great dreams that the Bodhisatta had before his awakening, each interpreted as a sign of it.

  • The mothers of the Jinas. Jain tradition holds that the mother of every Tīrthaṅkara sees a series of auspicious dreams at his conception — fourteen according to the Śvetāmbaras, sixteen according to the Digambaras — including an elephant, a bull, a lion, the goddess Śrī, the moon and the sun. The dreams are a favourite subject of Jain manuscript painting (Chapter 12).

docs.title: 7.5.1 Dreams in Epic and Drama
docs.text:
Dreams play important parts in Indian narrative literature. In the Rāmāyaṇa’s Sundarakāṇḍa, the demoness Trijaṭā, one of Sītā’s guards in Laṅkā, tells the others of a dream in which she saw Rāma in white garments on a celestial chariot and Rāvaṇa, shaven and smeared with oil, dragged southwards on a donkey — images that match the omens of death listed by the physicians — and warns them to treat Sītā kindly. In the play Svapnavāsavadatta (“Vāsavadattā in a Dream”), attributed to Bhāsa, King Udayana, half asleep, speaks to his queen, whom he believes dead, and the play turns on the ambiguity between dream and waking. Dreams in such works serve as omens, as devices of plot, and as explorations of longing and memory — uses that show how familiar the theories of the physicians and dream-interpreters were to poets and their audiences.

Dream interpretation was also a learned specialism. The Atharvaveda contains hymns against bad dreams, the Purāṇas and astrological works contain chapters on dream omens, and Jagaddeva’s Svapnacintāmaṇi (c. 12th century) is a manual devoted to the subject, classifying auspicious and inauspicious dreams and prescribing rites to avert the bad ones. Dreams also had a place in religious foundation stories: many temple traditions tell how a deity appeared to a king, a priest or a devotee in a dream and commanded that an image be found or a shrine built, and Sufi hagiography is full of dreams in which a saint appears to his disciples. Islamic dream interpretation (taʿbīr), with its own manuals in Arabic and Persian, circulated in India alongside the Sanskrit tradition (Section 7.6). These texts belong to the history of divination; they are not psychological theories of dreams in the modern sense, though they reveal what images were charged with meaning in the culture.

docs.title: 7.6 Dreams in the Islamic and Sufi Traditions
docs.text:
From the eleventh century India also had a second learned tradition of dream interpretation, in Arabic and Persian. Its starting point was a ḥadīth, transmitted in the collections of al-Bukhārī and Muslim, that divides dreams into three kinds. A good dream is glad tidings from God; a distressing dream comes from Satan; and a third kind arises from what a person has been “talking to himself” about, his own preoccupations. Another ḥadīth calls the true dream of a believer one of the forty-six parts of prophecy. Dreams were therefore taken seriously as a possible channel of knowledge, but most dreams were not thought to be of this kind. The threefold division is close to the classifications of the Milindapañha and of Caraka, which also set aside dreams arising from habit and bodily disturbance before admitting a small class of meaningful ones.

The philosophers gave the true dream a psychological explanation. In Ibn Sīnā’s account the imagination (Chapter 8) is busy in sleep with the residues of the day and the effects of the body’s humours, which produce most dreams. When it is quiet, the rational soul can receive knowledge from the higher intellects, and the imagination then translates this knowledge into images. The images of a meaningful dream are thus symbols that need interpretation (taʿbīr, literally “carrying across”), and a large Arabic and Persian literature of dream books, many ascribed to the eighth-century scholar Ibn Sīrīn, catalogued them. Unani physicians, like Caraka, also read dreams as signs of the body’s state: a person dominated by black bile was expected to have dark and fearful dreams.

The Sufis made dreams part of the spiritual path. Disciples reported their dreams to the master, who interpreted them as signs of the disciple’s inner state and progress. A seeker could be initiated in a dream by a dead master, the so-called uwaysī initiation, and dreams of the Prophet were valued as a confirmation of a teaching or a vocation. The practice of istikhāra, a prayer for guidance after which the answer is sought in a dream, was and is widespread among Indian Muslims. The malfūẓāt of the Chishtī masters record dreams as part of their teaching, and the Mughal emperors noted their dreams and those of their courtiers in their memoirs. In the Indian setting this tradition met the Sanskrit and vernacular dream lore at many points. Mughal and Rajput painting depicts dreams in both traditions, and the dream of the beloved that sets a hero on his quest is a stock motif of the Sufi romances in Avadhi (Chapter 8).

docs.title: 7.7 Sleep in Āyurveda
docs.text:
The Carakasaṃhitā names three “supports” (upastambha) of life: food, sleep and regulated sexual conduct (Sūtrasthāna 11.35). Its chapter on sleep (Sūtrasthāna 21) begins from a strong claim:

Carakasaṃhitā, Sūtrasthāna 21.36

nidrāyattaṃ sukhaṃ duḥkhaṃ puṣṭiḥ kārśyaṃ balābalam | vṛṣatā klībatā jñānam ajñānaṃ jīvitaṃ na ca || Happiness and unhappiness, plumpness and leanness, strength and weakness, virility and impotence, knowledge and ignorance, life and its absence depend on sleep.

Caraka explains sleep as occurring when the mind, together with the senses, becomes exhausted and withdraws from its objects. He distinguishes sleep born of tamas, of kapha, of mental and of bodily exhaustion, sleep that is adventitious (for example from injury), sleep that accompanies disease, and sleep that arises naturally at night (rātrisvabhāvaprabhavā), which he calls the “nurse of all beings” (Sūtrasthāna 21.58–59). Sleeping by day is generally discouraged, except in the hot season and for the weak, the elderly and those exhausted by labour or travel; staying awake at night is said to cause dryness and sleeping by day unctuousness. For sleeplessness Caraka recommends measures such as massage, bathing, nourishing foods with milk, a comfortable bed and pleasant surroundings; for excessive sleep, fasting, purification and activity.

Caraka’s explanations are framed in terms of the doṣas and guṇas, and his remedies have not been tested as he describes them. Some of his advice — regular hours, a calm environment — overlaps with the commonsense elements of cognitive-behavioural therapy for insomnia, the treatment best supported by modern evidence; others of its elements, such as deliberately restricting time in bed, have no classical counterpart. Traditional advice of this kind needs testing rather than assuming.

Health and Safety Note

Persistent insomnia, excessive daytime sleepiness, loud snoring with breathing pauses and similar problems can be signs of medical or psychiatric conditions that need professional assessment. Herbal sedatives sold as traditional remedies can interact with medicines and may be contaminated; see Chapter 3.

docs.title: 7.8 Sleep in Monastic Discipline
docs.text: The Buddhist and Jain monastic codes regulated sleep as part of the discipline of the mind. Buddhist monks were taught to sleep in the “lion’s posture” (sīhaseyyā), lying on the right side with one foot on the other, “mindful and clearly comprehending”, having noted the time to rise; the Buddha is described as dividing the night into three watches and sleeping only in the middle one. Over-sleeping and attachment to the pleasure of sleep are listed among the things that hinder a monk’s progress, and “wakefulness” (jāgariyā) is praised as one of the disciplines of the path. The Visuddhimagga recommends particular meditations for those troubled by drowsiness. These rules show that sleep, like eating, was treated as an occasion for mindfulness and restraint rather than as a private matter outside the religious life.

docs.title: 7.9 Sleep and Dream in Yoga
docs.text: The Yogasūtra, as noted in Chapter 3, counts dreamless sleep among the fluctuations of the mind: it is “the fluctuation that rests on the cognition of absence” (YS 1.10). Vyāsa’s commentary argues that sleep must be a cognition, since on waking one remembers it: “I slept well; my mind is clear”, or “I slept badly; my mind is dull and wandering”. Sleep is thus a fluctuation of the mind to be stilled like any other. The Advaitins, too, held that deep sleep is an experience later remembered, but for them it is an experience of the witness, of bliss and of ignorance, in which the mind itself is in abeyance (Section 4.4); the contrast lies in where the experience is located and how it is valued, not in whether sleep is experienced at all. Patañjali also lists among the means of steadying the mind “taking as support the knowledge gained in dream and sleep” (svapnanidrājñānālambanaṃ vā, YS 1.38). The commentators understood this in different ways: as meditation on an auspicious image seen in a dream, or on the tranquillity experienced in sleep. In either case, the states of sleep were seen as material for contemplative practice.

docs.title: 7.10 Yogic Sleep
docs.text: The term yoganidrā, “yogic sleep”, has several meanings. In the Purāṇas it is the cosmic sleep of Viṣṇu between creations, personified in the Devīmāhātmya as the Goddess. In some medieval Haṭha and Rāja Yoga texts it denotes a state of meditative absorption. The modern practice called “Yoga Nidra” is different again: a guided relaxation technique developed by Swami Satyananda Saraswati of the Bihar School of Yoga and published in 1976 (Satyananda Saraswati, Swami 1976), which combines a resolution (saṅkalpa), the rotation of attention through the body (adapted, according to its creator, from the Tantric rite of nyāsa), awareness of the breath, the evocation of opposite sensations and guided visualisation. The practice is widely taught and is used in some clinical settings; the evidence for its effects is discussed in Chapter 13. It should be understood as a modern synthesis drawing on traditional elements, not as an ancient technique preserved unchanged.

docs.title: 7.11 Dream Yoga
docs.text: The most systematic Indian-derived practice of awareness in dreams is the “dream yoga” (Tibetan rmi lam) taught among the Six Doctrines attributed to the Indian adept Nāropa (11th century) and transmitted in Tibetan Buddhism. The practitioner learns to recognise dreams as dreams while dreaming, to transform their contents, and to understand all appearances, waking and dreaming, as mind-made; the practice is also regarded as preparation for the intermediate state (bar do) after death. Lucid dreaming — awareness that one is dreaming while the dream continues — was long regarded by Western psychologists as doubtful, until experiments in the late 1970s and early 1980s showed that dreamers in REM sleep could signal, by pre-arranged eye movements, that they had become lucid (LaBerge et al. 1981). It has since been studied in sleep laboratories, and some researchers have drawn on Tibetan practices for techniques of inducing it. The laboratory findings establish that lucid dreaming occurs; they say nothing about the doctrinal claims — about the illusory nature of all appearances or the preparation for death — that give the Tibetan practice its meaning. Here again, the tradition and the laboratory research have different aims, and the one does not validate the other.

docs.title: 7.12 Between Death and Birth
docs.text: Several Indian traditions extended their analysis of the states of consciousness beyond sleep to death and rebirth. The Upaniṣads describe the departure of the self at death, gathering the senses into itself “as a caterpillar, reaching the end of a blade of grass, draws itself together” to step onto the next (BU 4.4.3). Buddhist schools disagreed about whether there is an “intermediate existence” (antarābhava) between death and rebirth. The Sarvāstivādins, as set out in the Abhidharmakośa (chapter 3), held that there is: a subtle being, nourished by smells, that seeks its next birth. Vasubandhu records several opinions on how long it lasts — some masters held seven days, others seven weeks, others that there is no fixed limit and it lasts until the conditions for rebirth come together (Vasubandhu 1988–1990) — and the figure of forty-nine days later became standard in Tibetan teaching. The Theravādins denied the intermediate existence, holding that the last moment of consciousness in one life is followed immediately by the first moment of the next. The Tibetan teachings on the intermediate states (bar do), which include the states of dream, meditation and dying, developed the Indian Buddhist idea in elaborate detail. These doctrines belong to the religious cosmology of their traditions; they show how far the analysis of states of consciousness was extended, and why dream and sleep could be seen as rehearsals for death.

docs.title: 7.13 Dreams and the Modern Reader
docs.text: Modern dream research offers no single theory to set against the Indian ones. Freud’s view of dreams as disguised wish-fulfilment, Jung’s view of dreams as compensating messages from the unconscious, and later neuroscientific theories that relate dreaming to memory consolidation, emotional processing or the simulation of threats have all had their advocates, and none commands universal assent. Against this background, some of the Indian classifications look remarkably sensible — Caraka’s recognition that most dreams rework the day’s experiences, wishes and imaginings, and the Milindapañha’s list of bodily, habitual and other sources of dreams — while others, such as the prognostic interpretation of dream images, belong to a world of omens that modern science does not share. Reading the texts well means recognising both.

docs.title: 7.14 Comparing the Traditions
docs.text:
Table 7.2. Approaches to dreams in Indian traditions. Tradition Key texts View of dreams Upaniṣads Bṛhadāraṇyaka 4.3; Chāndogya 8.7–12; Māṇḍūkya Evidence of the self’s creative, self-luminous nature; a stage on the way to the self Advaita Gauḍapāda; Śaṅkara on BS 2.2.29 For Gauḍapāda, proof of the world’s unreality; for Śaṅkara, a lower order of reality than waking Yogācāra Vasubandhu, Viṃśatikā Proof that experience does not require external objects Āyurveda Carakasaṃhitā, Indriyasthāna 5 Seven kinds; dreams of disease and omens of death Buddhist narrative Milindapañha; Aṅguttara 5.196 Six kinds of dreamer; prophetic dreams Jain Lives of the Jinas Auspicious dreams of the Tīrthaṅkaras’ mothers Omen literature Svapnacintāmaṇi Classification of auspicious and inauspicious dreams Islamic and Sufi Ḥadīth collections; Ibn Sīnā; dream books Three kinds of dream; the true dream as symbolic knowledge; dreams in initiation and guidance Tibetan Buddhism Six Doctrines of Nāropa Recognition and transformation of dreams in meditation

What unites the approaches compared in Table 7.2 is the conviction that dreams matter — as evidence about the self, as signs, or as an opportunity for practice. On what dreams are, where they come from and what they show, the traditions part company. A careful history of Indian thought about dreams should resist both the temptation to read modern dream science into the texts and the temptation to dismiss the texts as superstition. They record serious attempts, within their own frameworks, to make sense of a universal and puzzling experience.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text:

  • O’Flaherty (1984): a wide-ranging study of dreams and illusion in Indian myth and philosophy, with many stories from the Yogavāsiṣṭha.

  • Thompson (2015): Indian and Tibetan contemplative accounts of dreaming and sleep in dialogue with modern sleep science.

  • Sharma (1981–1994): the Carakasaṃhitā on sleep and dreams.

docs.title: Chapter 8: Self, Heart and Spirit: Islamic, Sufi and Sikh Psychology in India
docs.text: āī panthī sagal jamātī man jītai jag jīt Make the fellowship of all people your sect of yogis; conquer the mind, and you conquer the world. — Guru Nānak, Japjī 28 (Guru Granth Sāhib, p. 6)

docs.title: 8.1 Introduction
docs.text:
The chapters so far have followed accounts of the mind composed in Sanskrit, Pali, Prakrit and Tamil. Arabic learning had reached Sindh with Arab rule in the eighth century, but it was from the eleventh century, with Ghaznavid rule at Lahore, that another body of thought about the inner life took lasting root in India. It was written in Arabic and Persian and, later, in Hindavi, Panjabi, Sindhi, Dakani and Urdu. Its roots lay in the Qurʾān, in the Greek philosophy and medicine that had been translated into Arabic, and in the Sufi literature of Iraq, Khurasan and Central Asia. By the sixteenth century it had become fully Indian, in the sense that some of its most influential works were written in Lahore, Delhi, Sirhind and Gulbarga by authors who never left the subcontinent. In the same period the Sikh Gurus, beginning with Guru Nānak (1469–1539), composed in the Panjab a body of devotional poetry with its own diagnosis of the human condition and its own discipline of the mind.

These traditions are often treated in surveys of “Indian psychology” as a postscript, or are absorbed into Vedānta as if they were variations on it. This chapter treats them on their own terms. It sets out the vocabulary of the self in the Qurʾān (Section 8.2); the faculty psychology and ethics that Muslim philosophers and physicians inherited from the Greeks and that were taught in Indian madrasas (Section 8.3); the psychology of the Sufi path as it was written and taught in India (Section 8.4); and the Sikh teaching on the mind (man) and on self-centredness (haumai) (Section 8.5). The general history of Islam, Sufism and Sikhism in India is given in Volume 24, Samanvaya, and the Sufi engagement with yoga, including Guru Nānak’s dialogue with the Nāth yogis, in Volume 5, Yoga Taraṅgiṇī. Neither is repeated here. The institutions in which these traditions were taught — the maktab, the madrasa, the Sufi hospice and the Sikh dharamsāl — are described in Chapter 11.

Two cautions apply throughout. First, the Arabic, Persian and Panjabi terms do not map neatly onto Sanskrit ones. Nafs is not ahaṃkāra, qalb is not manas, and haumai is not simply the Sāṃkhya “I-maker”, although each invites comparison. Secondly, these are religious psychologies. Their accounts of the self are inseparable from their accounts of God, revelation and grace, and they should not be stripped of that context to make them look like modern therapies.

docs.title: 8.2 The Qurʾānic Vocabulary of the Inner Person
docs.text:
The Qurʾān does not set out a theory of the mind, but it supplied the words in which every later Muslim theory was framed. Four are central.

Nafs means “self” or “soul”, and in ordinary Arabic simply “oneself”. Three Qurʾānic phrases became the basis of a moral psychology. In the story of Joseph the self is said to “command to evil” (al-nafs al-ammāra bi’l-sūʾ, 12:53); in another passage God swears by “the self that blames” (al-nafs al-lawwāma, 75:2); and a third addresses “the self at peace” (al-nafs al-muṭmaʾinna, 89:27) and bids it return to its Lord. Later writers read the three phrases as three conditions or stages of one self.

The three conditions of the self (nafs)

al-nafs al-ammāra bi’l-sūʾ (Qurʾān 12:53) “The self that commands to evil”: the self ruled by its appetites. al-nafs al-lawwāma (75:2) “The self that blames”: the self that has begun to accuse itself. al-nafs al-muṭmaʾinna (89:27) “The self at peace”: the self that has come to rest in God and is bidden to return to its Lord.

A further passage (91:7–10) swears by the soul “and the One who proportioned it and inspired it with its wickedness and its righteousness”, and declares that whoever purifies it has succeeded. This verse made the purification of the self (tazkiyat al-nafs) a religious task.

Qalb, the heart, is in the Qurʾān the organ of understanding as well as of feeling. It is the heart that can be sealed, hardened or diseased, and that can also be guided and find rest. “It is not the eyes that are blind,” says one verse, “but the hearts within the breasts” (22:46); another declares that “in the remembrance of God hearts find rest” (13:28). On the Day of Judgement only the one who comes to God “with a sound heart” (qalb salīm, 26:89) will be saved. A well-known ḥadīth, transmitted in the collections of al-Bukhārī and Muslim, adds that there is a piece of flesh in the body which, when it is sound, keeps the whole body sound, and when it is corrupt, corrupts it — and that this is the heart. Islamic psychology is thus, from the start, a psychology of the heart, not of the head.

Rūḥ, the spirit, is what God breathed into Adam (15:29, 38:72). When people ask about it, the Prophet is told to answer that “the spirit is of the command of my Lord” (17:85), and that they have been given only a little knowledge. Many later writers took this as a warning against speculating about the spirit; the Sufis took the phrase “of the command” (min amr) as the starting point for a distinction between a world of command and a world of creation (Section 8.4.5).

ʿAql, reason or intellect, is curiously absent as a noun from the Qurʾān. The verb from the same root, “to understand, to use one’s reason”, occurs many times, usually in the challenge “will you not then understand?”. The noun entered the vocabulary through theology and philosophy, where it named the rational faculty and, in the Neoplatonic cosmology, the cosmic Intellect.

docs.title: 8.3 The Philosophers and the Physicians: Faculties of the Soul
8.3.1 The Internal Senses
docs.text:
The philosophers of Baghdad, Khurasan and Andalusia took over Aristotle’s account of the soul and refined it. The most influential version was that of Ibn Sīnā (Avicenna, 980–1037), whose Kitāb al-Nafs (“Book of the Soul”) and its abridgement in the Kitāb al-Najāt became the standard Islamic psychology (Rahman 1952). Ibn Sīnā distinguished the vegetative soul (nutrition, growth, reproduction), the animal soul (perception and voluntary movement) and the rational soul. Between the five external senses and the intellect he placed five internal senses, each assigned to a region of the brain’s ventricles:

  1. the common sense (al-ḥiss al-mushtarak), which unites the reports of the different senses into a single percept;

  2. the retentive imagination (khayāl), which stores the forms of things perceived;

  3. the compositive imagination (mutakhayyila), which combines and separates images, and which in human beings, when governed by reason, becomes the cogitative faculty (mufakkira);

  4. the estimative faculty (wahm), which grasps the non-sensible meanings in things perceived — the sheep’s perception that the wolf is to be fled;

  5. memory (ḥāfiẓa), which stores what estimation has grasped.

The scheme invites comparison with the Indian analyses of perception and memory (Chapters 3 and 5). Like Nyāya, it treats perception as a process in stages; like the Abhidharma, it gives a separate place to the grasping of a thing’s significance for the perceiver. Unlike either, it places the faculties in the organs of the body, and it subordinates them all to a rational soul that is immaterial and survives death.

In India this psychology was taught in two settings. In the madrasa it formed part of the philosophical curriculum, studied through Athīr al-Dīn al-Abharī’s thirteenth-century handbook Hidāyat al-Ḥikma and its commentaries, which remained set texts of the Dars-i Niẓāmī into the twentieth century (Chapter 11). In medicine it formed part of the theory of Unani (Yūnānī, “Greek”) physicians, for whom the “psychic” faculty (quwwa nafsāniyya) seated in the brain governed sensation, movement and thought (Volume 13, Āyurveda). The physicians described disorders of the mind in these terms: melancholia (mālīkhūliyā), attributed to an excess of black bile affecting the brain; madness (junūn); and, following Ibn Sīnā’s Qānūn, lovesickness (ʿishq) treated as a melancholic illness. The treatment combined regimen, diet and drugs with conversation, music and the management of the patient’s surroundings. The dār al-shifāʾ (hospital) founded by Sultan Fīrūz Shāh Tughluq in Delhi in the fourteenth century is among the earliest institutions in India for which the care of the sick in this tradition is recorded.

docs.title: 8.3.2 Ethics as the Medicine of the Soul
docs.text:
The most widely read psychological literature in Muslim India, however, was not the technical philosophy of the soul but the Persian literature of ethics (akhlāq). Its foundation was the Tahdhīb al-Akhlāq (“Refinement of Character”) of Miskawayh (d. 1030), which joined Plato’s division of the soul to Aristotle’s theory of virtue as a mean. Naṣīr al-Dīn Ṭūsī rewrote it in Persian as the Akhlāq-i Nāṣirī (1235), adding books on the household and on the state; Jalāl al-Dīn Dawānī’s Akhlāq-i Jalālī (late fifteenth century) restated Ṭūsī’s work in a more elegant style. Both were read throughout Mughal India, and Muzaffar Alam has shown how the akhlāq tradition shaped the outlook of the Mughal nobility and its Hindu and Muslim secretaries (Alam 2004). The literary and political sides of this literature are treated in Volume 8 and Volume 18; its psychology concerns us here.

Table 8.1. The faculties of the soul and the cardinal virtues in Ṭūsī’s Akhlāq-i Nāṣirī, after Miskawayh. Each virtue is a mean between two vices. Faculty Virtue Vice of excess Vice of deficiency rational (nāṭiqa) wisdom (ḥikmat) folly, misplaced cleverness (safah) stupidity (balah) irascible (ghaḍabī) courage (shujāʿat) rashness (tahawwur) cowardice (jubn) appetitive (shahwānī) temperance (ʿiffat) greed, licence (sharah) torpor (khumūd) the three in harmony justice (ʿadālat) doing injustice (ẓulm) submitting to injustice (inẓilām)

The scheme is summarised in Table 8.1. Its psychological interest lies less in the table than in the therapeutics that followed it. Ṭūsī, following Miskawayh, describes the “diseases of the soul” — among them anger, fear, above all the fear of death, and grief — and prescribes their cure as a physician prescribes for the body. Health is preserved by keeping good company and good habits; disease is treated by opposites, and anger is cured by reflecting on its causes and consequences and by deliberately cultivating forbearance. Fear of death is analysed as a mistake arising from ignorance of what death is, and grief as the result of attachment to things that are by nature transient. The treatise also offers a theory of education: since character (khulq) is formed by habit, children must be trained early, praised for good conduct, kept from bad company and taught to love knowledge before they can understand its reasons (Ṭūsī 1964). The resemblance to the Indian medical idea of “conquering the mind” (sattvāvajaya, Chapter 3) is real, though the two traditions developed independently.

Alongside the philosophical akhlāq stood al-Ghazālī’s (1058–1111) great synthesis of law, ethics and Sufism, the Iḥyāʾ ʿUlūm al-Dīn (“Revival of the Religious Sciences”), whose books on “the wonders of the heart” and “the discipline of the soul” gave the Sufi psychology of the heart a systematic form. Its Persian abridgement, the Kīmiyā-yi Saʿādat (“Alchemy of Happiness”), was widely read in India. Al-Ghazālī compared the heart to a king, reason to his minister, and the appetites and anger to unruly servants and soldiers who must be governed rather than destroyed. The image of the self as a kingdom to be ruled, not a prison to be escaped, is characteristic of the Islamic ethical tradition. Indian thought had images of self-governance of its own, from the chariot of the Kaṭha Upaniṣad (Section 2.4) to the Gītā’s discipline of action (Section 4.9), but al-Ghazālī’s image gives the appetites a legitimate, governed place in a life lived within the religious law.

docs.title: 8.4.1 The Vocabulary of the Path
docs.text:
From the thirteenth century, Sufi orders became one of the most important channels of religious teaching in India, and they brought with them a developed vocabulary of the self and its transformation. Drawing on the Qurʾān and on earlier Persian and Arabic Sufi writers, Indian Sufis distinguished levels of the lower self (nafs): the self that “commands to evil” (ammāra), the self that “blames” itself (lawwāma), and the self “at peace” (muṭmaʾinna). The heart (qalb) was the organ of spiritual perception, to be polished like a mirror. The path was described as a sequence of “stations” (maqām) attained by effort — repentance, abstinence, patience, trust in God, contentment — and of “states” (ḥāl) granted by grace, such as longing, intimacy and ecstasy.

The goal of the path was described in a pair of terms: the passing away (fanāʾ) of the self’s attributes in God, and the abiding (baqāʾ) in God that follows. Sufi writers disagreed about how these were to be understood — whether as the extinction of the self’s awareness of itself, as the replacement of its qualities by divine qualities, or as the return of a transformed self to ordinary life — and much of the Indian Sufi literature is concerned with that question. Annemarie Schimmel’s Mystical Dimensions of Islam remains the best introduction to the vocabulary (Schimmel 1975).

docs.title: 8.4.2 Al-Hujwīrī’s Unveiling of the Veiled
docs.text:
The first Sufi treatise written in India is also, as its translator called it, the oldest Persian treatise on Sufism. ʿAlī ibn ʿUthmān al-Hujwīrī, born near Ghazna, settled in Lahore, where he died about 1072 (some sources give a few years later); his shrine there, known as the Dātā Darbār, is still one of the most visited in South Asia. His Kashf al-Maḥjūb (“The Unveiling of the Veiled”) is a handbook for the seeker, translated into English by R. A. Nicholson in 1911 (al-Hujwīrī 1911). It begins with knowledge, poverty and the nature of Sufism, gives lives of the Prophet’s companions and of the early masters, and then surveys twelve “schools” of Sufis — ten of which Hujwīrī approves and two of which he condemns. Each school is identified with a characteristic doctrine, and the survey amounts to a typology of inner states: sobriety and intoxication, presence and absence, union and separation, the mortification of the self, passing away and abiding. The last part of the book is arranged as the lifting of a series of “veils”, from the knowledge of God and the profession of unity through prayer, almsgiving, fasting and pilgrimage to companionship, the technical language of the Sufis, and listening to music.

Three of Hujwīrī’s distinctions became standard in Indian Sufism. First, he insists on the difference between a station and a state: the station belongs to the seeker’s effort and conduct, the state is a gift that descends on the heart and cannot be acquired. Secondly, in the long-running debate between the partisans of “intoxication” (sukr), associated with Abū Yazīd (Bāyazīd) of Bisṭām, and of “sobriety” (ṣaḥw), associated with al-Junayd of Baghdad, he sides with sobriety: the ecstatic utterances of the intoxicated are to be excused, not imitated, and the higher condition is the one in which the seeker keeps full possession of his faculties and of the religious law. Thirdly, he treats the lower self as the chief obstacle on the path. His discussion of the school of Sahl al-Tustarī is an extended account of the “struggle against the self” (mujāhadat al-nafs), in which the self is to be disciplined by hunger, wakefulness and the opposition of its desires, but never trusted, because its tricks grow subtler as the seeker advances. These three themes — the gratuitousness of spiritual experience, the priority of sobriety, and the cunning of the self — run through the later Indian literature.

docs.title: 8.4.3 The Chishtī Masters: Teaching by Conversation
docs.text:
Sufi teaching was organised around the relationship between master (shaykh, pīr) and disciple (murīd), and took place in the hospice (khānqāh). The conversations of the Chishtī master Niẓām al-Dīn Awliyāʾ (d. 1325) of Delhi, recorded between 1307 and 1322 by his disciple Amīr Ḥasan Sijzī in the Fawāʾid al-Fuʾād, show a teacher who instructed through anecdote, counsel and example, attending to the inner states of his hearers and emphasising humility, generosity and the service of others (Sijzī 1992). The Chishtīs also cultivated listening to music (samāʿ) as a means of inducing spiritual states, a practice that connected them with Indian musical traditions.

The Fawāʾid al-Fuʾād created a genre, the malfūẓāt or “utterances” of a master, which became the characteristic form of Indian Sufi teaching. The conversations of Niẓām al-Dīn’s successor Naṣīr al-Dīn Maḥmūd, “the Lamp of Delhi” (d. 1356), were recorded as the Khayr al-Majālis, and those of Sayyid Muḥammad Gēsū Darāz (d. 1422), who carried the Chishtī teaching to Gulbarga in the Deccan, by his son. Collections attributed to the earlier Chishtī masters, from Muʿīn al-Dīn of Ajmer to Farīd al-Dīn of Pakpattan, were judged by the historian Mohammad Habib and others to be later compositions; Ernst and Lawrence point out that they were nevertheless read as authoritative and shaped the image of those masters (Ernst and Lawrence 2002).

The psychological interest of the genre lies in its method. The master’s sayings are almost always addressed to a particular person in a particular condition, and the recorder notes the effect of a story on the hearers — tears, silence, a change of resolve. The master diagnoses the disciple’s state and prescribes accordingly: a proud man is set to menial service, an anxious one reassured, a scholar warned against the vanity of learning. The teaching also turns constantly on the management of emotion: on forgiving injuries, on bearing hostility without returning it, and on hope and fear of God held in balance. The Chishtī insistence on the conditions of samāʿ reflects a similar attention to state. The listener, the singer, the words sung and the company present all had to be fit, and Niẓām al-Dīn is reported to have disapproved of musical instruments, because music was a powerful means of moving the heart and could move it in the wrong direction.

docs.title: 8.4.4 Remembrance and the Heart
docs.text:
The central practice of the Sufi orders was remembrance (dhikr): the repetition of the profession of faith, of the name Allāh, or of other divine names, aloud (jahrī) or silently in the heart (khafī), alone or in assembly. The Chishtīs and Qādirīs in India practised vocal dhikr as well as silent; the Naqshbandīs were known for silent remembrance of the heart. The Qurʾānic promise that “in the remembrance of God hearts find rest” gave the practice its rationale, and Sufi manuals describe its stages: the repetition first occupies the tongue, then the heart, until the remembrance continues of itself and finally the one who remembers is absorbed in the One remembered. Dhikr was supported by contemplation and watchful attention (murāqaba), by examination of conscience (muḥāsaba), and by periods of seclusion, of which the forty-day retreat (chilla) was the best known; hagiographies attribute extreme forms of it to Farīd al-Dīn. Some Indian Sufis combined dhikr with the holding of the breath, and the extent to which this drew on yoga was debated among the Sufis themselves (Volume 5).

The comparison with the Indian practices of recollection — the Buddhist recollections (anussati), the smaraṇa and nāmasaṅkīrtana of the bhakti traditions, and the Sikh nām simran (Section 8.5.6) — is obvious, and was made by Indian Sufis and devotees themselves. The differences are equally important. Dhikr is directed to a personal God who is wholly other than the creature, and it is bound up with the observance of the religious law; its aim is not the discovery of an inner self identical with the absolute, but the purification of the heart so that it can reflect the divine attributes.

docs.title: 8.4.5 The Naqshbandī Subtle Centres and Aḥmad Sirhindī
docs.text:
The Naqshbandī order was brought to India from Central Asia by Khwāja Bāqī Billāh (1564–1603), who settled in Delhi around 1599. His most important disciple, Shaykh Aḥmad Sirhindī (1564–1624), gave the Indian Naqshbandīs — known after him as the Mujaddidīs, from his title Mujaddid-i Alf-i Thānī, “Renewer of the Second Millennium” — a distinctive psychology and a distinctive metaphysics. Both are set out in his Maktūbāt, more than five hundred letters to disciples and to nobles of the Mughal court (Friedmann 1971).

Sirhindī systematised a doctrine of subtle centres (laṭāʾif, singular laṭīfa) in the human being. Taking up the Qurʾānic distinction between God’s “command” (amr) and his “creation” (khalq), he taught that the human being is composed of ten subtle centres. Five belong to the “world of command”, whose roots lie beyond the created cosmos: the heart (qalb), spirit (rūḥ), secret (sirr), hidden (khafī) and most hidden (akhfā). Five belong to the “world of creation”: the self (nafs) and the four elements of the body. In Mujaddidī practice each of the first five was located at a point on the chest, as in Table 8.2, and the disciple was led through them one by one in a graded series of lessons. The master directed his concentrated attention (tawajjuh) to the disciple’s heart and the disciple performed silent dhikr at each centre in turn, until each was “awakened” and returned to its origin. Arthur Buehler has shown how this graded and supervised method made the Mujaddidī shaykh a “mediating” teacher, responsible for guiding the disciple’s inner experience step by step (Buehler 1998).

Table 8.2. The ten subtle centres (laṭāʾif) of the Mujaddidī Naqshbandīs. Locations follow a common later scheme; manuals differ in detail. Realm Subtle centre Location in practice world of command heart (qalb) below the left breast (ʿālam al-amr) spirit (rūḥ) below the right breast secret (sirr) above the left breast hidden (khafī) above the right breast most hidden (akhfā) centre of the chest world of creation self (nafs) the forehead (in some schemes, below the navel) (ʿālam al-khalq) earth, water, fire, air the whole body

The laṭāʾif are sometimes equated in modern writing with the cakras of Tantric and Haṭha yoga (Chapter 3). The equation should be resisted. The laṭāʾif are not arranged along a central channel, are not associated with a rising energy, and are defined by their relation to the divine command, not to the elements of the subtle body. What the two systems share is a practice of fixing attention on points in the body as a way of training the mind, and a conviction that inner experience can be mapped and guided.

Sirhindī’s metaphysics was also, in part, a theory of experience. The dominant metaphysics of Indian Sufism, derived from Ibn ʿArabī (1165–1240), was the “unity of being” (waḥdat al-wujūd): only God truly exists, and the world is his self-manifestation. Sirhindī, who had himself passed through the experience of unity, argued that it was a stage on the path and not its end. The experience of oneness, he wrote, is real as an experience, but its content is a “unity of witnessing” (waḥdat al-shuhūd), not of being. When the sun rises the stars are no longer seen, but they have not ceased to exist; so the mystic overwhelmed by God no longer perceives the world, though the world remains distinct from God. Beyond the station of unity lay a higher station of servanthood (ʿabdiyya), in which the mystic returns to the world, recognises the distance between creature and Creator, and lives by the religious law. Sirhindī’s doctrine is, among other things, an argument that mystical experience cannot by itself establish metaphysical conclusions. It thus addresses a question that also divided the Advaitins from their Buddhist and Vedāntic opponents (Chapter 4).

Sirhindī is often remembered as the champion of Islamic orthodoxy against Akbar’s religious policies, and his letters to Mughal nobles do urge the restoration of the religious law. Yohanan Friedmann has shown, however, that this image owes much to later admirers; most of his letters concern the mystical path, and in his lifetime he was controversial chiefly for his claims about his own spiritual rank, for which the emperor Jahāngīr briefly imprisoned him (Friedmann 1971).

docs.title: 8.4.6 Shāh Walī Allāh
docs.text:
Shāh Walī Allāh of Delhi (1703–1762), the son of the founder of the Madrasa-yi Raḥīmiyya (Chapter 11), was the most systematic Muslim thinker of eighteenth-century India. His Arabic Ḥujjat Allāh al-Bāligha (“The Conclusive Argument from God”) sets out to explain the reasons behind the commandments of Islam, and to do so it develops an account of human nature (Walī Allāh 1996; Rizvi 1980).

Walī Allāh’s psychology has three elements. First, he describes a subtle vital body, the nasama or “breath”, arising in the heart from the finest vapours of the blood, through which the rational soul acts on the body. Secondly, he describes two opposing dispositions in every person, an “angelic” (malakiyya) and an “animal” (bahīmiyya) one. People differ according to the strength of each and the degree to which they are in harmony or conflict, and he offers a typology of characters built on these variables. Thirdly, he names four basic virtues through which the human being attains happiness: purity (ṭahāra), humble reverence before God (ikhbāt), magnanimity, or freedom from domination by base desires (samāḥa), and justice (ʿadāla). These are psychological capacities rather than rules, and the religious law is, in his account, a means of cultivating them in a whole community.

What distinguishes Walī Allāh is that he joins this individual psychology to a theory of society. Human beings, he argues, develop “supports” or arrangements of life (irtifāqāt) in four stages: the basic skills of livelihood, the household and its dealings, the city-state, and finally a universal order embracing many states. The virtues of the individual and the institutions of society are thus parts of one account of human flourishing. In the Sufi controversies of his time he argued that the “unity of being” and the “unity of witnessing” differed more in expression than in substance. His descendants and pupils shaped Indian Islamic learning for the next century.

docs.title: 8.4.7 Meeting Points
docs.text:
The encounter between Sufi and Indian ideas produced deliberate comparisons. The Mughal prince Dārā Shukōh argued in his Majmaʿ al-Baḥrayn (“The Meeting of the Two Oceans”, 1655) that the Sufi and Vedāntic vocabularies of the self and God express the same truths, and the Persian Sirr-i Akbar (“The Great Secret”, 1657), made under his direction, rendered fifty Upaniṣads for readers of Persian. Persian versions of the Yogavāsiṣṭha and other texts circulated widely. The resemblance that Dārā saw between the Sufi “unity of being” and Advaita is real at the level of formulas, but the Sufi doctrine came from Ibn ʿArabī and the Qurʾān, not from Vedānta.
