It also kept a personal God, a revealed law and a created world, and Sirhindī’s critique shows that it was contested within Indian Sufism itself. In the devotional poetry of the regional languages, Sufi and bhakti images of longing and of the inner beloved mingled freely. The Persian and Arabic works on yoga and the meetings of Sufis and yogis are described in Volume 5, and the general history of these exchanges in Volume 24.

One body of literature deserves mention here because it is, among other things, a psychology of love. The Sufi romances (premākhyān) composed in Avadhi between the late fourteenth and the mid-sixteenth centuries — among them Quṭban’s Mirigāvatī (1503), Malik Muḥammad Jāyasī’s Padmāvat (1540) and Manjhan’s Madhumālatī (1545) — tell stories of a prince who sees or hears of a beautiful woman, falls in love, becomes a yogi in search of her, and wins her after trials. Aditya Behl has argued that the poets fused the Sufi idea of the transforming power of love with the Indian aesthetics of rasa (Chapter 6), developing a “rasa of love” (prem-rasa) in which the hearer’s emotional response to the story became a means of spiritual education (Behl 2012). The literary history of these poems is given in Volume 8. For a history of Indian psychology they show how the Indian analysis of aesthetic emotion could be taken up into a different religious framework without losing its own technical vocabulary.

docs.title: 8.5.1 Sources and Interpretation
docs.text:
The primary source for Sikh teaching on the mind is the Guru Granth Sāhib, the scripture compiled by Guru Arjan in 1604 and, in its later recension, declared by Guru Gobind Singh to be the Guru after him. Its standard printed edition runs to 1,430 pages. It contains hymns of six of the Gurus and of earlier saints and court bards, arranged by musical mode (rāg); its history is given in Volume 24. The hymns are poetry, composed for singing, not treatises. Their language is a literary idiom that Christopher Shackle has called the “sacred language of the Sikhs” or “Sant Bhāṣā”, mixing old Panjabi, Hindavi and Braj forms with Sanskrit and Persian vocabulary (Shackle 1983). Many key terms are therefore polyvalent, and translation is already interpretation. The Vārāṅ of Bhāī Gurdās (d. 1636), which the tradition regards as a key to the scripture, are the earliest extended commentary.

Modern interpretation has taken several directions. The Singh Sabha scholars of the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries produced influential works of exegesis and reference. W. H. McLeod’s Guru Nanak and the Sikh Religion (1968) gave the first analysis in English of Nānak’s thought as a coherent system — the nature of God, the condition of “unregenerate man”, the means of God’s self-revelation and the discipline of the name — and its categories have been widely used, even by those who reject his historical conclusions about Nānak’s life (McLeod 1968). Arvind-pal Singh Mandair has argued that the very act of rendering Sikh terms as “God”, “soul”, “salvation” or “ego” carried a Christian and colonial theology into Sikh self-understanding, and has proposed readings of haumai and nām that stay closer to the poetry’s own logic (Mandair 2013). Shackle and Mandair’s selection, Teachings of the Sikh Gurus, offers careful translations with this problem in view (Shackle and Mandair 2005), and Pashaura Singh has studied how the text was compiled and how its meanings were fixed (Singh 2000). The account below follows the scripture’s own vocabulary as far as possible and notes where readings differ.

docs.title: 8.5.2 Man: The Mind as Problem and as Place of Change
docs.text:
The word man (from Sanskrit manas) is among the most frequent in the Guru Granth Sāhib. It does not denote a faculty in the Sāṃkhya sense but the whole inner person: the seat of thought, desire, emotion and will. Many hymns address the mind directly, in the second person, scolding, pleading with and instructing it. The mind is restless and runs in all directions; it is ensnared by māyā, the world of attachment and illusion; it is driven by the five “thieves” or vices — lust (kām), anger (krodh), greed (lobh), attachment (moh) and pride (ahaṅkār). Yet the mind is also the place where the change happens. The Japjī declares that to conquer the mind is to conquer the world (man jītai jag jīt, stanza 28), and a hymn of Guru Amar Dās tells the mind that it is “an embodiment of the divine light” and bids it recognise its own origin (Guru Granth Sāhib, p. 441).

This double view of the mind — as the root of bondage and as itself divine in origin — recalls the Upaniṣadic saying that the mind is the cause of both bondage and liberation, and the Yogācāra and Kashmir Śaiva teachings that consciousness is obscured but not destroyed by its defilements. The Sikh view is, however, distinct in one respect. The mind is not to be stilled or dissolved into a witness-consciousness; it is to be turned around, from facing itself to facing the Guru. The Gurus describe the two orientations with a pair of terms. The manmukh, “one whose face is towards the mind”, follows his own will; the gurmukh, “one whose face is towards the Guru”, lives by the Guru’s word (sabad).

docs.title: 8.5.3 Haumai
docs.text:
The fundamental disorder of the manmukh is haumai, a compound of two forms of the first-person pronoun, “I” and “me”. It is usually translated “ego” or “self-centredness”, and McLeod defines it as the self-assertion that binds a person to the round of birth and death because it sets the individual against the divine order (McLeod 1968). It is not a belief that can be refuted, nor a single emotion, but a pervasive orientation. In a famous ślok of the Āsā kī Vār Guru Nānak lists the acts of a human life — coming and going, being born and dying, giving and taking, earning and losing, speaking truth and falsehood — and says of each that it is done “in haumai”. A second ślok, by Guru Aṅgad, adds that haumai is a chronic disease but that its remedy also lies within it (Guru Granth Sāhib, p. 466): the same self that is turned in on itself can be turned towards God.

The diagnosis has a structural similarity to the Buddhist analysis of craving and of the conceit “I am” (Chapter 5), and to the Sāṃkhya and Yoga accounts of the “I-maker” and the affliction of “I-am-ness” (asmitā, Chapter 3). The difference lies in the cure. For the Buddhist the conceit “I am” is uprooted by insight into the impersonal flow of events; for Yoga the seer is discriminated from the seen. For the Gurus haumai is overcome by recognising the divine order and the divine name, through the Guru’s word and by grace. The self is not shown to be unreal; it is reoriented.

docs.title: 8.5.4 Hukam, Grace and the Limits of Effort
docs.text:
The Japjī, Guru Nānak’s composition that opens the scripture and is recited daily, begins by examining the means by which a person might hope to become “true”. Its first stanza rejects them one by one. Cleansing (or thinking) a hundred thousand times does not achieve what is sought — the key word, soch, is read either as “purity” or as “thought”, and the ambiguity has generated much commentary — nor does keeping silence bring inner silence, nor do the riches of the worlds satisfy hunger, nor will any amount of cleverness go along with one at the end. The stanza ends with the answer: to walk in the divine will or order (hukam). The second stanza adds that everything is within the hukam, and that “one who understands the hukam”, in Nānak’s words, “does not speak in haumai”.

The psychological point is subtle. Effort — ritual, ascetic, intellectual — cannot by itself overcome self-centredness, because effort undertaken by the self tends to strengthen the self. The fourth stanza of the Japjī adds that “by deeds one obtains the garment” of a body, “but by grace (nadar) the door of liberation”. Grace does not, however, make effort pointless. The Sikh tradition holds the two together, much as Sufi writers held together the station acquired by effort and the state given by grace.

docs.title: 8.5.5 The Five Realms
docs.text:
Stanzas 34–37 of the Japjī describe a sequence of five “realms” (khaṇḍ), which later Sikh writers and modern scholars have read as stages of spiritual growth.

  1. The realm of duty (dharam khaṇḍ): the earth, set amid the seasons and the elements as a place of moral action, where each is judged by deeds.

  2. The realm of knowledge (giān khaṇḍ): the dawning awareness of the vastness of creation, its countless worlds, gods and teachers, which humbles the self.

  3. The realm of saram: translated by McLeod as “effort”, by others as “beauty” or “spiritual endeavour”. Here, the stanza says, the mind, intellect and understanding are fashioned anew.

  4. The realm of grace (karam khaṇḍ): karam here is the Persian word for grace, not the Sanskrit karma. It is the realm of power and of those filled with the divine.

  5. The realm of truth (sach khaṇḍ): the dwelling of the Formless One, which the stanza says is “hard as iron” to describe.

The interpretation of the third realm illustrates the problem of translation noted above. Read as “effort”, it makes the sequence a progression from moral action and knowledge through discipline to grace; read as “beauty”, it makes the transformation of the mind an aesthetic and devotional event. Either way the sequence moves from outward action to the reshaping of the mind itself, and ends in a condition that cannot be described.

docs.title: 8.5.6 Nām Simran, Sahaj and the Householder’s Life
docs.text:
The discipline that overcomes haumai is nām simran, “remembrance of the name”. Nām is not simply a word for God but, in McLeod’s analysis, the whole of the divine self-expression in creation; to remember it is to bring the mind into accord with the order that runs through everything. The practice ranges from the repetition of a divine name such as Vāhigurū to the singing of the scripture in congregation (kīrtan) and to a continuous inward awareness. It is related to the smaraṇa of the bhakti poets and to the Sufi dhikr (Section 8.4.4), and the scripture itself includes the verses of Kabīr, Nāmdev and Bābā Farīd. The Sikh tradition nevertheless insists that the Gurus’ teaching is a revelation in its own right, not a combination of others (Volume 24).

The fruit of the discipline is sahaj, a word inherited from the Nāth and Sant traditions and meaning “natural” or “spontaneous”. In the Guru Granth Sāhib it names a state of equipoise in which the turmoil of the mind has ceased and the person lives in harmony with the divine order. McLeod treats it as the ultimate condition of the Sikh path, beyond adequate description (McLeod 1968). It is attained in the midst of ordinary life. The Gurus rejected the renunciation of the yogi (Volume 5) and of the ascetic orders: the householder who earns an honest living (kirat karnī) and shares with others (vaṇḍ chhakṇā) is the model, and the mind is to be disciplined within family and work, not by leaving them.

docs.title: 8.5.7 Sevā, Saṅgat and Chaṛhdī Kalā
docs.text:
Sikh psychology is also a social psychology. Selfless service (sevā) — cooking and serving in the community kitchen (laṅgar), cleaning the shoes of the congregation, tending the gurdwara — is understood not only as charity but as a direct discipline against haumai, since it is done without reward and often in humble roles. The congregation (saṅgat) is the place where the mind is shaped by the company of the faithful and by the singing of the scripture; the Sufi insistence on companionship (ṣuḥbat) offers an obvious parallel. The daily congregational prayer (Ardās) ends with a petition for “rising spirits” (chaṛhdī kalā) and for the welfare of all. The ideal of chaṛhdī kalā — an undefeated, optimistic resilience grounded in trust in the divine will — is associated in Sikh memory with the persecutions of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, and is often cited by Sikhs today as a resource for facing adversity.

The scripture’s teaching on the mind is addressed to all human beings, and Guru Nānak’s verse asking why woman should be called inferior, when kings are born of her (Āsā kī Vār, Guru Granth Sāhib, p. 473), is often cited as evidence of its egalitarian intent. Nikky-Guninder Kaur Singh has drawn attention to the feminine imagery of the divine and of the soul in the scripture (Singh 1993). Doris Jakobsh has shown, however, that Sikh social practice did not always follow the scripture, and that the place of women in Sikh history was reshaped in the colonial period (Jakobsh 2003). As in the other traditions surveyed in this volume, the psychology of the texts and the social history of their communities must be distinguished.

docs.title: 8.6 Comparing the Vocabularies
docs.text:
Table 8.3 sets the Sufi and Sikh accounts beside three of the Indian accounts discussed in earlier chapters. The table simplifies traditions that are internally diverse, and its columns name analogous roles, not equivalent concepts.

Table 8.3. What obscures the self, where change takes place, and how: five accounts compared (simplified). Tradition The disorder Locus of change Main practice Goal Yoga (Ch. 3) ignorance and the afflictions (kleśa) citta and its fluctuations practice and dispassion; the eight limbs isolation of the seer (kaivalya) Advaita (Ch. 4) superimposition (adhyāsa) the inner instrument hearing, reflection, contemplation knowledge of identity with brahman Abhidharma (Ch. 5) craving, ignorance, latent tendencies citta and mental factors calm and insight nibbāna Sufism the self that commands to evil the heart and the subtle centres dhikr, watchfulness, companionship with a master passing away and abiding in God; the self at peace Sikh teaching haumai and the five vices man, turned from manmukh to gurmukh nām simran, sevā, saṅgat sahaj, union by grace in the householder’s life

Three contrasts stand out. First, the Islamic and Sikh traditions locate the decisive transformation in the heart or the whole inner person rather than in a cognitive faculty, and treat emotion — love, longing, fear, hope — as the material of the path rather than as an obstacle to be quietened. In this they are closer to the bhakti traditions (Chapter 4) than to classical Yoga or Advaita. Secondly, both give grace a place that the classical Sāṃkhya, Yoga and Abhidharma accounts do not, while still demanding sustained effort. Thirdly, both insist on the life of the community — the religious law and the Sufi hospice in one case, the congregation, kitchen and household in the other — as the setting of inner change. None of these contrasts is absolute. Devotional Vedānta gives grace a central place, the Buddhist and Jain monastic orders are communities of practice, and Sufis were among the most austere renouncers of medieval India.

docs.title: 8.7 Assessment
docs.text: Indo-Islamic and Sikh thought about the mind has often been left out of histories of Indian psychology, either because it was not written in Sanskrit or because it was assumed to be derivative. Neither reason holds. The Persian and Arabic literature of India includes what is often called the oldest Persian treatise on Sufism, an influential Persian ethics of the soul, the Mujaddidī psychology of subtle centres and Shāh Walī Allāh’s theory of human nature and society. The Sikh scripture contains a sustained and original analysis of self-centredness and its cure. These works deserve to be read alongside the Upaniṣads, the Yogasūtra and the Abhidharma, with the same attention to their own categories and the same caution about easy equivalences. The Indian traditions of the mind were, from the eleventh century at least, multilingual and multi-religious, and their meetings — in Dārā Shukōh’s comparisons, in the Sufi romances, in the shared vocabulary of the Sant poets and the Gurus — are part of their history.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text:
• Schimmel (1975): the standard introduction to Sufi thought and practice, with much on the Indian masters; Schimmel (1980) surveys Islam in the subcontinent.

  • al-Hujwīrī (1911): the Kashf al-Maḥjūb in R. A. Nicholson’s English translation.

  • Sijzī (1992): the conversations of Niẓām al-Dīn Awliyāʾ, translated by Bruce Lawrence; Ernst and Lawrence (2002) on the Chishtī order.

  • Friedmann (1971) and Buehler (1998): Sirhindī’s thought and the Mujaddidī method of guidance.

  • Walī Allāh (1996): Marcia Hermansen’s translation of the Ḥujjat Allāh al-Bāligha, with an introduction to Walī Allāh’s psychology.

  • Ṭūsī (1964) and Alam (2004): Ṭūsī’s ethics and its place in Mughal India.

  • McLeod (1968), Shackle and Mandair (2005) and Mandair (2013): Guru Nānak’s thought, the Sikh scriptures in translation, and the problems of translating Sikh concepts.

docs.title: Chapter 9: The Teacher’s Household: Brahmanical Education
docs.text: mātṛdevo bhava | pitṛdevo bhava | ācāryadevo bhava | atithidevo bhava | Treat your mother as a god. Treat your father as a god. Treat your teacher as a god. Treat your guest as a god. — Taittirīya Upaniṣad 1.11.2

docs.title: 9.1 Introduction
docs.text: The word gurukula, “the teacher’s family”, has become in modern India a byword for an idealised traditional education: a boy living in the forest home of a sage, serving him, learning from him by heart and by example. The ideal has a real basis in the Vedic and Dharmaśāstra sources, which describe in detail a period of studentship (brahmacarya) spent living with a teacher. But those sources are normative texts written by and for a Brahmin elite. They describe what their authors thought should happen, and they restricted Vedic education to a minority of the population: boys of the three upper varṇas, and in practice mainly Brahmin boys. This chapter describes the model as the texts present it, its methods and curriculum, and its exclusions. The broader landscape of Indian education — monasteries, colleges, vernacular schools, madrasas — is the subject of Chapter 11. The standard scholarly account is Scharfe (2002); the older surveys by Altekar (1965) and Mookerji (1947) are still useful for their collections of evidence but are more celebratory in tone.

docs.title: 9.2.1 Terms
docs.text:
The Vedic and Dharmaśāstra texts use several words for teachers and students. The ācārya is the teacher who initiates a student and teaches him the Veda with its ritual and esoteric parts; the upādhyāya teaches a portion of the Veda or the auxiliary sciences for a living (Manu 2.140–141). The guru (“weighty one”) is a general term of respect that includes parents. The student is a brahmacārin, “one who lives the life of the Veda”, or an antevāsin, “one who dwells near” the teacher; the word śiṣya, “one to be taught”, is general.

The popular etymology of guru as “remover (ru) of darkness (gu)” comes from late texts such as the Advayatāraka Upaniṣad; linguistically, guru simply means “heavy, weighty”. The etymology is nonetheless a fair expression of how the role was understood.

docs.title: 9.2.2 The Qualified Teacher
docs.text:
The Upaniṣads expect a student who seeks knowledge of Brahman to approach a qualified teacher with humility:

Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 1.2.12

tadvijñānārthaṃ sa gurum evābhigacchet samitpāṇiḥ śrotriyaṃ brahmaniṣṭham To know that, he should go, firewood in hand, to a teacher who is learned in the Veda and grounded in Brahman.

Carrying firewood was the student’s sign of willingness to serve: tending the teacher’s fire was one of his daily duties. The two qualifications — learning in the texts (śrotriya) and personal grounding in what they teach (brahmaniṣṭha) — became the standard description of the ideal teacher.

docs.title: 9.2.3 The Student’s Conduct
docs.text: The Dharmasūtras of Āpastamba, Gautama, Baudhāyana and Vasiṣṭha (composed in the last centuries BCE) and the Manusmṛti (c. 2nd century CE) regulate the student’s life minutely (Olivelle 2005). He must rise before the teacher and go to bed after him; beg food from households and hand it over to the teacher; fetch water and firewood; tend the sacred fire; avoid honey, meat, perfumes, ornaments, dancing, gambling and the company of women; speak truthfully; and treat the teacher, the teacher’s wife and the teacher’s family with deference. The teacher in turn must teach the student without withholding anything and treat him like a son. The texts permit physical punishment, though some restrict it to a rope or a thin cane applied to the back, and threaten the teacher with penalties if he goes further.

docs.title: 9.2.4 Teaching and Payment
docs.text:
The normative texts held that Vedic knowledge should not be sold. A teacher received gifts and the student’s service, and at the end of studentship a final gift (gurudakṣiṇā), but teaching for a stipulated fee was frowned upon: Manu lists the “paid teacher” (bhṛtakādhyāpaka) and the student who pays a fee among those who should not be invited to an ancestral offering. In practice teachers depended on the gifts of students’ families, on royal and temple endowments, and on land grants (Chapter 11), and the epics and Jātakas speak of students who paid fees as a matter of course. The ideal of knowledge as a gift rather than a commodity was real, but it was sustained by an economy of patronage.

The relationship was thus both affectionate and hierarchical. Its modern image as a model of mentoring should not obscure the degree of control the teacher exercised and the dependence of the student, who might spend many years in another man’s household as an unpaid servant.

docs.title: 9.3 The Rites of Childhood
docs.text:
Brahmanical education was framed by the life-cycle rites (saṃskāra) prescribed in the Gṛhyasūtras and Dharmaśāstras (Kane 1941). Before initiation a child of the twice-born classes passed through a series of rites: the birth rite (jātakarman), in which the father touches the newborn’s lips with honey and ghee and whispers in its ear; the naming (nāmakaraṇa); the first outing; the first feeding with solid food (annaprāśana); and the tonsure (cūḍākaraṇa), usually in the first or third year. Later texts add a rite for beginning to learn the alphabet (vidyārambha; see below). Initiation followed, and the end of studentship was marked by the first shaving of the beard (keśānta) and the ceremonial bath (samāvartana).

These rites expressed the idea that a person is formed, not merely born: the child is ritually “made” (saṃskṛta) into a full member of the community in stages, and education is one of those stages. The same idea underlies the use of the word saṃskāra for the impressions that experience leaves in the mind (Chapter 3): in both senses a saṃskāra is a “making” that shapes what a person becomes. Like initiation itself, the full series of rites applied to boys of the twice-born classes; for girls most of the rites were performed without Vedic mantras, and marriage took the place of initiation.

docs.title: 9.4 Initiation: Upanayana
docs.text:
Vedic study began with the rite of initiation, upanayana, “leading near” — that is, to the teacher. In it the boy was invested with a girdle (mekhalā), a staff and an antelope skin (later, the sacred thread, yajñopavīta), was taught the sāvitrī verse (Ṛgveda 3.62.10, the “Gāyatrī”), and was formally accepted by the teacher. Initiation was regarded as a second birth; hence the three upper classes are called “twice-born” (dvija).

The texts prescribe initiation in the eighth year (counted from conception) for a Brahmin, the eleventh for a Kṣatriya and the twelfth for a Vaiśya, with outside limits of sixteen, twenty-two and twenty-four years (Manu 2.36–38); the Gṛhyasūtras assign the three classes to spring, summer and autumn respectively. A twice-born man who was not initiated in time became an outcaste (vrātya) unless he performed expiation. Śūdras were not initiated, and by the time of Manu girls were not initiated either: for a woman, Manu says, the marriage ceremony takes the place of initiation, service to her husband takes the place of residence with the teacher, and household work takes the place of tending the sacred fire (Manu 2.67).

The duration of study was long. The Chāndogya Upaniṣad (6.1.2) tells of Śvetaketu, who went to his teacher at twelve and returned at twenty-four, “having learned all the Vedas”; Manu (3.1) prescribes thirty-six years for the three Vedas, or half or a quarter of that, “or until he has learned them”. These are ideal figures; in practice many students learned only part of the Veda of their own school.

docs.title: 9.5.1 The Veda and Its Auxiliaries
docs.text:
The core of Brahmanical education was the memorisation of the Veda of the student’s own branch (svādhyāya), in the manner described in Chapter 10. Alongside it stood the six “limbs of the Veda” (vedāṅga): phonetics (śikṣā), metre (chandas), grammar (vyākaraṇa), etymology (nirukta), astronomy and calendrics (jyotiṣa) and ritual (kalpa).

A verse found in the Pāṇinīya Śikṣā pictures the auxiliaries as the limbs of the Veda’s body: metre its feet, ritual its hands, astronomy its eye, etymology its ear, phonetics its nose — and grammar its mouth, the most important of all. The image explains why grammar came to stand at the head of the traditional curriculum.

docs.title: 9.5.2 Why Study Grammar?
docs.text:
Patañjali opens his “Great Commentary” (Mahābhāṣya, 2nd century BCE) on Pāṇini’s grammar by asking what the purpose of grammar is. He gives five principal reasons, summed up in a mnemonic compound (rakṣohāgamalaghvasandehāḥ): the preservation (rakṣā) of the Veda; the ability to adapt (ūha) Vedic formulas correctly to new ritual contexts; the injunction of scripture (āgama) that a Brahmin should study the Veda with its auxiliaries; economy (laghu), since grammar teaches the language through general rules rather than by listing every word; and the removal of doubt (asandeha) about the correct form of words. The passage includes the warning about the wrongly accented word quoted in Chapter 10, and the remark, attributed to an earlier teacher, that one should not teach the language word by word: even Bṛhaspati, teaching Indra word by word for a thousand divine years, did not reach the end. Grammar’s claim to be the “mouth” of the Veda rested on its power to generalise.

The study of Pāṇini became the foundation of all advanced Sanskrit learning, Brahmanical, Buddhist and Jain alike; Yijing found it at the start of the Buddhist curriculum at Nālandā (Chapter 11). Its method — a compact rule-system learned by heart and then applied through commentary and practice — set the pattern for much of Indian technical education. On Pāṇini and the grammatical tradition see Volume 10 of this series.

docs.title: 9.5.3 Lists of Sciences
docs.text:
Later texts list the branches of learning in different ways.

  • The Yājñavalkyasmṛti (1.3) names fourteen “sources of knowledge and law” (vidyāsthāna): the four Vedas, the six Vedāṅgas, and Purāṇa, Nyāya (logic), Mīmāṃsā (Vedic exegesis) and Dharmaśāstra.

  • Later authorities, such as Madhusūdana Sarasvatī in his Prasthānabheda (16th century), add four “secondary Vedas” (upaveda) to make eighteen: Āyurveda (medicine), Dhanurveda (archery and warfare), Gāndharvaveda (music) and Arthaśāstra (polity).

  • The Arthaśāstra (a composite text, c. 50 BCE–300 CE in its present form; (Olivelle 2013)) prescribes for a prince four sciences: the Veda, investigative reasoning (ānvīkṣikī), economics (vārttā) and government (daṇḍanīti).

An earlier and more varied picture is given in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad (7.1), where Nārada comes to Sanatkumāra for instruction and lists what he has already studied: the four Vedas, the epics and ancient lore as a “fifth Veda”, grammar, the rites for the ancestors, mathematics (rāśi), the science of portents, chronology, logic, ethics, etymology, the sciences of spirits, of weapons, of the stars, and of serpents and celestial beings. All this, Nārada confesses, has made him merely “a knower of texts, not a knower of the self” — a reminder that the Upaniṣads valued one kind of knowledge above all the rest.

The Kāmasūtra (1.3) lists sixty-four arts (kalā) — music, dance, painting, garland-making, cookery, carpentry, word games, and many more — that the cultured townsman and the accomplished courtesan should know. The list shows the range of refined accomplishments valued in urban society; it does not describe the curriculum of any school.

docs.title: 9.5.4 Professional Learning
docs.text: Most practical skills — crafts, trade, agriculture, accountancy, the arts — were learned in families and guilds by apprenticeship, not in the teacher’s household. Medicine is an instructive intermediate case. The Carakasaṃhitā (Vimānasthāna 8) describes how a student should choose a teacher and a teacher a student, and records the address with which the teacher initiates a medical student, enjoining celibacy, truthfulness, obedience and care for patients. The Suśrutasaṃhitā (Sūtrasthāna 9) prescribes practical training for surgeons: incision on gourds, cucumbers and other vegetables; excision on leather bags filled with water or mud; scraping on hides with hair; puncturing veins on the vessels of dead animals and on lotus stalks; and so on. It insists that a student who has learned the texts without practice is like a coward on the battlefield. These passages are among the earliest descriptions of skills training in Indian literature.

docs.title: 9.6 How It Was Taught
docs.text:
The sources point to a number of characteristic methods.

  • Oral repetition. The teacher recited and the students repeated, phrase by phrase, until the text was fixed in memory (Chapter 10).

  • Exposition and commentary. In the śāstric disciplines, the teacher explained a root text through a commentary, and the student learned to explain it in turn.

  • Question and answer. The Upaniṣads are full of dialogues in which students question teachers — and teachers question students. Uddālaka’s demonstrations to Śvetaketu (Chapter 2) and Prajāpati’s staged instruction of Indra (Chapter 7) are teaching by inquiry.

  • Debate. Formal debate (vāda), with rules of argument codified by the Nyāya school, was central to advanced study and is discussed in Chapter 11.

  • Guided discovery. Varuṇa’s teaching of Bhṛgu in the Taittirīya Upaniṣad (3.1–6), in which the student is given only a definition and sent away to find the answer by his own effort, is the classic example.

  • Example. The student lived in the teacher’s household and learned conduct as much as texts.

Two Upaniṣadic stories show how varied the teacher–student relationship could be. In the Praśna Upaniṣad, six students come to the sage Pippalāda with questions; he tells them to live with him for another year in austerity, celibacy and faith, and only then to ask — a lesson that readiness must precede instruction. In the Chāndogya Upaniṣad (4.10–15), Upakosala serves his teacher Satyakāma Jābāla for twelve years, but the teacher goes on a journey without having instructed him. Distressed, Upakosala falls ill; the sacred fires he has tended then teach him themselves, and when the teacher returns he notices that the student’s face “shines like that of one who knows Brahman” and completes the teaching. The story suggests both the devotion expected of a student and the possibility of learning from one’s own practice when the teacher is absent.

No fixed daily timetable survives from antiquity; the timetables printed in some modern books are reconstructions. What the texts prescribe is a day framed by the morning and evening twilight rites (sandhyā), the tending of the fire and the begging round, with study fitted around them, and a calendar with an annual opening (upākaraṇa) and closing (utsarjana) of Vedic study and many days on which recitation was suspended (anadhyāya).

docs.title: 9.7 Learning a Śāstra
docs.text:
Beyond the Veda, advanced study meant mastering a śāstra, a systematic discipline such as grammar, logic, Mīmāṃsā, Vedānta, medicine, astronomy or poetics. The structure of śāstric literature shaped the way it was taught (Scharfe 2002).

  • The root text. Most disciplines had a root text (mūla), often in the extremely concise form of aphorisms (sūtra) or memorial verses (kārikā). The student learned it by heart. Pāṇini’s grammar, with nearly four thousand sūtras, is the most famous example; its rules are formulated with technical devices — abbreviations, markers, conventions of ordering — that make it compact enough to memorise but impossible to understand without instruction.

  • The commentaries. The root text was explained through layers of commentary: a bhāṣya expounding it, sub-commentaries (vārttika, ṭīkā) explaining the bhāṣya, and so on, sometimes over many centuries. Learning a śāstra meant learning to read this layered literature and, eventually, to write in it.

  • Method of exposition. A traditional analysis lists the elements of explaining a text: dividing it into words, giving their meanings, analysing compounds, construing the sentence, raising objections and answering them. The last two — objection (ākṣepa, pūrvapakṣa) and reply (samādhāna, siddhānta) — made dialectic part of every lesson.

  • Manuals and primers. Introductory works (prakaraṇa) such as the Tarkasaṅgraha in logic or the Laghusiddhāntakaumudī in grammar were written to lead beginners into a discipline, and are still used.

This pedagogy produced scholars of great precision and the habit of arguing every point from both sides. It also had characteristic limitations: the authority of the root text and its commentators could inhibit innovation, and learning was organised by school and lineage rather than by subject.

docs.title: 9.7.1 Learning Mathematics
docs.text: Mathematical astronomy (jyotiṣa) and arithmetic were taught within families of astronomers and in the schools of particular masters, and some mathematical works were written with teaching in mind. Bhāskara II’s Līlāvatī (1150), an arithmetic in verse, addresses many of its problems to a girl — “O Līlāvatī” — in the playful manner of a teacher setting exercises, and was used as a textbook across India for centuries; it was later translated into Persian at Akbar’s court. In sixteenth-century Kerala, Jyeṣṭhadeva’s Yuktibhāṣā, written in Malayalam rather than Sanskrit, set out the reasoning (yukti) behind the results of the Kerala school of mathematics and astronomy, including its infinite series, in a form designed for students. These works show that Indian mathematical pedagogy valued both memorable formulation and explanation of reasons. The history of Indian mathematics is the subject of Volume 11 of this series.

docs.title: 9.7.2 Learning Medicine
docs.text: Medical education combined study of the texts with practical training. Besides the exercises on fruits and leather described above, the Suśrutasaṃhitā (Śārīrasthāna 5) describes how a student should learn anatomy by examining a human corpse that has been left to decompose in a cage in a river for seven days and then gradually scraped with brushes of grass and bark, so that the layers of the body can be observed — one of the very few descriptions of systematic dissection in the ancient world. The text insists that a surgeon must know the body both from the texts and by direct observation. Caraka’s instructions on the choice of a teacher and the conduct of discussions (Chapter 11) complete a picture of a learned profession with a deliberate theory of training.

docs.title: 9.7.3 Learning Music
docs.text: The classical musical traditions have been transmitted orally from teacher to student within lineages for centuries, and in Hindustani music the lineages crystallised in the nineteenth century into gharānās associated with particular families and styles. A student would live with or near the teacher, serve him, and learn through years of imitation and practice; in some lineages the relationship is sealed by a ceremony of tying a thread on the student’s wrist. The modern institutionalisation of music teaching in colleges and universities, from the early twentieth century, was in part a response to the restrictiveness of the hereditary system. The history of music and its teaching is treated in Volume 9.

docs.title: 9.8.1 The Education of Princes
docs.text:
The Arthaśāstra (1.5) prescribes the education of a prince: after the tonsure ceremony he should learn writing and arithmetic; after initiation, the Veda and investigative reasoning from learned teachers, economics from officials, and government from theoreticians and practitioners. He should spend part of the day on training in elephants, horses, chariots and weapons, and part on hearing the epics and histories, and should keep company with elders to develop discipline. The epics describe the training of princes in archery and the use of weapons by teachers such as Droṇa. These texts show that the education of the ruling class combined literacy, practical administration, military skills and a moral formation through narrative.

The Arthaśāstra (1.5) also offers a short theory of education. Discipline (vinaya), it says, is of two kinds, innate and acquired; training can discipline only a suitable person, not an unsuitable one, just as work can shape only suitable material. The capacities of a good learner are listed as the desire to hear, hearing, grasping, retaining, understanding, reasoning for and against, and attachment to the truth. The same list of intellectual qualities — wishing to learn, listening, grasping, retaining, reasoning — recurs in many Indian texts as an account of the stages of learning.

docs.title: 9.8.2 Teaching through Stories: The Pañcatantra
docs.text: One of the most influential Indian works on education is a collection of animal fables. The Pañcatantra (perhaps 3rd–5th century CE) opens with a frame story: a king despairs of his three sons, who are dull and uninterested in learning, and the Brahmin Viṣṇuśarman undertakes to make them expert in the conduct of affairs (nīti) within six months. He does so by telling them stories, in five books, in which animals act out the dilemmas of friendship, alliance, war and statecraft, and in which maxims in verse comment on the action. The later Hitopadeśa reworks the same material for the same purpose. The frame embodies a pedagogical idea — that practical wisdom is best taught through narrative, to learners who would not respond to abstract instruction — and the collection became one of the most widely translated books of the pre-modern world, passing through Middle Persian and Arabic (as Kalīla wa Dimna) into the languages of Europe. Its view of the world is pragmatic, often cynical, and frankly hierarchical; it teaches prudence and self-interest as much as virtue. On the Pañcatantra as literature see Volume 8 of this series.

docs.title: 9.8.3 Craft and Apprenticeship
docs.text: The great majority of skills — weaving, metalwork, carpentry, pottery, sculpture, architecture, trade, agriculture — were learned by apprenticeship, usually within the family or the occupational caste, and sometimes in guilds (śreṇī). The law book of Nārada (perhaps 5th–6th century CE) regulates the relationship between a master and an apprentice (antevāsin) who lives with him to learn a craft: the master must teach him and feed him, may not make him do other work, and may discipline him; the apprentice must stay for the agreed term even if he learns the craft sooner. This model of hereditary and apprenticed learning, rather than schooling, was the normal form of education for most Indians until modern times; its knowledge was largely unwritten, and is treated in Volume 17 of this series.

docs.title: 9.8.4 Beginning to Read
docs.text: By the medieval period, a ceremony for beginning to learn the alphabet (vidyārambha or akṣarārambha), in which a small child traces letters in rice or sand, had become widespread, especially in the south, where it is still widely performed. It was not restricted to the twice-born in the way that upanayana was, and it marks the existence of a broader culture of elementary literacy alongside the Vedic schools (Chapter 11).

docs.title: 9.9 Testing and Recognition
docs.text:
Traditional Indian education had no written examinations, grades or diplomas of the modern kind. Mastery was tested in other ways. A Vedic student’s recitation was checked by his teacher and, in public recitations, by other reciters; a student of a śāstra demonstrated his learning by expounding texts and by debate, first with fellow students and then before assemblies of scholars (pariṣad, sabhā). Reputation was established by success in such assemblies and by the judgement of recognised teachers. In the later period, communities of scholars conferred honorific titles — in Bengal, for example, titles such as Tarkālaṅkāra (“ornament of logic”) or Vidyāsāgara (“ocean of learning”) — and royal courts honoured scholars with gifts and appointments. Tradition reports distinctive local practices, such as an examination in Mithilā in which a needle was pushed at random through a manuscript and the candidate had to explain the passage on the page where it stopped; such reports are difficult to verify but convey the expectation that a scholar must command the whole of a text, not selected parts.

Monastic institutions had their own procedures. Admission to Nālandā, according to Xuanzang, required success in a debate with the gatekeeper scholars (Chapter 11); Tibetan monastic colleges later developed formal examinations by debate leading to degrees such as geshe. The absence of written examinations should not be taken to mean the absence of rigorous assessment; it meant that assessment was oral, public and dependent on the judgement of masters.

docs.title: 9.10 Completion: Samāvartana
docs.text:
At the end of studentship the student performed the “return” (samāvartana), marked by a ceremonial bath, after which he was called a snātaka, “one who has bathed”. He offered his teacher a gift (gurudakṣiṇā) and was then expected to marry and become a householder. The Taittirīya Upaniṣad preserves the teacher’s final instruction:

Taittirīya Upaniṣad 1.11.1

satyaṃ vada | dharmaṃ cara | svādhyāyān mā pramadaḥ | ācāryāya priyaṃ dhanam āhṛtya prajātantuṃ mā vyavacchetsīḥ | Speak the truth. Practise dharma. Do not neglect your recitation. Having brought your teacher a gift that pleases him, do not cut off the line of offspring.

The passage continues with injunctions not to neglect truth, dharma, welfare, prosperity, recitation and the rites for gods and ancestors, and to treat parents, teacher and guest as gods. It ends with practical advice: when in doubt about conduct, follow the example of Brahmins who are thoughtful, devoted and gentle. It is often called the first “convocation address”; it is better understood as a summary of the duties of a Vedic householder.

docs.title: 9.11 Life-Stages
docs.text:
The period of studentship was later integrated into the scheme of four life-stages (āśrama): student, householder, forest-dweller and renouncer. Olivelle (1993) has shown that the āśramas were originally alternative ways of life between which an adult could choose; only later were they arranged as successive stages of a single life, and the age-ranges often quoted (“8 to 25”, “25 to 50” and so on) are modern conventions, not classical rules. The scheme applied, in any case, only to twice-born men.

The Atharvaveda devotes a whole hymn (11.5) to the Vedic student, whom it glorifies as sustaining the world by his discipline:

Atharvaveda (Śaunaka) 11.5.17

brahmacaryeṇa tapasā rājā rāṣṭraṃ vi rakṣati | ācāryo brahmacaryeṇa brahmacāriṇam icchate || By studentship and austerity the king protects the realm; by studentship the teacher seeks a student.

docs.title: 9.12 Who Could Learn? Caste, Gender and Exclusion
docs.text: Any account of the teacher’s household must face the fact that it was closed to most people. The restriction was not incidental; the normative texts state it repeatedly and sometimes violently.

docs.title: 9.12.1 Śūdras
docs.text:
The Dharmasūtras and Manu define the Śūdra as “once-born” (ekajāti), without initiation (Manu 10.4), and exclude him from Vedic study. The Gautama Dharmasūtra prescribes that if a Śūdra listens to a recitation of the Veda his ears are to be filled with molten tin or lac; if he recites it, his tongue is to be cut out; if he commits it to memory, his body is to be split apart (Gautama 12.4–6). Manu forbids giving a Śūdra advice or teaching him the law (Manu 4.80). Śaṅkara, as noted in Chapter 4, cites the Gautama rule in his commentary on Brahmasūtra 1.3.38. Whether such punishments were ever carried out is unknown; their importance lies in what they reveal about the ideology of knowledge as a hereditary possession of the twice-born.

The epics dramatise the exclusion. In the Mahābhārata (1.123 in the critical edition), the Niṣāda prince Ekalavya, refused as a pupil by the archery teacher Droṇa, teaches himself before a clay image of Droṇa and becomes the finest archer in the land; Droṇa, to protect the pre-eminence of his Kṣatriya pupil Arjuna, demands as his fee Ekalavya’s right thumb, which Ekalavya cuts off and gives him. In the Uttarakāṇḍa of the Rāmāyaṇa (7.64–67 in the critical edition), Rāma beheads the Śūdra Śambūka for practising austerities, an act forbidden to his class, and a Brahmin boy who had died is restored to life. Both stories have been retold, criticised and reinterpreted for centuries; in modern times they became central texts for anti-caste thinkers.

The tradition also preserves counter-currents. The Chāndogya Upaniṣad (4.4) tells of Satyakāma Jābāla, who does not know his father’s lineage and is accepted as a student by Hāridrumata Gautama because he tells the truth about it — though the teacher concludes that only a Brahmin could speak so honestly. The Aitareya Brāhmaṇa (2.19) tells of Kavaṣa Ailūṣa, the son of a slave woman, driven from a sacrifice but then recognised as a seer. The Mahābhārata gives important teaching roles to Vidura, born of a servant woman, and to the meat-seller of Mithilā who instructs a Brahmin in dharma. The Buddhist and Jain monastic orders admitted members of all castes (Chapter 11), and the Buddhist Vajrasūcī attacked the idea of birth-based superiority with arguments drawn from the Brahmanical texts themselves. The devotional poets of the second millennium — among them Nandanār, Cokhāmeḷā, Ravidās and Kabīr — were themselves from excluded or low-ranked communities and composed in the regional languages, outside the Sanskrit curriculum.

docs.title: 9.12.2 Women
docs.text:
The evidence on women’s education is mixed and changes over time. Several hymns of the Ṛgveda are attributed by the later index (Anukramaṇī) to women seers such as Ghoṣā, Apālā and Lopāmudrā. In the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad Gārgī Vācaknavī twice questions Yājñavalkya in a public debate (3.6, 3.8), and Maitreyī receives his teaching on the self (2.4, 4.5). In the Mahābhārata (12.308 in the critical edition) the female ascetic Sulabhā debates King Janaka and exposes his pretensions to liberation. The grammatical tradition, commenting on Pāṇini 4.1.49, distinguishes ācāryā, a woman who is herself a teacher, from ācāryāṇī, the wife of a teacher. A passage attributed to the lawgiver Hārīta and quoted in medieval digests distinguishes “women who speak of Brahman” (brahmavādinī), who were initiated and studied, from women who married directly.

But the normative texts from about the turn of the common era exclude women from initiation (Manu 2.67) and declare that rites for women are performed without Vedic mantras (Manu 9.18). Women’s access to Sanskrit learning thereafter depended on family circumstances, and was most often found among royal and courtly women, in families of scholars, and among nuns in the Buddhist and Jain orders. Feminist historians have analysed how the control of women’s education was bound up with the control of their sexuality and with the maintenance of caste boundaries (Chakravarti 2003).

docs.title: 9.12.3 Modern Critiques
docs.text: From the nineteenth century the exclusion of Śūdras, Dalits and women from education became a central issue of Indian social reform. Jotirao Phule (1827–1890) and Savitribai Phule (1831–1897) opened a school for girls in Pune in 1848 and later schools for children of the “untouchable” castes; Jotirao’s Gulāmgirī (1873) attacked Brahmin control of knowledge, and in 1882 he submitted a memorial to the Education Commission demanding universal primary education (O’Hanlon 1985). B. R. Ambedkar (1891–1956) analysed the Dharmaśāstra rules on Śūdras and argued that the denial of education had been one of the principal instruments of caste domination; his Annihilation of Caste (1936) remains the classic statement (Ambedkar 1936). These critiques are part of the history of Indian education and must be read alongside the texts that praise the teacher’s household.

docs.title: 9.13 The Legacy
docs.text:
The teacher’s household as an ideal has had a long afterlife. Traditional Vedic schools (pāṭhaśālās) continue to train students in recitation; Sanskrit śāstras are still taught by traditional teachers in some institutions. In the colonial period the ideal was revived in new forms: the Arya Samaj founded the Gurukul Kangri near Haridwar in 1902 as a residential school combining Vedic study with modern subjects; Rabindranath Tagore founded a school at Santiniketan in 1901, which grew into Visva-Bharati (1921), drawing on the image of the forest hermitage while rejecting its caste restrictions. The National Education Policy of 2020 invokes the tradition in general terms (Chapter 13).

What can fairly be claimed for the model is an emphasis on close, long-term relationships between teacher and student, on learning by heart and by example, and on education as the formation of character as well as the transmission of knowledge. What must also be acknowledged is that, as described in the normative texts, it was available to few, hierarchical in its relations, and bound up with an ideology of birth.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text:
• Scharfe (2002): the most thorough scholarly account of education in ancient India, Brahmanical and Buddhist.

  • Altekar (1965), Mookerji (1947) and Keay (1918): older surveys, rich in references but often uncritical.

  • Kane (1941): the standard compendium on upanayana, studentship and the rules of the Dharmaśāstra.

  • Olivelle (2005) and Olivelle (1993): Manu’s code and the history of the āśrama system.

  • Chakravarti (2003), Ambedkar (1936) and O’Hanlon (1985): gender, caste and the critique of Brahmanical education.

docs.title: Chapter 10: The Oral Tradition: Knowledge in the Living Voice
docs.text: yad eṣām anyo anyasya vācaṃ śāktasyeva vadati śikṣamāṇaḥ When one of them repeats the speech of another, as a learner repeats his teacher’s … — Ṛgveda 7.103.5 (the hymn to the frogs)

docs.title: 10.1 Introduction
docs.text:
The Vedic hymns were composed, collected and transmitted for many centuries without writing. The Ṛgveda, a collection of 1,028 hymns comprising some 10,500 verses whose core is dated c. 1500–1200 BCE, was handed down from teacher to student by word of mouth, together with the other Vedic collections, their ritual prose (the Brāhmaṇas) and their speculative appendices (the Āraṇyakas and Upaniṣads). Apart from the undeciphered Indus script of the third millennium BCE, which had long disappeared by the Vedic period, writing is first securely attested in India in the inscriptions of Aśoka in the third century BCE, and the Vedic texts seem to have been written down only much later; no surviving Vedic manuscript is older than the early second millennium CE, and most are far more recent. Yet the oral transmission was so precise that versions recited today in widely separated regions agree almost syllable for syllable, including the pitch accents that had long since disappeared from spoken Sanskrit.

This achievement rested on a specialised educational technique: the training of reciters through years of repetition, supported by elaborate “modifications” of the text and by a body of phonetic science. UNESCO proclaimed the tradition of Vedic chanting a Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity in 2003. This chapter describes how the system worked, what it achieved and what is claimed for it (Staal 1961; Staal 1986).

docs.title: 10.2 Why Oral?
docs.text:
Scholars have offered several explanations for the long preference for oral transmission of the Veda, which are compatible with each other.

  1. The power of exact sound. The Veda was śruti, “what is heard”. Its efficacy in ritual was believed to depend on exact pronunciation, including accent, and a written text could not guarantee this.

  2. Control of transmission. Oral teaching kept the Veda within the families and schools entitled to it. The prohibitions on Śūdras hearing or learning the Veda (Chapter 9) presuppose oral transmission, and the reluctance to write the Veda down was partly a reluctance to make it accessible.

  3. Prestige of memorised knowledge. A well-known saying holds that “knowledge that is in a book, and wealth that is in another’s hand” are useless when needed. Learning that existed only in a book was regarded as second-rate.

  4. Chronology. The Vedic corpus was largely composed before writing came into use; by the time writing was available, the oral system was well established and highly prestigious.

Writing, when it came, was used for many other purposes — administration, commerce, literature, the sciences — and the śāstric literature was transmitted both orally and in manuscripts (Chapter 12). But the most sacred texts remained, in principle, oral.

docs.title: 10.3 Branches of Transmission
docs.text:
Each Veda was transmitted in several “branches” (śākhā), recensions preserved by particular lineages of teachers and students, each with its own text, recitation style and ritual manuals. Patañjali’s Mahābhāṣya (2nd century BCE) gives the traditional numbers: twenty-one branches of the Ṛgveda, a hundred and one of the Yajurveda, a thousand “paths” of the Sāmaveda and nine of the Atharvaveda. Only a few survive (Table 10.1).

Table 10.1. Surviving branches (śākhā) of the Vedas. Veda Traditional number Surviving branches (text and/or recitation) Ṛgveda 21 Śākala (the extant saṃhitā); traces of others Yajurveda 101 White: Mādhyandina, Kāṇva. Black: Taittirīya, Maitrāyaṇī, Kaṭha (and fragments of Kapiṣṭhala) Sāmaveda 1,000 Kauthuma, Rāṇāyanīya, Jaiminīya Atharvaveda 9 Śaunaka, Paippalāda (the latter recited by a small community in Odisha)

The loss of most branches shows the vulnerability of oral transmission: when a lineage died out, its text disappeared with it. The survival of the others shows its robustness: where lineages continued, texts were preserved with extraordinary fidelity.

docs.title: 10.4.1 The Basic Texts
docs.text: A Vedic text was learned in several forms. The continuous text (saṃhitāpāṭha) presents the words as they are recited in ritual, joined by the rules of euphonic combination (sandhi), which can obscure word boundaries. The word-by-word text (padapāṭha) separates every word and gives it in its independent form, splitting compounds and noting suffixes; the padapāṭha of the Ṛgveda is attributed to Śākalya and is already an analysis of the text, making explicit its grammar. The step text (kramapāṭha) recites the words in overlapping pairs: 1–2, 2–3, 3–4, and so on.

docs.title: 10.4.2 The Eight Modifications
docs.text:
On these foundations the tradition built eight more complex “modifications” (vikṛti): jaṭā (“braid”), mālā (“garland”), śikhā (“crest”), rekhā (“line”), dhvaja (“flag”), daṇḍa (“staff”), ratha (“chariot”) and ghana (“dense”). Each permutes the words according to a fixed pattern. Two are commonly performed today. Table 10.2 shows how the basic forms and two of the modifications treat a sequence of four words.

Table 10.2. Recitation patterns for a sequence of four words A B C D. Pattern Recitation saṃhitā A B C D (with sandhi) pada A  |  B  |  C  |  D krama AB  |  BC  |  CD jaṭā AB BA AB  |  BC CB BC  |  CD DC CD ghana AB BA ABC CBA ABC  |  BC CB BCD DCB BCD  |  …

In the patterns that recite words backwards, sandhi must be applied anew to each reversed pair, and the accents must be adjusted according to strict rules. A reciter who can perform the ghana of a long text — a ghanapāṭhin — has therefore mastered not only the sequence of words but their grammatical form and accentuation. The permutations multiply the length of the text many times over.

docs.title: 10.4.3 How the System Checks Itself
docs.text: The patterns provide multiple, interlocking representations of the same text. An error in the continuous text would be exposed by the word-by-word text, and an error in the order of words by the step and braided patterns, since each word appears in several combinations with its neighbours. The redundancy is often explained by analogy with error-detecting codes (Section 1.10), but the system’s reliability depended as much on the discipline of teachers and the social organisation of the schools as on the patterns themselves.

docs.title: 10.5 Accent and Phonetics
docs.text:
Vedic Sanskrit had a pitch accent, which is marked in the saṃhitā and pada texts and preserved in recitation. The grammarians distinguish the raised (udātta), the not-raised (anudātta) and the “sounded” or falling (svarita) tones, the last typically following an udātta. In recitation the accents are often accompanied by movements of the head or hand, which differ from school to school; Sāmaveda singers use finger positions to mark the notes of the chants.

Every student was taught that accent could change meaning, and that an error could be dangerous. Patañjali, justifying the study of grammar at the opening of his Mahābhāṣya, quotes the verse that became the standard warning (the Pāṇinīya Śikṣā has a variant beginning mantro hīnaḥ):

Patañjali, Mahābhāṣya, introduction (Paspaśāhnika)

duṣṭaḥ śabdaḥ svarato varṇato vā mithyāprayukto na tam artham āha | sa vāgvajro yajamānaṃ hinasti yathendraśatruḥ svarato ’parādhāt || A word spoiled in accent or in sound and misused fails to say what is meant; it becomes a thunderbolt of speech that strikes the patron of the rite, like indraśatru with its misplaced accent.

The example, a compound whose meaning flips between “slayer of Indra” and “having Indra as slayer” with the position of the accent, comes from a Brāhmaṇa story retold in Volume 10, Śabda Vidyā. For the history of education its interest lies in the attitude it expresses: recitation was drilled not as an aesthetic accomplishment but under a sense of ritual danger, which helps explain the severity and length of the training described below.

To secure correct pronunciation, each Vedic school developed phonetic manuals. The prātiśākhyas state the rules by which the pada text is converted into the saṃhitā text for a particular branch, and the śikṣā texts describe the articulation of sounds by place and manner, the length of vowels and the qualities of good and bad recitation. This phonetic science, which classifies sounds by their point of articulation and the effort involved, is among the most precise in the ancient world and laid the foundation for Pāṇini’s grammar (Scharfe 2002). Its achievements are discussed further in Volume 10 of this series.

docs.title: 10.6 Chant: The Sāmaveda
docs.text: The Sāmaveda poses special problems of transmission, because its texts are melodies (sāman) sung to verses drawn mostly from the Ṛgveda. In singing, the words of the verse are transformed: syllables are lengthened, repeated and replaced by meaningless “stobha” syllables, and the melody is divided into sections sung by different priests. The songs are collected in “song-books” (gāna), and their notes were indicated in later manuscripts by numerals or syllables written above the text, and in performance by finger and hand positions. The three surviving branches — Kauthuma, Rāṇāyanīya and Jaiminīya — differ in their melodies and their styles of singing; the Jaiminīya tradition survives mainly among the Nambūdiris of Kerala and in parts of Tamil Nadu. Recordings and studies of these traditions since the mid-twentieth century have shown how much regional variation exists within a framework of strict fidelity to the inherited melodies.

docs.title: 10.7 A Rediscovered Branch
docs.text: The fate of the Paippalāda branch of the Atharvaveda illustrates both the fragility and the persistence of the oral tradition. For a long time the Paippalāda text was known in the West only from a single, damaged birch-bark manuscript from Kashmir, discovered in the nineteenth century. In the 1950s the Bengali scholar Durgamohan Bhattacharyya found that Brahmin families in Odisha still possessed palm-leaf manuscripts of the Paippalāda saṃhitā and preserved a tradition of reciting it. The Odisha manuscripts have since become the basis of new critical editions. The episode shows that branches of Vedic learning considered lost may survive in small communities, and that the oral and manuscript traditions supported each other.

docs.title: 10.8 How Students Learned
docs.text:
The texts and modern observation of traditional schools allow a fairly clear picture of the method.

  • The teacher recites a short segment — often half a verse — and the student repeats it, usually several times, until it is exact. The Ṛgvedic “frog hymn” (7.103) already compares the croaking of frogs to students repeating the words of their teacher.

  • New material is added daily while earlier material is repeated, so that the whole is revised at regular intervals.

  • The padapāṭha and kramapāṭha are learned after the saṃhitā, and the advanced modifications only by specialists.

  • Recitation is accompanied by hand and head movements marking the accents, which serve as a physical aid to memory.

  • Students recite together and correct one another, and large recitations in assemblies provide public checks.

  • Learning begins young, often at seven or eight, and continues for many years; full mastery of a Veda with its modifications may take a decade or more.

Psychologists who have looked at these methods note that they combine several techniques known to support retention: distributed practice over long periods, active recall, multiple overlapping encodings of the same material, rhythmic and melodic structure, and the use of movement. These observations help explain why the method works; its purpose, however — verbatim preservation of sound, often without attention to meaning — is not the purpose of most modern education (Section 13.17).

docs.title: 10.8.1 The Rhythm of the Year
docs.text: Vedic study was regulated by a calendar. It began each year with a ceremony of opening (upākaraṇa), usually in the rainy season, and was formally closed some months later (utsarjana). The Dharmasūtras list a great many occasions on which recitation must be suspended (anadhyāya): on certain lunar days, during storms, thunder and earthquakes, at the death of certain persons, in the presence of particular sounds or people, in a village where there is a corpse, and so on. Some of these rules served practical purposes — recitation in a thunderstorm would be inaudible — while others expressed ideas of ritual purity. Together they show that Vedic learning was embedded in ritual time, not organised as a continuous “course”.

docs.title: 10.8.2 Meaning and Sound
docs.text: A striking feature of the Vedic schools is that the preservation of sound was often separated from the understanding of meaning. Many reciters, past and present, learned the texts without studying their sense, which was the business of exegetes and ritualists. The Nirukta of Yāska (mid-first millennium BCE) complains of those who learn the Veda without understanding it, comparing such a person to a pillar or a bearer of burdens. The tradition thus contained an internal critique of rote learning even while it depended on it.

docs.title: 10.9 Feats of Memory: Avadhāna
docs.text: The culture of trained memory found other expressions beyond the Veda. In the literary tradition of the Telugu and Kannada regions, and in Sanskrit, a performance called avadhāna (“attention”) tests a poet’s memory and concentration in public. In the “eightfold” form (aṣṭāvadhāna) the performer deals simultaneously with eight questioners: composing verses on set themes and in set metres, under constraints such as the exclusion of certain letters; completing a verse of which one line is given; conversing on unrelated subjects; keeping count of bells rung at random intervals; and finally reciting all the compositions in order. Larger forms with a hundred (śatāvadhāna) or more participants are recorded; in the Jain tradition, Śrīmad Rājacandra (1867–1901), the spiritual guide of the young Gandhi, was famous in his youth for such performances. Avadhāna is a living art and a striking demonstration of the capacities that long training in memory and verse composition can develop.

docs.title: 10.10 Memorising the Śāstras
docs.text:
Memorisation was not confined to the Veda. The root texts of the śāstras — Pāṇini’s nearly four thousand grammatical rules, the Amarakośa (the standard Sanskrit thesaurus, in verse), the sūtras of the philosophical schools, the verse summaries of medicine and astronomy — were composed in forms designed to be memorised, and students learned them by heart before studying their meaning. The extreme concision of the sūtra style, in which a grammarian was said to rejoice over saving half a short vowel as much as over the birth of a son, made texts easy to memorise but impossible to understand without a teacher’s explanation; memory and commentary were thus two halves of a single method. Versification served the same purpose in the sciences: mathematical rules, medical prescriptions and astronomical procedures were cast in metrical form so that they could be carried in the mind and recalled when needed.

Scholarly Note: “Vedic Mathematics”

A set of rapid calculation techniques published in 1965 under the title Vedic Mathematics, by Bhāratī Kṛṣṇa Tīrtha, Śaṅkarācārya of Puri, is widely taught in Indian schools and coaching classes as an ancient system. The sixteen “sūtras” on which it is based do not occur in any Vedic text or Vedic appendix; the author stated that he had reconstructed them, and the methods are modern arithmetical shortcuts. They may be useful for mental arithmetic, but they have no historical connection with the Veda, and they should not be presented as part of India’s mathematical heritage. The genuine history of Indian mathematics is treated in Volume 11 of this series.

docs.title: 10.11 Ritual Performance
docs.text: Vedic recitation was originally inseparable from ritual. In the great solemn (śrauta) sacrifices, priests of the four Vedas each recited or sang their own texts in a fixed sequence, and the correctness of the ritual depended on the correctness of the recitation. Some of these rituals survive in a few families. In 1975 a twelve-day performance of the Agnicayana, the ritual of building the fire altar, by Nambūdiri priests at Panjal in Kerala was documented on film and in a two-volume study by Frits Staal and his collaborators (Staal 1983), preserving a detailed record of a ritual tradition of great antiquity. Such documentation is one way in which a tradition that was designed to be transmitted only from person to person is now also preserved in other media.

docs.title: 10.12 Research on Vedic Reciters
docs.text: A neuroimaging study published in 2016 compared the brains of a group of professional Vedic pandits, trained from childhood in intensive memorisation and recitation, with those of matched controls (Hartzell et al. 2016). The authors reported differences in grey-matter density and cortical thickness in several regions, including areas associated with language, memory (among them parts of the hippocampus) and vision. The study is of genuine interest as evidence that long training in a specialised skill is associated with differences in brain structure, as has been found for musicians, taxi drivers and other experts. Its limitations should also be noted: it was cross-sectional and relatively small, so it cannot show that recitation training caused the differences, and its findings concern a highly selected group. It does not show that Vedic recitation improves general intelligence or that it should be adopted as an educational method.

docs.title: 10.13 Other Oral Traditions
docs.text:
The Vedic schools were not the only oral traditions of India.

  • Buddhist recitation. According to tradition, the Buddha’s teachings were recited and fixed at a council soon after his death, and the canon was transmitted orally by specialised reciters (bhāṇaka) for several centuries; the Sri Lankan chronicles say the Pali canon was written down in the first century BCE. Communal recitation remained central to monastic life.

  • The Pali word for these councils, saṅgīti, means literally “chanting together”: a council was an assembly at which the community recited the teachings in unison, establishing an agreed text by collective performance. The Theravāda chronicles describe three or four such councils before the canon was committed to writing, and modern Buddhist countries have held further councils on the same model, the most recent in Burma in 1954–56.

  • Jain transmission. The Jain scriptures were likewise transmitted orally, with periodic councils to reconcile versions, until the council at Valabhī (fifth century CE) had them written down (Chapter 11).

  • Epic and Purāṇic narration. The epics and Purāṇas present themselves as narrated by bards (sūta) and storytellers. Unlike the Vedic texts, they were transmitted with much variation; the critical edition of the Mahābhārata prepared at Pune shows how freely the text grew in different regions. Public recitation and exposition (kathā, pravacana) of the epics and Purāṇas, and musical narration such as Harikathā, remain living traditions.

  • Regional and folk traditions. Oral epics in the regional languages — the Rajasthani epic of Pābūjī, the Ālhā of north India, the epics of the Tamil and Telugu countries — are performed by hereditary bards, often with painted scrolls or cloths, and vary with each performance. Tribal communities transmit genealogies, myths and knowledge of the environment orally (Volume 23).

  • Music. Classical music was taught orally from teacher to student within lineages (gharānā, paramparā) until the twentieth century and is still largely so taught (Volume 9).

Comparison with oral traditions elsewhere is illuminating. In the 1930s Milman Parry and Albert Lord studied the oral epic singers of Yugoslavia and showed that they composed their long poems anew in each performance, using a stock of traditional formulas and themes; they argued that the Homeric epics had been composed in the same way (Parry 1971; Lord 1960). The Indian epics and Purāṇas, and many regional oral epics, show features of this kind of composition-in-performance. The Vedic tradition is quite different: it aimed at, and achieved, verbatim reproduction of a fixed text, with techniques designed to eliminate variation. The contrast shows that “oral tradition” covers very different practices, and that the Vedic achievement is unusual among the world’s oral literatures.

Women’s oral traditions deserve special mention, because they are rarely represented in the textual record. Across India women have composed and transmitted songs for work, ritual and the life cycle — songs for grinding grain, for weddings, for the birth of children, for laments — in which they express their experiences, griefs and judgements of family and society. In Maharashtra, for example, the “grinding songs” (ovī) sung by women at the hand-mill have been collected in their tens of thousands by researchers since the 1980s, revealing a large body of women’s poetry about work, kinship, devotion and suffering. Such songs are part of the history of Indian knowledge and education: they are the means by which much of what women knew was taught to the next generation.

These traditions differ from the Vedic one in a fundamental way: they valued faithful transmission of a story, a style or a repertoire, not verbatim fixity of every syllable. Together they show that Indian oral culture was not one system but many.

docs.title: 10.14 The Living Tradition
docs.text:
Vedic recitation continues in traditional schools in many parts of India — among the Nambūdiri Brahmins of Kerala, whose Ṛgvedic and Sāmavedic traditions were documented by Frits Staal (1961); in Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh and Maharashtra; in Vārāṇasī; and elsewhere. Some branches survive in only a handful of families. Government and private bodies, including the Maharshi Sandipani Rashtriya Veda Vidya Pratishthan at Ujjain, support Vedic schools, and recordings have been made of many branches. Changes in the economy and in family occupations have reduced the number of full-time reciters, and the long-term survival of several branches is uncertain.

The social basis of the tradition has also begun to change. Vedic recitation was for most of its history restricted to males of particular Brahmin families. In the twentieth century reform movements such as the Arya Samaj taught the Veda to women and to members of other castes, and today a number of institutions train women in Vedic recitation and as ritual officiants, though this remains contested in some traditional circles. The Veda itself, once guarded from those not entitled to hear it, has been printed — the first complete edition of the Ṛgveda with Sāyaṇa’s commentary was published by Friedrich Max Müller in 1849–1874 — and is now freely available in print, in recordings and online.

The oral tradition is an achievement that historians of every persuasion admire. Admiration need not mean uncritical celebration: the same system that preserved the Veda so faithfully also kept it within a narrow circle, and its methods were designed to preserve sound rather than to cultivate understanding. Both facts are part of its history.
